[4] Answer: desert animals are active at night because they avoid the daytime heat and save the water in their bodies.

qadamlar.doska: Cactus too: spiny leaves → loses little water
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Plants are adapted in the same way: a desert cactus saves water with its spiny leaves.

qadamlar.doska: What protects a walrus from the cold?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] What protects a walrus from the cold in icy water? Write one or two words.
qadamlar.javob: fat|layer of fat|thick fat|its fat|thick layer of fat|blubber

qadamlar.doska: What happens to the pupil in a dark room?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] You walked from a bright place into a dark room. Does the pupil of your eye get bigger or smaller? Write one word.

qadamlar.sarlavha: How to solve an international question
qadamlar.doska:
1) Identify the environment: cold, hot, water?
2) Find the problem: cold, lack of water, predators
3) How does the feature solve that problem?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] First, identify what kind of environment the animal lives in: cold, hot, desert, or water. [2] Then think: What difficulty is there in this environment? Is it cold, is there little water, are there predators? [3] Finally, connect the feature to the problem. Use the word “because” in your answer.

qadamlar.doska:
Adaptation — a feature for survival
In the body: fat, fur, spines, webbed feet
In behavior: active at night, migrating, warming eggs
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Remember: an adaptation helps an organism survive in its environment. [2] It can be in the body: fat, fur, spines, webbed feet. [3] Or in behavior: being active at night, migrating to warm regions, warming eggs. Great work!

q1.doska: Adaptation = a feature that suits the environment
q1.ovoz: Every animal has a “tool” that suits the place where it lives. That is an adaptation.

q1.doska: In winter you dress warmly too
q1.ovoz: In winter you wear a thick jacket, and in summer a light shirt. Animals are also adapted to the cold with thick fur or fat.

q1.doska: Environment → problem → solution (feature)
q1.ovoz: Three steps: what the environment is like, what problem there is, and which feature of the animal solves it.

q2.doska:
Cold → fat, fur
Hot → coming out at night, saving water
q2.ovoz: In the cold, fat and fur keep an animal warm. In the hot desert, animals come out at night and save water.

q2.doska: Kyzylkum: quiet by day, alive at night
q2.ovoz: In the Kyzylkum Desert, everything is quiet during the day, and the animals are in their burrows. At night, snakes, mice, and hedgehogs come out looking for food.

q2.doska: Experiment: a fat-filled glove in icy water
q2.ovoz: If you put a glove filled with fat on one hand and dip it into icy water, that hand gets less cold. A walrus's fat works the same way.

q3.doska: Spines — protection, webbing — swimming, talons — grabbing
q3.ovoz: Spines give protection, webbed feet help with swimming, and sharp talons help with catching prey.

q3.doska: The fox could not bite the hedgehog
q3.ovoz: A hungry fox saw a hedgehog. The hedgehog curled up into a spiny ball. The fox pricked its nose and went away.

q3.doska: Foot = tool: oar, hook
q3.ovoz: Imagine a bird's foot as a tool: a duck's foot is an oar, and an eagle's foot is a hook.

q4.doska: Little food in winter → birds fly away
q4.ovoz: In winter there is not enough food for birds, so they fly to warm places.

q4.doska: Storks fly south in the fall and return in spring
q4.ovoz: In the fall, storks fly away to warm lands in the south, and in spring they return to their nests.

q4.doska: Mirror experiment: turn the light off and on
q4.ovoz: Look in a mirror, turn off the light, then turn it on. You will see your pupils get smaller in the light.

tipik_xatolar: Thinking birds fly away only because it is cold; the main reason is that food becomes scarce
Thinking desert animals come out at night “because they can't sleep”
Mistakenly thinking the pupil gets smaller in the dark
Thinking a bird sits on its eggs only to guard them; the main purpose is to keep them warm
Thinking an animal changes its adaptations because it wants to
strategiyalar: Build the chain: environment → problem → feature
Give the reason in your answer using the word “because”
If several options seem correct, choose the one that best fits the environment in the question

maqsad: Build and read food chains; understand predator–prey relationships, where plants get their energy, and human impact

qadamlar.doska:
Grass → rabbit → fox: who eats whom?
TIMSS: 56% of fourth graders answered correctly
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Grass grows in a field, a rabbit eats the grass, and a fox hunts the rabbit. How do we read this chain? [2] In the international TIMSS study, on average 56 percent of fourth-grade students around the world answered questions on this topic correctly. Questions about animals dying out were the hardest. Today you will learn to answer these questions with ease!

qadamlar.doska:
Sun → plant: makes food
The plant uses energy to grow and live
Animals get food by eating other living things
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Green plants make their own food with the help of sunlight. That is why they are called producers. [2] A plant uses this energy to grow, put out new leaves, flower, and make seeds. [3] Animals cannot make their own food; they get energy by eating plants or other animals.

qadamlar.doska:
Grass → grasshopper → frog → snake
Arrow points from “eaten” → “eater”
Herbivore — eats plants; predator — hunts animals
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] A food chain shows who eats whom. A chain always starts with a plant. [2] The arrow points from the one that is eaten to the one that eats it. In other words, it shows where the energy goes. [3] An animal that eats plants is a herbivore, and one that hunts and eats other animals is a predator. An animal that is hunted is called prey.

qadamlar.doska:
If one link changes, the others change too
Fewer foxes → more rabbits → less grass
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] The animals in a chain depend on each other. If the number of one changes, the numbers of the others change too. [2] For example, if there are fewer foxes, fewer animals hunt the rabbits, and the rabbits multiply. And many rabbits eat a lot of grass.

qadamlar.doska:
Causes of extinction: habitat loss, hunting
Pollution also does harm
Protection: nature reserves, bicycles, buses
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] The main reasons animals die out are habitat loss when forests are cut down, and too much hunting. [2] Air and water pollution also harm plants and animals. [3] We can protect nature: creating nature reserves and using a bicycle or bus instead of a car pollute the air less.

qadamlar.doska:
Chain: leaf → caterpillar → sparrow → hawk
The caterpillar eats the leaf → herbivore
The sparrow and hawk eat animals → predators
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Example one. We made a chain from a leaf, a caterpillar, a sparrow, and a hawk. Find the predators here. [2] The caterpillar eats the leaf, so it is a herbivore. [3] The sparrow hunts the caterpillar, and the hawk hunts the sparrow. So both are predators, and the hawk is at the end of the chain.

qadamlar.doska: Leaf — producer, the start of the chain
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] The leaf at the start of the chain makes food from sunlight; it is a producer. The energy of all the animals starts with it.

qadamlar.doska:
Grass → rabbit → fox. All the foxes were hunted
Step 1: nobody hunts the rabbits → they multiply
Step 2: many rabbits → less grass
Step 3: not enough grass → rabbits decrease too
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Example two, a reasoning question. In one area, people hunted all the foxes. What happens next? [2] Step one: now nobody hunts the rabbits, so their number goes up. [3] Step two: many rabbits eat a lot of grass, and the grass runs low. [4] Step three: when there is not enough food, the rabbits go hungry, and later their number goes down too. See, everything is connected!

qadamlar.doska: Conclusion: if one species disappears, the balance is upset
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] You see, the loss of one species changed the whole chain. That is why we must protect the balance of nature.

qadamlar.doska: Grass → grasshopper → frog → snake. Who eats the grasshopper?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Look at this chain. Who eats the grasshopper? Write one word.

qadamlar.doska: If the frogs disappear, what happens to the number of grasshoppers?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] If the frogs disappear from this chain, what happens to the number of grasshoppers: does it go up or down?

qadamlar.sarlavha: How to solve an international question
qadamlar.doska:
1) Write the chain starting with the plant
2) Check the direction of the arrows
3) Follow the change step by step
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] In a food chain question, first write the chain with arrows, starting with the plant. [2] Check that each arrow points from the one that is eaten to the one that eats it. A backward arrow is a common trap. [3] If an animal disappears, think step by step about what happens first to its prey, and then to the animal that eats it.

qadamlar.doska:
Energy: Sun → plants → animals
Arrow from the eaten to the eater
If one link changes, the whole chain changes
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Remember: energy passes from the Sun to plants, and from plants to animals. [2] The arrow points from the one that is eaten to the one that eats it. [3] Every living organism in the chain is important, and we must protect them. Well done!

q1.doska: Plants — from the Sun, animals — from food
q1.ovoz: A plant gets its energy from the Sun, while an animal gets it by eating food.

q1.doska: The flower on the windowsill grew toward the sun
q1.ovoz: The flower by your window stretched toward the sun. It made food with the help of light and put out new leaves.

q1.doska:
The Sun = the cook's fire
The leaf = the kitchen
q1.ovoz: The leaf is a kitchen, and sunlight is the fire. In this kitchen, the plant cooks its own food.

q2.doska: The arrow means “passes to,” not “eats”
q2.ovoz: The arrow from the grass points to the rabbit: the grass's energy passes to the rabbit.

q2.doska: In the garden: leaf → aphid → ladybug
q2.ovoz: An aphid sucks the sap of a rose leaf in your garden, and a ladybug eats the aphid. This is a food chain in the garden.

q2.doska: Make a chain out of paper rings
q2.ovoz: Write the name of one living organism on each ring. If you break one ring, the chain falls apart.

q3.doska: Fewer hunters → more prey
q3.ovoz: If there are fewer hunting animals, the prey multiplies.

q3.doska: The cat left — the mice multiplied
q3.ovoz: In one house, the cat went away to another place. A month later, the mice in the storeroom had multiplied and eaten the grain.

q3.doska: Dominoes: if one falls, the next one falls
q3.ovoz: A food chain is like dominoes: if one tile falls, the ones after it are affected too.

q4.doska: If its home is destroyed, an animal disappears
q4.ovoz: If an animal's home — a forest or a tugai thicket — is destroyed, it cannot survive.

q4.doska: The Turan tiger disappeared after the tugai forests were cut down
q4.ovoz: Long ago, the Turan tiger lived in the tugai forests along the Amu Darya. Because the forests were cut down and the tigers were hunted, it died out.

q4.doska: Compare: 1 bus or 40 cars
q4.ovoz: If forty people travel in forty cars, the air gets very polluted. If they go in one bus, it is much less.

tipik_xatolar: Reading the arrow in the wrong direction (fox → rabbit)
Thinking plants get their energy from the soil; in fact, it comes from sunlight
Thinking that if predators decrease, prey decreases too
Blaming the loss of animals only on natural causes and forgetting human impact
Starting the chain with an animal
strategiyalar: Always write the chain starting with a plant
Follow the change step by step: what happens to the prey, then to the predator
Check the direction of the arrows in the options

maqsad: Understand healthy eating (calcium and other nutrients), how infectious diseases spread and how to prevent them, body temperature, and physical activity

qadamlar.doska:
Why is drinking milk good for your bones?
TIMSS: 41% of fourth graders answered correctly
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Your mother says, “Drink your milk, and your bones will be strong.” Is that true? Today we will find out. [2] In the international TIMSS study, on average 41 percent of fourth-grade students around the world answered questions on this topic correctly. This topic is considered quite difficult, especially the question about calcium. Today you will learn to answer these questions with ease!

qadamlar.doska:
Calcium — makes bones and teeth strong
Sources of calcium: milk, yogurt, cheese, cottage cheese
Protein — growth; fruits, vegetables — vitamins
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Calcium makes our bones and teeth strong. A growing child needs especially a lot of it. [2] Milk and milk products have the most calcium: yogurt, cheese, cottage cheese. [3] Meat, eggs, and beans are rich in protein, which helps the body grow. Fruits and vegetables contain vitamins.

qadamlar.doska:
The flu — caused by a virus
Spread: coughing, sneezing, dirty hands
Protection: washing hands with soap, covering your mouth
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] The flu is an infectious disease. It is caused by a virus, which is so tiny it cannot be seen. [2] When a sick person coughs or sneezes, the virus spreads through the air. It also spreads through dirty hands and shared dishes. [3] To protect ourselves, we wash our hands with soap, and when we sneeze, we cover our mouth and nose with a tissue or our elbow.

qadamlar.doska:
Healthy body temperature — about 36.6 °C
When running: the body warms up, the heart beats fast
When we rest, it slowly returns to normal
High temperature for a long time — a sign of illness
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] A healthy person's body temperature is about thirty-six point six degrees. We measure it with a thermometer. [2] When we run or play, our muscles work, the body warms up, the heart beats faster, and breathing speeds up. [3] When we rest, our temperature, heartbeat, and breathing slowly return to how they were before. [4] If a person's temperature rises well above 37 degrees even while sitting quietly, this is a fever — a sign of illness.

qadamlar.doska:
Which is richest in calcium: an apple, bread, or cheese?
Calcium — in milk products
Answer: cheese (it is made from milk)
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Example one. An apple, bread, and cheese — which is richest in calcium? [2] Let's remember: there is the most calcium in milk products. [3] Cheese is made from milk, so the answer is cheese.

qadamlar.doska: Also rich in calcium: yogurt, cottage cheese, sesame
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Yogurt, cottage cheese, and sesame seeds also have a lot of calcium. Drinking a glass of milk or yogurt every day is good for you.

qadamlar.doska:
Ali ran for 10 minutes: 36.6 °C → 37.2 °C
Reason: his working muscles gave off heat
Not sick: when he rests, his temperature drops
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Example two, a reasoning question. Ali ran for ten minutes, and his temperature rose from thirty-six point six to thirty-seven point two degrees. Why? [2] When we run, our muscles work hard and give off heat. That is why the body warms up a little. [3] This is not an illness. When Ali rests, he sweats, and his temperature returns to normal.

qadamlar.doska: If it is 38 °C while sitting quietly — a fever
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] But if Ali had been sitting quietly and his temperature was thirty-eight degrees, that would be a fever. Then he should see a doctor.

qadamlar.doska:
What protects against the flu: sweets or washing hands?
The virus also spreads through hands → hand washing
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Example three. Which helps protect against the flu: eating sweets or washing your hands with soap? [2] The virus gets into the mouth and nose from dirty hands. Soap washes the virus away. So the answer is washing your hands with soap.

qadamlar.doska: Which nutrient makes bones and teeth strong?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Write the name of the nutrient that makes bones and teeth strong. One word.

qadamlar.doska: When you run, does your heartbeat speed up or slow down?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] What happens to your heartbeat when you run: does it speed up or slow down? Write one word.

qadamlar.sarlavha: How to solve an international question
qadamlar.doska:
1) How does the disease spread? Find the way
2) Protection must block that way
3) If asked “Why?” — give the reason
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] If a question is about a disease, first figure out how it spreads: through the air, hands, or food. [2] The correct answer blocks that way: for example, washing hands or covering the mouth. [3] In an open question, do not just write “for health.” Write the exact reason: “calcium makes bones strong.”

qadamlar.doska:
Calcium: bones and teeth; milk products
Flu: virus; wash hands, cover your mouth
The body warms up after exercise — this is normal
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Remember: calcium is needed for bones and teeth, and milk products have a lot of it. [2] The flu is spread by a virus. Wash your hands and cover your mouth when you sneeze. [3] The body warms up after exercise, and it passes when we rest. Stay healthy!

q1.doska: Milk → calcium → strong bones
q1.ovoz: If you drink milk, you get calcium, and your bones become strong.

q1.doska: Sardor drank yogurt and grew fast
q1.ovoz: Sardor eats yogurt and cheese every day. Even when he falls while playing soccer, his bones are strong.

q1.doska:
Food → job table:
milk — bones, meat — growth, fruit — vitamins
q1.ovoz: Make a small table: milk is for bones, meat is for growth, and fruit is for vitamins.

q2.doska: Sneeze → virus → another person
q2.ovoz: If a sick person sneezes, the virus passes through the air to another person.

q2.doska: A child in class sneezed...
q2.ovoz: A child in class sneezed without covering his mouth. The next day, the two children sitting next to him got sick too. If he had covered his mouth, this would not have happened.

q2.doska: Experiment: sprinkle flour on your hand and touch the door
q2.ovoz: Sprinkle a little flour on your hand and touch the door handle. Viruses stay behind in the same way as the flour does.

q3.doska: We ran → warmed up → rested → normal
q3.ovoz: When we run, we warm up; when we rest, we go back to normal.

q3.doska: Your face turns red after soccer
q3.ovoz: After playing soccer, your face turns red and you sweat. This is your body getting rid of extra heat.

q3.doska: Count your heartbeat: at rest and after jumping
q3.ovoz: Stand quietly for one minute and count your heartbeats, then jump twenty times and count again. The second number will be higher.

tipik_xatolar: Choosing fruit or sweets as a source of calcium
Thinking the flu comes from the cold by itself; it is caused by a virus
Thinking a rise in temperature after exercise is an illness
Writing “good for your health” instead of an exact reason
Forgetting that washing hands, not just eating well, also protects you
strategiyalar: Find how the disease spreads and choose the answer that blocks it
In an open question, write the exact cause and result
Look at the situation: is the person resting or have they been active?

maqsad: Understand the solid, liquid, and gas states of matter, changes of state, solutions and mixtures, and the properties of materials

qadamlar.doska:
Ice, water, and steam — one substance!
TIMSS: 46% of fourth graders answered correctly
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] The ice in the freezer, the water in a glass, and the steam from a teapot are all one substance: water. How can that be? [2] In the international TIMSS study, on average 46 percent of fourth-grade students around the world answered questions on this topic correctly. Questions about identifying a gas and about condensation were the hardest. Today you will learn to answer these questions with ease!

qadamlar.doska:
Solid: shape and volume do not change
Liquid: has a volume, takes the shape of its container
Gas: fills the whole container
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] A solid — for example, ice or a stone — keeps its own shape and volume. [2] A liquid — for example, water or milk — flows and takes the shape of whatever container we pour it into, but its volume does not change. [3] A gas has neither its own shape nor its own volume; it fills the whole container. Air and water vapor are gases. Often they cannot be seen.

qadamlar.doska:
Heating: ice → water (melting) → vapor (evaporation)
Cooling: vapor → water (condensation) → ice
Water freezes at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C
Drops on a cold window — condensation
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] If we heat ice, it melts and turns into water. If we heat the water further, it evaporates and turns into a gas. [2] If we cool water vapor, it turns into drops of water — this is condensation. If we cool water, it freezes. [3] Pure water freezes at zero degrees and boils at one hundred degrees. [4] The drops that appear on the outside of a cold glass form from water vapor in the air. This is condensation too.

qadamlar.doska:
Salt dissolves in water — you can't see it, but it is there
Fine salt, hot water, stirring — faster
Mixture: sand + water, rice + beans
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] If we put salt in water and stir, it dissolves and can no longer be seen. But the salt does not disappear: the water tastes salty. [2] Fine salt dissolves faster than coarse salt. Hot water and stirring also make it dissolve faster. [3] In a mixture, several substances are together, and they can be separated. For example, we separate sandy water by filtering it.

qadamlar.doska:
Same size — different weight
Ice floats in water: most of it is underwater
A magnet attracts iron; wood and paper burn
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] If we take a brick, an apple, and a piece of foam of the same size, the brick is the heaviest and the foam is the lightest. [2] Ice is lighter than water, so it floats. But most of it is underwater, and only a small part sticks out on top. [3] A magnet attracts iron objects but does not attract aluminum or copper. Paper and wood burn; stone and glass do not.

qadamlar.doska:
Ice, water, steam — order by temperature
Ice ≤ 0 °C, water — from 0 to 100 °C
Steam ≈ 100 °C → ice < water < steam
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Example one. Ice, water, and the steam from boiling water — which is the hottest, and which is the coldest? [2] Ice is at zero degrees or colder. Liquid water is between zero and one hundred degrees. [3] The steam from boiling water is about one hundred degrees. So the coldest is ice, and the hottest is steam.

qadamlar.doska: Heating: ice → water → steam (temperature rises)
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] That is why, when we heat ice, it turns first into water and then into steam. At each stage we add heat.

qadamlar.doska:
Water in the glass: 200 g, salt: 20 g
The salt dissolved and could no longer be seen
The salt did not disappear — it spread through the water
$200 + 20 = 220$ g
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Example two, a reasoning question. Laylo weighed the water in a glass on a scale — two hundred grams — and the salt separately — twenty grams. [2] Then she put the salt in the water and dissolved it. The salt could no longer be seen. If we weigh it now, what will the scale show? [3] The salt did not disappear; it broke up into tiny particles and spread through the water. That is why the water is salty. [4] So the mass of the solution is two hundred twenty grams. Mass does not change when something dissolves.

qadamlar.doska: If we evaporate the water, the salt stays at the bottom
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Here is more proof that the salt did not disappear: if we heat the solution and evaporate the water, white salt is left at the bottom of the container.

qadamlar.doska: What state is the steam that forms when water boils?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] When water boils, what state is the water vapor that forms: solid, liquid, or gas? Remember, the white cloud above a teapot is made of tiny droplets that formed from the vapor.

qadamlar.doska: 10 g of sugar was dissolved in 100 g of water. Mass = ? g
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] We put ten grams of sugar into one hundred grams of water and dissolved it. What is the mass of the solution in grams? Write only the number.

qadamlar.sarlavha: How to solve an international question
qadamlar.doska:
1) Identify the state: solid, liquid, gas?
2) Was it heated or cooled?
3) “Can't be seen” ≠ “disappeared”
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] First, figure out what state the substance is in. Even if you can't see it, it may be a gas. [2] For a change of state, ask: was it heated or cooled? Heating causes melting and evaporation; cooling causes freezing and condensation. [3] A dissolved substance does not disappear. In a question about mass, add everything together.

qadamlar.doska:
Solid, liquid, gas — three states
Heating: melting, evaporation; cooling: freezing, condensation
Mass is conserved when something dissolves
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Remember: matter can be solid, liquid, or gas. [2] Heating causes melting and evaporation; cooling causes freezing and condensation. [3] When something dissolves, it does not disappear, and its mass is conserved. You're great!

q1.doska:
Solid — stays, liquid — flows
Gas — spreads out
q1.ovoz: A solid stays in place, a liquid flows, and a gas spreads out everywhere.

q1.doska: Blowing up a balloon: air fills the balloon
q1.ovoz: When you blow up a balloon, the air fills it completely and takes the shape of the balloon. You can't see air, but it is there — it is a gas.

q1.doska:
Classmates: solid — standing in rows
liquid — walking, gas — running
q1.ovoz: Compare particles to students: in a solid they stand firmly in place, in a liquid they slide past one another, and in a gas they run all around the hall.

q2.doska:
Heat → melting, evaporation
Cold → freezing, condensation
q2.ovoz: If we add heat, a substance melts or evaporates; if we cool it, it freezes or turns into drops.

q2.doska: The ice cream melted in the sun
q2.ovoz: In summer you left your ice cream in the sun, and it melted. If you put it in the freezer, it will harden again.

q2.doska: Mirror experiment: the bathroom mirror fogs up
q2.ovoz: After a hot shower, the mirror fogs up: water vapor in the air touches the cold mirror and turns into drops. That is condensation.

q3.doska: Dissolved = can't be seen, but still there
q3.ovoz: Even when sugar dissolves in tea, the tea tastes sweet. So the sugar is still there.

q3.doska: Grandma dissolves salt in hot water
q3.ovoz: To dissolve salt quickly, your grandmother uses hot water and stirs it with a spoon.

q3.doska: Experiment: 2 glasses — fine and coarse salt
q3.ovoz: Pour the same amount of water into two glasses. Put fine salt in one and coarse salt in the other. The fine salt dissolves faster.

q4.doska: Ice floats in water, a magnet attracts iron
q4.ovoz: Ice floats in water, and a magnet attracts only metals like iron.

q4.doska: A layer of ice on a pond in winter
q4.ovoz: In winter the surface of a pond freezes. The ice stays on top, and underneath there is still water where fish live.

q4.doska: In two hands: a brick and foam
q4.ovoz: Hold a brick in one hand and a piece of foam of exactly the same size in the other. They are the same size, but their weights are very different.

tipik_xatolar: Thinking “there is nothing there” because a gas cannot be seen
Thinking the white cloud from a teapot is a gas; in fact, it is tiny water droplets
Mixing up condensation and evaporation
Thinking dissolved salt disappears and the mass goes down
Drawing ice lying entirely on the surface of water; in fact, most of it is underwater
strategiyalar: First identify the state, then whether there was heating or cooling
In mass questions, add up all the parts
Remember that if the size is the same, the weight depends on the material

maqsad: Understand light sources, reflection and shadows, heat transfer and conductors, electric circuits, and how magnets interact

qadamlar.doska:
Why does a light bulb light up, and why do shadows form?
TIMSS: 54% of fourth graders answered correctly
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] In the evening you turn on the light — the room gets bright, and your shadow appears on the wall. All of this has to do with energy. [2] In the international TIMSS study, on average 54 percent of fourth-grade students around the world answered questions on this topic correctly. Questions about light bulb circuits and magnets were the hardest. Today you will learn to answer these questions with ease!

qadamlar.doska:
Light sources: the Sun, a lamp, fire
The Moon and mirrors reflect light
White light is made of the colors of the rainbow
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Things that give off their own light are called light sources: the Sun, a lamp that is on, a fire, a candle. [2] The Moon does not shine by itself; it reflects sunlight. Mirrors and the still water of a lake also reflect light. [3] The Sun's white light is actually made up of seven colors. We see these colors in a rainbow after the rain.

qadamlar.doska:
Light travels in straight lines
A shadow is on the side of the object opposite the source
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Light travels in straight lines and cannot pass through an opaque object. [2] The object blocks the light, and a shadow forms behind it, that is, on the side opposite the light source.

qadamlar.doska:
Heat moves from hot to cold
Metal conducts heat well, wood poorly
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Heat always moves from a hot object to a colder one. If we put a spoon in hot tea, the spoon gets hot. [2] Metal conducts heat well, so a metal spoon heats up quickly. Wood and plastic conduct heat poorly.

qadamlar.doska:
Circuit: battery + wires + bulb
If the circuit is closed, the bulb lights up
Metal conducts; plastic and rubber do not
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] A simple electric circuit is made of a battery, wires, and a light bulb. The battery is the source of electrical energy. [2] For current to flow, the circuit must be an unbroken, closed loop. The bulb's two contact points are connected to the two ends of the battery. [3] Metals such as copper and iron conduct electricity. Plastic, rubber, and wood do not conduct electricity; they are insulators.

qadamlar.doska:
A magnet has two poles: N and S
Like poles repel, unlike poles attract
An iron paper clip is attracted to a magnet
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Every magnet has two poles: north, N, and south, S. [2] The like poles of two magnets, for example N and N, push each other away. Unlike poles, N and S, attract each other. [3] A magnet attracts an iron paper clip. A paper clip stuck to a magnet can become a temporary magnet itself and attract another paper clip.

qadamlar.doska:
The Sun is on the left. Where is the tree's shadow?
The shadow is on the side opposite the source
Answer: on the right
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Example one. In the evening, the Sun is to the left of a tree. Which side does the tree's shadow fall on? [2] Let's remember: a shadow is on the side opposite the light source. [3] So if the Sun is on the left, the shadow falls on the right side of the tree.

qadamlar.doska:
Circuit: battery, bulb, 2 wires, and a ruler
Plastic does not conduct → the circuit is broken
A copper spoon instead of the ruler → it lights up
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Example two, a reasoning question. A circuit has a battery, a bulb, and two wires, and a plastic ruler is placed between the wires. Will the bulb light up? [2] Plastic does not conduct electricity, so the circuit is broken. The bulb will not light up. [3] If we put a metal spoon in place of the ruler, current will flow and the bulb will light up.

qadamlar.doska: Two carts: their N poles face each other
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] One more situation: magnets are placed on two carts with their N poles facing each other. If we push them close together and let go, they move away from each other in opposite directions.

qadamlar.doska: To light the bulb: a rubber band or a copper wire?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] You can put a rubber band or a copper wire in the gap in the circuit. With which one will the bulb light up? Write one word.

qadamlar.doska: If S and S poles come close, do they attract?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] We brought the S and S poles of two magnets close together. Do they attract or repel? Write one word.

qadamlar.sarlavha: How to solve an international question
qadamlar.doska:
1) Trace the picture with your finger
2) Draw the path of light as a straight line
3) Label the poles
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] In a circuit question, trace the path of the current with your finger, starting from the battery: Is the circuit closed? Is there a break? [2] In a shadow question, draw a straight line from the source through the object — the shadow lies along that line. [3] In a magnet question, write down which pole faces which: like poles repel, unlike poles attract.

qadamlar.doska:
Shadow — on the side opposite the source
Heat goes from hot to cold; metal conducts well
Closed circuit — the bulb lights; N–N repel
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Remember: light travels in straight lines, and a shadow is on the side opposite the source. [2] Heat moves from hot to cold, and metal conducts it well. [3] A bulb lights up in a closed circuit, and like poles repel. You did a wonderful job today!

q1.doska:
Gives off its own light — a source
Reflects — not a source
q1.ovoz: If something gives off its own light, it is a source; if it only reflects light, it is not a source. The Moon is not a source.

q1.doska: At night, a bicycle reflector shines
q1.ovoz: At night, when a car's headlights hit a bicycle reflector, it shines. It does not light up by itself; it reflects light — just like the Moon.

q1.doska: List: Sun ✓, lamp ✓, Moon ✗, mirror ✗
q1.ovoz: Make a two-column list: things that shine by themselves and things that reflect light. The Moon and a mirror go in the second column.

q2.doska: Lamp → object → shadow
q2.ovoz: The lamp, then the object, then the shadow — all three are on one line.

q2.doska: In the morning your shadow points west, in the evening east
q2.ovoz: In the morning the Sun is in the east, and your shadow falls to the west. In the evening the Sun is in the west, and your shadow stretches to the east.

q2.doska: Hand shadow theater
q2.ovoz: In a dark room, make a rabbit with your hand in front of a lamp. A rabbit shadow appears on the wall, on the side of your hand opposite the lamp.

q3.doska:
Hot → cold
Metal heats up fast
q3.ovoz: Heat moves from hot to cold. A metal spoon heats up quickly, but a wooden spoon does not.

q3.doska: We put a hot boiled egg in cold water
q3.ovoz: Your mother put a hot boiled egg in cold water. The egg cooled down, and the water warmed up a little — heat passed from the egg to the water.

q3.doska: Experiment: a metal and a wooden spoon in hot water
q3.ovoz: Put a metal spoon and a wooden spoon in hot water. After one minute, touch the handles: the metal spoon is hotter.

q4.doska: If the loop is not broken, the bulb lights up
q4.ovoz: Current flows around a loop. If the loop is broken, the bulb goes out.

q4.doska: The light switch at home breaks the circuit
q4.ovoz: When you press the light switch at home, it breaks or connects the circuit. That is why the light goes off or on.

q4.doska: Current = children running, circuit = a track
q4.ovoz: Compare current to children running around a track. If one part of the track is broken, nobody can get around.

q5.ovoz: Like poles repel, and unlike poles attract.

q5.doska: A fridge magnet sticks to the door
q5.ovoz: The refrigerator door is made of iron, so a magnet sticks to it. But it will not stick to a wooden door.

q5.doska: Experiment: try turning two magnets around
q5.ovoz: Bring two magnets close with one pair of ends facing — they repel. Turn one around — now they attract.

tipik_xatolar: Thinking the Moon is a light source
Drawing the shadow on the same side as the source
Thinking it is enough to connect just one end of the bulb
Thinking cold moves into a hot object; in fact, heat moves from hot to cold
Thinking a magnet attracts all metals (it does not attract aluminum or copper)
Mistakenly thinking like poles attract
strategiyalar: In a circuit question, trace the path of the current with your finger, starting from the battery
In a shadow question, draw a straight line through the source and the object
In a heat question, ask “Which one is hotter?” — heat flows out of it

maqsad: Understand force as a push or a pull, gravity, friction, and wind force, and analyze balance on a scale and a seesaw

qadamlar.doska:
Why does an apple fall down and not up?
TIMSS: 60% of fourth graders answered correctly
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] An apple that comes off a tree always falls down. What pulls it? [2] In the international TIMSS study, on average 60 percent of fourth-grade students around the world answered questions on this topic correctly. Reasoning questions about balance on a scale and a seesaw were harder. Today you will learn to answer these questions with ease!

qadamlar.doska:
Force — a push or a pull
A force starts or stops motion
A force changes direction and shape
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] A force is a push or a pull. We use force when we open a door and when we pull a cart. [2] A force can make something at rest start moving or make something moving stop. [3] A force can change the direction of motion; for example, you kick a ball and change its direction. If you press modeling clay, its shape changes.

qadamlar.doska:
Earth pulls everything toward itself
That is why things fall down
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Earth pulls everything toward its center. This pulling force is called gravity. [2] That is why a pencil you drop falls down and does not fly up.

qadamlar.doska:
Friction slows motion down
Ice — smooth (little friction), sand — rough
Wind pushes the sail — the boat moves
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] When two surfaces touch and slide against each other, friction appears. It slows motion down. [2] There is little friction on smooth ice, so we slip. There is a lot of friction on a rough surface. [3] Wind is a force too: it pushes the sail, and the sailboat moves.

qadamlar.doska:
Balance scale: the heavier pan goes down
Pans level — the weights are equal
Seesaw: the heavier child sits closer to the middle — balance
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] On a balance scale, the pan with the heavier object goes down, and the pan with the lighter one goes up. [2] If the two pans are level, the objects on both sides weigh the same. [3] On a seesaw for two, the heavier child goes down. For balance, the heavier child should sit closer to the pivot.

qadamlar.doska:
Scale: apple on the left, pear on the right. Left is down
The lower pan is heavier
Answer: the apple is heavier than the pear
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Example one. There is an apple on the left pan of a scale and a pear on the right. The left pan went down. Which one is heavier? [2] The object on the pan that went down is heavier. [3] So the apple is heavier than the pear.

qadamlar.doska: If the pans are level, the weights are equal
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] If the pans stopped level, the apple and the pear would weigh the same.

qadamlar.doska:
1) A and B: A went down → A > B
2) B and C: pans level → B = C
3) C and D: D went down → D > C
We have not compared A and D yet!
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Example two, a reasoning question. There are four cubes: A, B, C, and D. In the first weighing, A went down, so A is heavier than B. [2] In the second weighing, B and C balanced, so they are equal. [3] In the third weighing, D went down, so D is heavier than C. [4] Which is the lightest? B and C. But to know which of A and D is heavier, we would need to weigh them against each other too. Be careful!

qadamlar.doska: Seesaw: father 70 kg, son 30 kg
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Another situation: a father sits on one end of a seesaw and his son on the other. For balance, the father should move closer to the pivot.

qadamlar.doska: The right pan of the scale went down. Which side is heavier?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] The right pan of the scale went down. Which object is heavier: the one on the left or the one on the right? Write one word.

qadamlar.doska: What force pulls an apple that falls from a tree?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] What force pulls an apple down when it comes off a tree? Write the name of the force.
qadamlar.javob: gravity|force of gravity|gravitational force|Earth's gravity|weight|pull of the Earth

qadamlar.sarlavha: How to solve an international question
qadamlar.doska:
1) Write each weighing separately
2) Use the signs >, <, =
3) Draw conclusions only from what you know
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] In a scale question, write each weighing on a separate line: which is heavier, which is lighter, or whether they are equal. [2] If you write the results with the greater than, less than, and equal signs, you won't get confused. [3] Do not guess about things that were not compared. Check whether you have enough information.

qadamlar.doska:
Force — a push or a pull
Gravity pulls down; friction slows things down
On a scale, the heavier pan goes down
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Remember: a force is a push or a pull, and it changes motion, direction, and shape. [2] Gravity pulls things down, and friction slows motion down. [3] On a scale, the heavier pan goes down. Well done — you did a wonderful job!

q1.doska: Push or pull = force
q1.ovoz: When you push or pull something, you are using a force.

q1.doska: In soccer we kicked the ball, and the goalkeeper caught it
q1.ovoz: You kicked the ball, and it started moving. The goalkeeper caught it, and it stopped. Both times, a force was at work.

q1.doska: Observe: door — push, drawer — pull
q1.ovoz: Look around the classroom: we push the door to open it and pull the desk drawer to open it.

q2.doska: Earth pulls → everything falls down
q2.ovoz: Earth pulls everything toward itself, so everything falls down.

q2.doska: You threw a ball up — it came back down
q2.ovoz: No matter how high you throw a ball, it comes back down. Earth pulls it.

q2.doska: Earth is like a big magnet (but it pulls everything)
q2.ovoz: Imagine Earth as a huge ball that pulls everything toward itself. But unlike a magnet, it pulls wood and stone too.

q3.doska:
Smooth — slides fast
Rough — slows down
q3.ovoz: On a smooth surface, an object slides a long way; on a rough one, it stops quickly.

q3.doska: In winter people sprinkle sand on icy sidewalks
q3.ovoz: In winter people sprinkle sand on icy sidewalks. The sand increases friction, so people do not fall.

q3.doska: Experiment: roll a car on a carpet and on the floor
q3.ovoz: Push a toy car the same way on a smooth floor and on a carpet. On the floor it goes farther.

q4.doska: Heavy — down, light — up
q4.ovoz: On a scale, the heavy object goes down and the light object goes up.

q4.doska: At the bazaar, a seller weighed apples on a scale
q4.ovoz: At the bazaar, a seller put a one-kilogram weight on one pan and apples on the other. When the pans were level, the apples also weighed one kilogram.

q4.doska: Try it yourself on a seesaw
q4.ovoz: Get on a seesaw with a friend. If the heavier of you moves closer to the middle, you will balance.

tipik_xatolar: Thinking the higher pan on a scale is heavier
Drawing conclusions about things that were not compared
Thinking gravity acts only on heavy things
Thinking friction is always harmful (we need it to walk, too)
Thinking the heavier child should sit at the end of the seesaw for balance
strategiyalar: Write the result of each weighing using the signs >, <, =
Draw conclusions only from the information given
In a force question, ask “Who is pushing or pulling?”

maqsad: Analyze Earth's surface, types of soil and how soil changes, the use of water and air, saving natural resources, and life along a river

qadamlar.doska:
Where does drinking water come from?
TIMSS: 42% of fourth graders answered correctly
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] When you turn on the tap, clean water flows. Where does this water come from, and why should we save it? [2] In the international TIMSS study, on average 42 percent of fourth-grade students around the world answered questions on this topic correctly. This topic was quite difficult, especially the questions about using air and the energy of a waterfall. Today you will learn to answer these questions with ease!

qadamlar.doska:
Most of Earth's surface is covered by water
Most water is salty; there is little fresh water
Fresh water: rivers, lakes, glaciers, underground
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Most of Earth's surface — more than about two thirds — is water: oceans and seas. [2] But almost all of this water is salty. There is very little fresh water that is fit to drink. [3] Fresh water is found in rivers, lakes, glaciers, and underground. Drinking water is cleaned and comes to our homes through pipes.

qadamlar.doska:
Soil: small rocks, sand, clay, and humus
Soil rich in humus — the most fertile
Sand lets water through fast, clay holds it
Wind and water wear soil away
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Soil is made of tiny pieces of rock, sand, clay, and humus. Humus is rotted plant and animal remains. [2] The best soil for plants is dark soil rich in humus. It has a lot of nutrients and holds water well. [3] Sandy soil lets water through quickly, while clay soil holds water. [4] In nature, wind and rainwater wash or blow soil away. This wearing away is called erosion.

qadamlar.doska:
Air: breathing, burning, wind energy
Water: drinking, irrigation, making electricity
We save water: we turn off the tap
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] We need air to breathe, and fire burns using the oxygen in the air. Wind turns wind turbines and gives us electricity. [2] We drink water and use it to irrigate crops. At a hydroelectric power station, electricity is produced by the force of water falling from a waterfall or a dam. [3] To save water, we turn off the tap while brushing our teeth, get dripping taps fixed, and do not stay in the shower for a long time.

qadamlar.doska:
Renewable: the Sun, wind, flowing water
Nonrenewable: coal, oil, gas
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Sunlight, wind, and flowing water do not run out. They are renewable resources. [2] Coal, oil, and natural gas formed over millions of years. If we use them up, they are gone, so they are nonrenewable resources.

qadamlar.doska:
Farming by a river: what is the advantage?
Advantage: water for irrigation is close by
Disadvantage: a flood may wash away the crops
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Example one. Farmers often plant crops along a river. What is the advantage of this? [2] Water for irrigating the crops is close by. Besides, the silt brought by the river makes the soil fertile. [3] There is also a disadvantage: if the river floods in spring, the water may wash away the crops and flood homes.

qadamlar.doska: Protection: a levee is built along the river
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] To protect themselves from floods, people build an earth wall, a levee, along the river.

qadamlar.doska:
3 pots: sand, clay, soil with humus
Sand: the water drained away fast, few nutrients
Clay: water stood in puddles, the roots got no air
Answer: plants grow best in soil with humus
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Example two, a reasoning question. We filled three pots with sand, clay, and soil with humus, planted the same seeds, and watered them the same way. [2] In the sandy pot, the water drained away quickly, and the plant did not get enough water and nutrients. [3] In the clay pot, the water collected on top, and the roots did not get enough air. [4] But the soil with humus had enough water, air, and nutrients. So the plant grows best in this pot.

qadamlar.doska: A fair test: only the type of soil changed
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Notice: the seeds, water, and light were the same; only the type of soil changed. That is why we can confidently link the result to the soil.

qadamlar.doska: What do we get from the force of a waterfall?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] What kind of energy do we get from the force of water falling from a waterfall or a dam? Write one or two words.

qadamlar.doska: Is coal a renewable resource? (yes / no)
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Is coal a renewable resource? Write “yes” or “no.”

qadamlar.sarlavha: How to solve an international question
qadamlar.doska:
1) “Write two ways” — two different answers
2) Be specific: “I turn off the tap”
3) Keep advantages and disadvantages separate
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] International questions often say, “Write two ways.” Write two different answers, not two that mean the same thing. [2] Do not write “I will save water.” Write a specific action: “I turn off the tap while brushing my teeth.” [3] If an advantage is asked for, write the benefit; if a disadvantage is asked for, write the harm. Do not mix them up.

qadamlar.doska:
Fresh water is scarce — we save it
Soil with humus — the most fertile
Sun, wind, water — renewable; coal, oil — not
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Remember: there is little fresh water on Earth, and we must save it. [2] The best soil for plants is soil rich in humus. [3] The Sun, wind, and flowing water are renewable, but coal and oil run out. Wonderful work!

q1.doska: Lots of water, but little that is drinkable
q1.ovoz: There is a great deal of water on Earth, but only a small part of it is drinkable.

q1.doska: A thirsty sailor at sea
q1.ovoz: A sailor suffers from thirst even though he is surrounded by water. That is because seawater is salty, and you cannot drink it.

q1.doska: Out of 100 glasses of water, only 3 are fresh
q1.ovoz: If we imagine all the water on Earth as one hundred glasses, only about three would be fresh water; the rest would be salty.

q2.doska: Dark soil with humus — the best
q2.ovoz: The best soil for plants is dark, soft soil rich in humus.

q2.doska: Grandpa puts manure and fallen leaves in the garden
q2.ovoz: In the fall, your grandfather puts manure and fallen leaves in the garden. They rot, turn into humus, and make the soil fertile.

q2.doska: Experiment: pour water through sand and clay
q2.ovoz: Put sand in one funnel and clay in another, and pour water over them. The water flows through the sand quickly, but through the clay slowly.

q3.doska:
Air — breathing, fire, wind
Water — drinking, irrigation, electricity
q3.ovoz: Air is needed for breathing, fire, and wind. Water is needed for drinking, irrigation, and making electricity.

q3.doska: The Charvak Dam produces electricity
q3.ovoz: At the Charvak Reservoir in the Tashkent Region, water falling from the dam turns turbines and produces electricity.

q3.doska:
Ways to use air:
balloons, drying laundry, sails, breathing
q3.ovoz: There are many ways to use air: blowing up balloons, drying laundry, sailing boats, and breathing.

q4.doska:
Doesn't run out — renewable
Runs out — nonrenewable
q4.ovoz: Resources that do not run out are renewable; those that run out when we use them are nonrenewable.

q4.doska: A box of candy and apples on a tree
q4.ovoz: If you eat a whole box of candy, it does not fill up again — coal is like that. But an apple tree gives fruit again every year.

q4.doska: Two columns: renewable | nonrenewable
q4.ovoz: Draw two columns. Write the Sun, wind, and water in the first column, and coal, oil, and gas in the second.

tipik_xatolar: Thinking most of the water on Earth is fit to drink
Writing two answers that mean the same thing in a “write two ways” question
Limiting the uses of air to breathing only
Seeing only the benefits of farming along a river and forgetting the risk of flooding
Thinking coal and oil are renewable
strategiyalar: In an open question, write specific and different answers
Think about advantages and disadvantages separately
In an experiment question, notice that only one thing (the type of soil) changed

maqsad: Understand weather observation, the water cycle, the direction rivers flow, and how fossils tell us about the past

qadamlar.doska:
Where does rainwater come from?
TIMSS: 37% of fourth graders answered correctly
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] The water in a puddle disappears in the sun, then clouds appear and it rains. Where does this water go, and where does it come back from? [2] In the international TIMSS study, on average 37 percent of fourth-grade students around the world answered questions on this topic correctly. This was one of the hardest topics, especially the question about fossils. Today you will learn to answer these questions with ease!

qadamlar.doska:
Weather: temperature, precipitation, wind, clouds
Thermometer — temperature, wind vane — wind direction
Rain gauge — how much rain fell
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Weather is the condition of the air at a certain place and time: temperature, precipitation, wind, and clouds. [2] We measure temperature with a thermometer. A wind vane shows which direction the wind is blowing from. [3] We find out how much rain fell with a rain gauge.

qadamlar.doska:
1) Evaporation: the Sun heats water → vapor
2) Condensation: vapor cools → clouds
3) Precipitation: drops → rain, snow
4) Water flows back to rivers and seas
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] The Sun heats the water in seas, lakes, and rivers. The water evaporates and rises into the air as invisible vapor. [2] High up, the air is cold. The vapor cools and turns into tiny droplets, which together form clouds. This is condensation. [3] When the droplets grow bigger and heavier, they fall to the ground as rain or snow. [4] Water that falls on the ground flows through rivers to the sea or soaks into the ground. Then it all starts over again.

qadamlar.doska:
A river flows from high ground to low ground
It starts in the mountains and flows to the lowlands
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] A river always flows from higher ground to lower ground, because Earth's gravity pulls the water down. [2] Rivers start from melting snow and glaciers in the mountains and flow down to low plains, to a lake or the sea.

qadamlar.doska:
Fossil — a trace of an ancient living thing turned to stone
Fossils formed millions of years ago
Lower layer — older
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] A fossil is the trace or remains of a plant or animal that lived very long ago, preserved in rock. [2] Many fossils come from organisms that lived millions of years ago. Turning to stone takes a very long time. [3] Rocks lie in layers. Usually a lower layer formed earlier, so a fossil in it is older.

qadamlar.doska:
Put in order: precipitation, evaporation, clouds
Start: the Sun evaporates water
Evaporation → clouds → precipitation
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Example one. Put the stages of the water cycle in order: precipitation, evaporation, cloud formation. [2] First, the Sun heats the water and evaporates it. [3] The vapor cools and forms clouds, and precipitation falls from the clouds. The correct order is evaporation, clouds, precipitation.

qadamlar.doska: The Sun's energy drives the cycle
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] The Sun's energy drives this whole cycle: if the Sun did not heat the water, there would be no evaporation.

qadamlar.doska:
A fossil seashell was found on a mountain
Shellfish live only in the sea
So millions of years ago this place was the seafloor
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Example two, a reasoning question. A fossil of a seashell was found in rocks high on a mountain. What does this tell us? [2] Shellfish live only in seawater; they cannot climb a mountain by themselves. [3] So very long ago, millions of years ago, this place was the bottom of a sea. Later the layers of the earth rose up and formed a mountain.

qadamlar.doska: A fossil in a lower layer — older
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] If there are two fossils in the same rock, the one in the lower layer lived earlier than the one above it.

qadamlar.doska: What do we call vapor cooling into clouds?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] What is the process called when water vapor cools, turns into tiny droplets, and forms clouds? Write one word.

qadamlar.doska: Which way does a river flow: from high to low or the other way?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Which way does a river flow: from high ground to low ground, or from low ground to high ground? Write your answer.
qadamlar.javob: from high to low|high to low|downhill|down|from the mountains down

qadamlar.sarlavha: How to solve an international question
qadamlar.doska:
1) Break the process into stages
2) “What causes it?” — find the force or energy
3) Fossil: ask “Where did it live?”
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] In a question about a natural process, break it into stages and write them with arrows. [2] If the cause is asked for, find what drives it: the Sun's heat causes evaporation, and gravity makes water flow down. [3] In a fossil question, think about where and when the organism lived — this shows the past of that place.

qadamlar.doska:
Evaporation → condensation → precipitation → runoff
Rivers flow from high to low
Fossils — a history of millions of years
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Remember: water evaporates, forms clouds, falls as precipitation, and flows back. [2] Gravity makes a river flow from high ground to low ground. [3] Fossils show life from millions of years ago. Well done!

q1.doska: What is it like outside today? — that is the weather
q1.ovoz: Is it hot today, rainy, windy? That is the weather.

q1.doska: The weather report on TV in the morning
q1.ovoz: In the morning your mother watched the weather report and said, “It will rain today — take an umbrella.” We need to know the weather.

q1.doska: Journal: write down the temperature and clouds every day
q1.ovoz: For one week, write down the temperature and what the sky looks like every day. This will be your weather journal.

q2.doska: Water → vapor → cloud → rain → water
q2.ovoz: Water turns into vapor, vapor into clouds, clouds into rain, and rain into water again.

q2.doska: The laundry dried — the water went into the air
q2.ovoz: Your mother hung the washed laundry in the sun. The laundry dried because its water evaporated into the air. Later that water will join a cloud.

q2.doska: Experiment: a cold lid over hot water
q2.ovoz: Put a cold lid over a glass of hot water. Drops appear under the lid and drip down — a tiny rain!

q3.doska: Water flows downward
q3.ovoz: Water always flows downward, and so does a river.

q3.doska: The Chirchiq River starts in the mountains
q3.ovoz: The Chirchiq River begins with waters flowing from the Chatkal and Pskem Mountains and flows down into the Syr Darya.

q3.doska: Experiment: pour water on a tilted board
q3.ovoz: Tilt a board and pour water on the top. The water always flows to the lower end.

q4.doska: Fossil — an ancient trace in rock
q4.ovoz: A fossil is the trace of a plant or animal from very, very long ago, left in rock.

q4.doska: A leaf print was found in coal
q4.ovoz: Miners found the print of a fern leaf in a piece of coal. This plant lived millions of years ago.

q4.doska: A stack of books: the bottom one was put down first
q4.ovoz: Stack books on a table one on top of another. The bottom one was put down first. Rock layers are the same.

tipik_xatolar: Thinking clouds are made of vapor, that is, gas; they are made of tiny droplets
Thinking fossils formed a few years or centuries ago; in fact, it took millions of years
Thinking rivers flow from north to south; the direction depends on height
Mixing up the order of the stages of the water cycle
Thinking weather and climate are the same thing
strategiyalar: Break the process into stages and write them with arrows
Explain the cause in terms of a force or energy
In a fossil question, think about where and when the organism lived

maqsad: Understand the positions and motions of the Sun, Earth, and Moon, the causes of day and night and the seasons, and the importance of the Sun's energy

qadamlar.doska:
Why does night come after day?
TIMSS: 48% of fourth graders answered correctly
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Every morning the Sun rises, and every evening it sets. Is this because the Sun moves, or is there another reason? [2] In the international TIMSS study, on average 48 percent of fourth-grade students around the world answered questions on this topic correctly. Explaining the cause of day and night was the hardest question. Today you will learn to answer these questions with ease!

qadamlar.doska:
The Sun — a star at the center of the system
8 planets orbit the Sun
The Moon — Earth's satellite
The Sun gives Earth light and heat
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] The Sun is a star. It gives off its own light and heat and is at the center of the solar system. [2] Eight planets orbit the Sun. Earth is the third planet from the Sun. [3] The Moon orbits Earth; it is Earth's natural satellite. The Moon is about four times smaller than Earth. [4] The Sun gives Earth light and heat. Without it, plants would not grow, and there would be no life on Earth.

qadamlar.doska:
Earth spins on its axis
One full turn — 24 hours
The side facing the Sun — day, the other side — night
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Earth spins on its axis like a top. [2] It takes Earth about twenty-four hours, or one full day, to make one complete turn. [3] It is day on the side of Earth facing the Sun and night on the opposite side. The Sun does not go around Earth!

qadamlar.doska:
Earth goes around the Sun in 1 year
The cause of the seasons — the tilt of Earth's axis
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] It takes Earth one year, or about three hundred sixty-five days, to go once around the Sun. [2] Earth's axis is slightly tilted. That is why in summer the Sun's rays hit us more directly and the days are long, and in winter it is the opposite.

qadamlar.doska:
The Moon does not shine by itself — it reflects sunlight
The Moon goes around Earth in about 1 month
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] The Moon does not give off its own light. What we see on the Moon is reflected sunlight. [2] The Moon goes around Earth in about one month. During this time, the Moon's shape seems to change: new moon, half moon, full moon.

qadamlar.doska:
It is daytime in Tashkent. What about America?
Earth is a sphere: one side lit, one side dark
On the opposite side — night
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Example one. It is lunchtime, daytime, in Tashkent. What is happening at the same moment in America, on the opposite side of Earth? [2] Earth is shaped like a ball, and the Sun lights up only one half of it. [3] If Tashkent is on the side facing the Sun, America is on the opposite side. So it is night there.

qadamlar.doska: After half a day, everything switches
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Earth keeps spinning. After about half a day, Tashkent will be on the side facing away from the Sun, and night will begin there.

qadamlar.doska:
3 balls in a model: large, medium, small
The largest, in the center — the Sun
Goes around the Sun — Earth
Goes around Earth — the Moon
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Example two, a reasoning question. A picture shows three balls: a large one, a medium one, and a small one. The small ball goes around the medium one, and the medium one goes around the large ball. Which is which? [2] The largest one, in the center, is the Sun. It is more than a hundred times larger than Earth. [3] The medium ball going around the Sun is Earth. [4] The smallest ball going around Earth is the Moon.

qadamlar.doska: The Moon goes around the Sun together with Earth
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] The Moon goes around Earth, and together with Earth it also travels around the Sun.

qadamlar.doska: How many hours does it take Earth to spin once on its axis?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] How many hours does it take Earth to make one complete turn on its axis? Write the number.

qadamlar.doska: Does the Moon give off its own light? (yes / no)
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Does the Moon give off its own light? Write “yes” or “no.”
qadamlar.javob: no|it does not|no, it reflects light

qadamlar.sarlavha: How to solve an international question
qadamlar.doska:
1) What goes around what?
2) Tell two motions apart: day and year
3) In your explanation, mention Earth's spinning
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] First write down: Earth goes around the Sun, and the Moon goes around Earth. [2] Spinning on its axis gives day and night; going around the Sun gives a year. Do not mix them up. [3] For the question “Why do day and night happen?”, do not write “the Sun sets.” Write “Earth spins on its axis.”

qadamlar.doska:
Sun — star; Earth — planet; Moon — satellite
Spinning on its axis in 24 hours — day and night
Around the Sun in 1 year; seasons — from the tilt of the axis
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Remember: the Sun is a star, Earth is a planet, and the Moon is Earth's satellite. [2] Earth spins on its axis in twenty-four hours, which is why day and night take turns. [3] It goes around the Sun in one year, and the seasons happen because of the tilt of its axis. You did great work!

q1.doska: The Sun in the center, Earth around it, the Moon around Earth
q1.ovoz: The Sun is in the middle, Earth goes around it, and the Moon goes around Earth.

q1.doska: At a holiday, children circle around the tree
q1.ovoz: At a holiday party, children dance in a circle around the decorated tree. The Sun is the tree, and the planets are the children.

q1.doska: Model: the Sun — a 1-meter ball, Earth — a pea
q1.ovoz: If the Sun were a big ball one meter across, Earth would be like a pea, and the Moon like a grain of millet.

q2.doska: Earth spins → night, day
q2.ovoz: Earth spins, and that is why our nights and days take turns.

q2.doska: A child turning around next to a campfire
q2.ovoz: If you turn around next to a campfire, your face points sometimes toward the fire and sometimes toward the darkness. The fire stays put — you are the one turning.

q2.doska: Experiment: a lamp and a globe
q2.ovoz: In a dark room, turn on a lamp and spin a globe. The side facing the lamp is lit — day — and the back side is dark — night.

q3.doska: Once around the Sun = 1 year
q3.ovoz: When Earth goes once around the Sun, one year has passed.

q3.doska: Your birthday comes back every year
q3.ovoz: Your birthday comes every year because in that time Earth goes all the way around the Sun and returns to the same place.

q3.doska: Flashlight: straight down — warm, slanted — cool
q3.ovoz: If you shine a flashlight straight down on paper, the spot is small and bright. If you shine it at a slant, the spot is wide and dim. In summer sunlight comes in steeply, and in winter at a slant.

q4.doska: The Moon — like a mirror, it reflects sunlight
q4.ovoz: Like a mirror, the Moon reflects sunlight; it does not shine by itself.

q4.doska: The Moon's shape changes every night
q4.ovoz: Look at the Moon every night for a month: it changes from a thin crescent to a full moon and then back to a crescent.

q4.doska: Experiment: a lamp and a white ball
q4.ovoz: In the dark, shine a lamp on a white ball. The ball does not glow by itself, but it looks bright — the Moon is the same.

tipik_xatolar: Thinking day and night happen because the Sun goes around Earth
Mistakenly thinking Earth spins once on its axis in a year
Thinking the seasons happen because Earth moves closer to and farther from the Sun
Thinking the Moon gives off its own light
Drawing the Moon going around the Sun in a model
strategiyalar: First write down what goes around what
Tell apart a day (spinning on its axis) and a year (going around the Sun)
In your explanation, give Earth's motion as the cause

maqsad: Use prime factorization, find the GCF and LCM, and apply the properties of powers and division with remainder to real-life problems

qadamlar.doska:
Natural numbers: 1, 2, 3, 4, ...
TIMSS: on average, 42% of 8th graders answered correctly
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Hello everyone! Today we will uncover the secrets of the most familiar numbers of all, the natural numbers: prime numbers, powers, and division with remainder. [2] In the international TIMSS study, on average forty-two percent of students worldwide answered questions on this topic correctly. By the end of the lesson, you will be able to solve such questions with ease!

qadamlar.doska:
Prime number: divisible only by 1 and itself: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11
$36 = 2 \cdot 18 = 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 9 = 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 3$
$36 = 2^2 \cdot 3^2$
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] A prime number is a number greater than one that is divisible only by one and itself: two, three, five, seven, eleven. [2] We divide thirty-six by the smallest primes one after another: by two, by two again, then by three. [3] We write repeated factors as powers: two squared times three squared.

qadamlar.doska:
$12 = 2^2 \cdot 3$,  $18 = 2 \cdot 3^2$
GCF: common factors, lowest power: $2 \cdot 3 = 6$
LCM: all factors, highest power: $2^2 \cdot 3^2 = 36$
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] We write the prime factorizations of twelve and eighteen. [2] For the GCF, we take the factors found in both numbers, each to its lowest power. The result is six. [3] For the LCM, we take all the factors, each to its highest power. The result is thirty-six.

[1] When we multiply powers with the same base, we add the exponents. [2] For example, eight is two cubed, sixteen is two to the fourth power, and their product is two to the seventh power. [3] To rewrite a power of four as a power of two, we multiply the exponent by two.

qadamlar.doska:
$a = b \cdot q + r$,  $0 \le r < b$
$100 = 12 \cdot 8 + 4$
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Any number can be written as the divisor times the quotient plus the remainder, and the remainder is smaller than the divisor. [2] If we pack one hundred eggs into boxes of twelve, we get eight full boxes and four eggs are left over.

qadamlar.doska: Write the prime factorization of 180
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Example one: let's find the prime factorization of one hundred eighty.

qadamlar.doska:
$180 = 2 \cdot 90 = 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 45$
$45 = 3 \cdot 15 = 3 \cdot 3 \cdot 5$
$180 = 2^2 \cdot 3^2 \cdot 5$
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] One hundred eighty is even, so we divide by two: ninety; by two again: forty-five. [2] Forty-five is odd but divisible by three: fifteen, and fifteen is three times five. [3] Answer: two squared, three squared, and five. Check: four times nine times five is one hundred eighty.

qadamlar.doska:
A farm has 250 eggs, packed 12 to a box
How many boxes are filled? How many boxes are needed for all of them?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Example two: a farm has two hundred fifty eggs, and each box holds twelve. [2] The question has two parts: how many boxes will be full, and how many boxes are needed in total for all the eggs?

qadamlar.doska:
$250 = 12 \cdot 20 + 10$
20 full boxes, 10 eggs left over
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] We divide two hundred fifty by twelve with remainder: the quotient is twenty and the remainder is ten. [2] So twenty boxes are full and ten eggs are left over.

qadamlar.doska:
For all of them: 20 + 1 = 21 boxes
Read the question carefully: 20 or 21?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] To pack the ten leftover eggs too, we need one more box, so twenty-one in total. [2] This is exactly where TIMSS sets a trap: is the question asking for full boxes or for the boxes needed? Pay attention.

[1] Example three: let's write sixty-four times one thousand twenty-four as a power of four. [2] First we write both as powers of two: two to the sixth and two to the tenth. [3] We add the exponents: sixteen. Since sixteen is even, this is four to the eighth power.
[1] Now solve this yourself: find the greatest common factor of twenty-four and thirty-six. First write the prime factorization of each.
[1] Eight squared times eight cubed equals two to what power? Start by writing eight as a power of two.

qadamlar.sarlavha: How to solve an international question
qadamlar.doska:
1) Write the prime factorization of the numbers
2) Think about what the remainder means
3) Check the answer by multiplying
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Step one: break large numbers into prime factors or powers right away. Many questions are solved this way. [2] Step two: in division with remainder, use the text to decide what to do with the remainder: drop it or add one more. [3] Step three: check your answer with the inverse operation. Multiply back, and you should get the starting number.

qadamlar.doska:
$36 = 2^2 \cdot 3^2$ — prime factors
GCF: lowest power, LCM: highest power
$a^m \cdot a^n = a^{m+n}$;  $a = bq + r$
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Remember: every natural number can be written as a product of primes in exactly one way. [2] For the GCF, we take the lowest power of the common factors; for the LCM, the highest power of all factors. [3] When we multiply powers, we add the exponents, and the remainder is always smaller than the divisor. You did great work today!

q1.doska:
12 = 2 · 6 = 2 · 2 · 3
Keep dividing until you can't
q1.ovoz: We keep dividing by the smallest prime until the quotient is itself a prime. Twelve is two times six, and six is two times three. So twelve is made of two, two, and three.

q1.doska:
Lego tower = smallest bricks
36 = 2 · 2 · 3 · 3
q1.ovoz: Imagine taking a Lego tower apart down to its smallest pieces. Prime numbers are the smallest bricks that can't be split any further. Thirty-six is built from two bricks of two and two bricks of three.

q1.doska:
Factor tree: 36 → 4 and 9
4 → 2·2,  9 → 3·3
q1.ovoz: Try the tree method: split thirty-six into four and nine, four into two and two, and nine into three and three. If you multiply all the primes on the leaves of the tree, you get thirty-six.

q2.doska:
Factors of 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12
Factors of 18: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18
Greatest common one: 6
q2.ovoz: List the factors of both numbers and mark the common ones. The greatest is six, and that is the GCF.

q2.doska:
12 apples, 18 pears — identical gift bags
At most 6 gift bags
q2.ovoz: You have twelve apples and eighteen pears, and you want to split them into identical gift bags. You can make at most six bags, each with two apples and three pears. That is the GCF.

q2.doska:
Multiples of 12: 12, 24, 36, ...
Multiples of 18: 18, 36, ...
First common one: 36 = LCM
q2.ovoz: You can also find the LCM by listing multiples: write the multiples of twelve and of eighteen. The first number they have in common is thirty-six.

q3.ovoz: Write the powers out in full: three twos and two more twos, so five twos multiplied together. That is why the exponents add.

q3.doska:
Bacteria double every hour
3 hours, then 4 hours: 2⁷ times
q3.ovoz: Bacteria double every hour. If three hours pass and then four more, that is seven hours in total, so they multiply two to the seventh power times.

q3.doska:
4 = 2², 16 = 2⁴, 64 = 2⁶
Powers of 4 are even powers of 2
q3.ovoz: Memorize the table of powers of two: two, four, eight, sixteen, thirty-two, sixty-four. The powers of four are exactly the even powers of two.

q4.ovoz: If we divide seventeen by five, five goes in three times with two left over. Check: five times three is fifteen, plus two is seventeen.

q4.doska:
30 students, 8 seats per minibus
30 = 8 · 3 + 6 → 4 minibuses
q4.ovoz: Thirty students are going on a trip in eight-seat minibuses. Three minibuses are filled and six people are left, and they need a minibus too, so four in total.

tipik_xatolar: Ignoring the leftover part in a remainder problem: saying 20 boxes for 250 eggs
Multiplying the exponents when multiplying powers: writing 2³ · 2⁴ = 2¹²
Thinking 1 is a prime number
Mixing up the GCF and the LCM
Leaving a composite number in a prime factorization: 36 = 4 · 9
strategiyalar: Write large numbers as prime factors or powers first
In division with remainder, reread what the question is asking
Check your answer with the inverse operation
If the greatest result is asked for, try putting the largest digits in the highest places

maqsad: Convert between fractions and decimals, compare them, perform operations, place them on a number line, and estimate

qadamlar.doska:
$\frac{3}{8}$ of a pizza = 0.375
TIMSS: on average, 50% of 8th graders answered correctly
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Imagine we cut a pizza into eight slices and ate three of them. That is three eighths, or zero point three seven five. [2] In the international TIMSS study, on average fifty percent of students worldwide answered questions on this topic correctly. Today we won't join the other half: we will learn to solve them all!

qadamlar.sarlavha: Converting a fraction to a decimal
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Every fraction means dividing the numerator by the denominator. [2] Three fifths: we divide three by five and get zero point six. [3] In a mixed number, the whole part stays the same and we divide only the fraction part: dividing five by six gives zero point eight three three three, and so on.

[1] Four hundredths means four in the hundredths place, and three thousandths means three in the thousandths place. Together they make zero point zero four three. [2] When we add decimals, we line up the decimal points, and we can write a zero in an empty place.

qadamlar.doska:
Common denominator first!
$\frac{5}{6} - \frac{1}{4} = \frac{10}{12} - \frac{3}{12} = \frac{7}{12}$
Wrong: $\frac{5}{6} - \frac{1}{4} \ne \frac{4}{2}$
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Before adding or subtracting fractions, the denominators must be the same. [2] The LCM of six and four is twelve. We change five sixths into ten twelfths and one fourth into three twelfths, then subtract the numerators. [3] Subtracting numerator from numerator and denominator from denominator is the most common mistake. Don't do it!

qadamlar.doska:
Interval length ÷ number of parts = one step
5 parts from 0 to 1 → step 0.2
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] To find a point on a number line, first find the length of one part: divide the length of the interval by the number of parts. [2] For example, if there are five equal parts from zero to one, each step is zero point two.

[1] Example one: let's write four and three eighths as a decimal. [2] The whole part, four, stays where it is. We divide three by eight: zero point three seven five. [3] Answer: four point three seven five.

qadamlar.doska:
The interval from 0.3 to 0.5 is divided into 5 equal parts
N is the 2nd mark after 0.3. N = ?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Example two, TIMSS style: on a number line, the interval from zero point three to zero point five is divided into five equal parts. [2] Point N is at the second mark after zero point three. Find N.

[1] First we find the length of the interval: zero point five minus zero point three is zero point two. [2] There are five parts, so one step is zero point zero four. [3] N is two steps away: we add zero point zero eight to zero point three and get zero point three eight.

qadamlar.doska:
Which number is closest to $\frac{5.92 \cdot 3.07}{2.96}$?
$\approx \frac{6 \cdot 3}{3} = 6$
Exact value: 6.14 — the estimate is right
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Example three: without calculating exactly, let's find the whole number closest to this expression. [2] We round each number: five point nine two is about six, three point zero seven is about three, and two point nine six is about three. Six times three, divided by three, is six. [3] A calculator gives six point one four, so our estimate is very close.

qadamlar.doska: Write $\frac{7}{20}$ as a decimal
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Now you try: write seven twentieths as a decimal. Hint: make the denominator one hundred.
qadamlar.savol: Write the answer as a decimal

qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Subtract one fourth from two thirds. First find a common denominator.
qadamlar.savol: Write the answer as a fraction

qadamlar.sarlavha: How to solve an international question
qadamlar.doska:
1) Narrow down the options by estimating
2) On a number line, find one step first
3) Write the fractions in the same form
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] First: in a multiple-choice question, round the numbers and rule out the options that can't be right straight away. [2] Second: on a number line, always divide the interval by the number of parts to find one step. Count the parts, not the marks. [3] Third: before comparing or adding, write all the numbers in the same form, either as decimals or as fractions with a common denominator.

qadamlar.doska:
$\frac{a}{b} = a : b$
Add and subtract only with a common denominator
Number line: interval ÷ number of parts
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Remember: a fraction is a division. Divide the numerator by the denominator and you get a decimal. [2] When adding and subtracting fractions, first find a common denominator. [3] On a number line, one step is the length of the interval divided by the number of parts. Well done, you worked brilliantly today!

q1.ovoz: Memorize the most common fractions: one half is zero point five, one fourth is zero point two five. Three fourths is three such parts: zero point seven five.

q1.doska:
