[2] An element is made of one kind of atom, and a compound is made of different atoms chemically bonded together. [3] In a mixture the substances are not bonded and can be separated by physical methods. [4] In a formula, the subscript shows the number of atoms, and the coefficient shows the number of molecules. Today you conquered even the hardest question. Well done!

q1.doska:
Atom: a Lego brick
Molecule: a shape built from the bricks
q1.ovoz: Imagine an atom as a Lego brick, and a molecule as a small shape built from these bricks.

q1.doska:
One drop of water has ≈ 1 600 000 000 000 000 000 000 molecules
That is why we cannot see them
q1.ovoz: A single drop of water contains billions upon billions of water molecules, more than one and a half sextillion. They are so small that you cannot see them even with the strongest ordinary microscope.

q1.doska:
If we open perfume in a corner of a room,
the smell spreads through the whole room: the particles are moving
q1.ovoz: If you open a bottle of perfume in a corner of a room, after a while the smell spreads through the whole room. This shows that matter is made of tiny particles and that they move.

q2.doska:
Element: ●● ●●
Compound: ●○ ●○;  Mixture: ●● ●○
q2.ovoz: Remember with a picture: only identical balls means an element; different balls bonded together, with all particles the same, means a compound; different particles mixed together means a mixture.

q2.doska:
In the kitchen: sugar is a compound
Sweet tea is a mixture
q2.ovoz: Look in the kitchen: sugar is a compound made of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen. If you put it in tea, the sweet tea is a mixture, and if you evaporate the tea, the sugar is left behind.

q2.doska:
Can it be separated physically?
Yes → mixture;  no → pure substance
q2.ovoz: Another method: can the substance be separated by physical methods such as filtering, evaporation, or a magnet? If it can, it is a mixture; if it cannot, it is a pure substance, that is, an element or a compound.

q3.doska:
$\mathrm{H_2O}$ = H, H, O
Subscript: how many; symbol: which atom
q3.ovoz: Reading a formula is easy: the letter tells you which atom, and the small number tells you how many. H two O means two hydrogens and one oxygen.

q3.doska:
Recipe: 2 eggs, 1 cup of flour
A formula is the “recipe” of a molecule too
q3.ovoz: Think of a formula as a recipe: like “two eggs and one cup of flour”, H two O is a recipe that says “two hydrogens and one oxygen”.

q3.doska:
Draw each atom as a circle:
$\mathrm{CO_2}$ → ○●○ → 3 circles
q3.ovoz: Draw each atom as a circle and count the circles. For C O two you get three circles, so three atoms.

q4.doska:
Metal: shiny, conducts current
Nonmetal: usually not
q4.ovoz: In short: a metal is shiny and conducts current, while a nonmetal usually does not.

q4.doska:
Electric wire: copper inside, plastic outside
Copper conducts current, plastic protects
q4.ovoz: Look at an electric wire at home: there is copper inside and plastic on the outside. Copper is a metal and conducts current, while plastic does not, and it protects us from the current.

q4.doska:
Experiment: battery + bulb + substance
The bulb lit up → conductor
q4.ovoz: A small experiment: connect a battery, a bulb, and the substance being tested in a circuit. When a nail or a coin is connected, the bulb lights up; when wood or rubber is connected, it does not.

tipik_xatolar: Thinking $\mathrm{O_2}$ or $\mathrm{N_2}$ is a compound: they are elements made of one kind of atom
Not counting an element without a subscript in a formula (for example, saying $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$ has 6 atoms)
Thinking a mixture of different particles is a compound
Thinking that the number of atoms changes when a substance is crushed or ground
Deciding that something is a metal based only on its shine
strategiyalar: For a particle picture, ask two questions: are the particles the same, are the atoms the same
In a formula, count each element separately, then add
If there is a coefficient, multiply the number of atoms in one molecule by it
Identify a metal using several properties

maqsad: Distinguish physical and chemical properties of substances, calculate with a solubility table, identify acids and bases by pH, and explain neutralization and the expansion of water when it freezes

qadamlar.doska:
Why do water pipes burst in winter?
TIMSS: on average 50% of grade 8 students answered correctly
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Why do water pipes burst in severe frost, and why do rocks crack over the years? Today we will study the properties of substances and find the answer. [2] In the international TIMSS study, on average fifty percent of students around the world answered questions on this topic correctly, that is, every second student. Today you will join those who solve them with confidence!

qadamlar.doska:
Physical properties: color, density, melting and boiling points
solubility, electrical and thermal conductivity
Chemical properties: flammability, reaction with acids
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Physical properties are found without changing the substance: color, smell, density, melting point, and boiling point. [2] Solubility and electrical and thermal conductivity are also physical properties. [3] A chemical property is a substance's ability to turn into another substance: for example, flammability or reacting with an acid.

qadamlar.doska:
Solution = solvent (water) + solute (salt)
Solubility: the greatest mass that can dissolve in 100 g of water
Most solids: temperature ↑ → solubility ↑
Gases: temperature ↑ → solubility ↓
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] A solution is a uniform mixture of a solvent and a solute, for example, a solution of salt in water. [2] Solubility is the greatest mass of a substance that can dissolve in one hundred grams of water at a given temperature. [3] For most solids, solubility increases as the temperature rises. [4] For gases it is the opposite: less gas dissolves in warm water, which is why soda water goes “flat” faster when it is warm.

qadamlar.doska:
pH scale: 0 ... 7 ... 14
pH < 7: acid: vinegar, lemon juice
pH = 7: neutral: pure water;  pH > 7: base: ammonia solution
Acid + base → salt + water (neutralization)
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] The pH scale shows whether a solution is acidic or basic: it runs from zero to fourteen. [2] If the pH is less than seven, the solution is acidic: vinegar, lemon juice. Acids taste sour and turn litmus red. [3] A pH of seven is neutral, for example, pure water. If it is greater than seven, the solution is basic: ammonia solution, soapy water. They turn litmus blue. [4] An acid and a base react with each other to form a salt and water. This is a neutralization reaction.

qadamlar.doska:
Water expands when it freezes: its volume increases by ≈9%
Density of ice $0.92$ g/cm³ < density of water 1 g/cm³
Water in a crack freezes and splits the rock
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Most substances contract when they cool, but water expands when it freezes: the volume of ice is about nine percent larger than that of the water. [2] That is why the density of ice, about zero point nine two grams per cubic centimeter, is less than that of water, and ice floats on water. [3] Water that gets into a crack in a rock freezes, expands, and makes the crack bigger. As this happens again and again, the rock breaks apart. This is physical weathering.

qadamlar.doska:
Ammonia solution is slowly added to vinegar (pH = 3)
The pH of the ammonia solution = 11. How does the pH change?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Example one. The pH of the vinegar in a glass is three. Ammonia solution is slowly being added to it. [2] The pH of the ammonia solution is eleven. How does the pH of the mixture change?

qadamlar.doska:
The base neutralizes the acid → the pH keeps rising
If enough is added, pH ≈ 7; if too much is added, pH > 7
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Ammonia solution is a base. It neutralizes the acid in the vinegar, so the pH rises gradually. [2] When enough has been added, the pH gets close to seven, and if too much is added, it goes above seven and the solution becomes basic.

qadamlar.doska: Answer: the pH rises from 3 and approaches 7
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Answer: the pH increases starting from three and approaches seven. Important: the pH never goes above eleven, because the most basic liquid is the ammonia solution being added.

qadamlar.doska:
Solubility of $\mathrm{KNO_3}$ (g / 100 g water):
20 °C: 32 g;  40 °C: 64 g;  60 °C: 110 g
At 40 °C, 80 g of $\mathrm{KNO_3}$ was added to 100 g of water
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Example two requires reasoning. The solubility of potassium nitrate is given in a table. [2] At twenty degrees, thirty-two grams dissolve; at forty degrees, sixty-four grams; and at sixty degrees, one hundred ten grams. [3] Eighty grams of potassium nitrate were added to one hundred grams of water at forty degrees. Will all of it dissolve? And what will happen if the solution is then cooled to twenty degrees?

qadamlar.doska:
At 40 °C only 64 g dissolve: $80 - 64 = 16$ g do not dissolve
The solution is saturated: 64 g dissolved
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] At forty degrees, at most sixty-four grams dissolve, so eighty minus sixty-four, that is, sixteen grams, stay undissolved at the bottom of the container. [2] This solution is saturated: it holds the most substance that can dissolve at this temperature, sixty-four grams.

qadamlar.doska:
At 20 °C, 32 g dissolve: $64 - 32 = 32$ g crystallize out
Total solid at the bottom: $16 + 32 = 48$ g
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] If the solution is cooled to twenty degrees, only thirty-two grams can stay dissolved. Sixty-four minus thirty-two: another thirty-two grams settle out as crystals. [2] In total there will be sixteen plus thirty-two, that is, forty-eight grams of solid at the bottom of the container. Reading the table step by step is the key to success.

qadamlar.doska: The pH of lemon juice is 2. Is it an acid or a base?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Now you try: the pH of lemon juice is two. Is it an acid or a base? Write one word.
qadamlar.savol: Write one word: acid or base

qadamlar.doska: At 60 °C, at most how many g of $\mathrm{KNO_3}$ dissolve in 50 g of water?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] One more question: according to the table, how many grams of potassium nitrate, at most, dissolve in fifty grams of water at sixty degrees? Write the number.

qadamlar.sarlavha: How to solve an international question
qadamlar.doska:
1. In a table or graph, read the unit: “in 100 g of water”
2. If the mass of water is different, set up a proportion
3. pH: less than 7 is an acid, greater is a base
4. Explain the event with particles and properties
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] First: on a solubility table or graph, read the unit: the value is usually given for one hundred grams of water. [2] Second: if the water is not one hundred grams, decrease or increase the value proportionally. [3] Third: in a pH question, use seven as the boundary, and remember that in neutralization the pH approaches seven. [4] Fourth: for a “why” question, state the property clearly: for example, water expands when it freezes, so the rock cracks.

qadamlar.doska:
Physical property: substance unchanged; chemical: new substance
Solubility: per 100 g of water; often rises with temperature
pH < 7 acid, = 7 neutral, > 7 base
Water expands when it freezes: ice floats, rocks crack
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Remember: when a physical property is found, the substance does not change, while a chemical property has to do with turning into a new substance. [2] Solubility is given for one hundred grams of water, and for many solids it increases with temperature. [3] A pH less than seven means an acid, seven is neutral, and greater than seven is a base; an acid and a base neutralize each other. [4] Water expands when it freezes: that is why ice floats and rocks crack. You did excellent work today!

q1.doska:
Physical: found by looking or measuring
Chemical: found when the substance changes
q1.ovoz: A simple difference: you find a physical property by looking or measuring, but you find a chemical property when the substance turns into another substance.

q1.doska:
Paper is white and light: physical properties
Paper burns: a chemical property
q1.ovoz: Take a sheet from your notebook: its white color and lightness are physical properties. But it can burn and turn into ash. This is its chemical property.

q1.doska:
Ask: did a new substance appear?
No → physical;  yes → chemical
q1.ovoz: Each time, ask yourself: when this property was tested, did a new substance appear? If not, it is physical; if so, it is chemical.

q2.doska:
Sugar dissolves fast and in large amounts in hot tea
Less dissolves in cold tea
q2.ovoz: In hot tea, sugar dissolves quickly and in large amounts, but in cold tea it stays at the bottom: when the temperature rises, solubility increases.

q2.doska:
We left a soda in the sun
When we opened it, it foamed and the gas escaped
q2.ovoz: Sardor left a soda in the sun. When he opened it, it foamed up and the gas quickly escaped, because less gas dissolves in a warm liquid.

q2.doska:
A saturated solution is a “full bus”
There is no room for new passengers
q2.ovoz: Compare a saturated solution to a full bus: there is no room for any more passengers, and the extra substance stays undissolved at the bottom.

q3.doska:
Sour → acid
Soapy → base
Pure water → neutral
q3.ovoz: Remember with everyday examples: sour things are acids, soapy slippery things are bases, and pure water is neutral. But never taste chemicals!

q3.doska:
An ant sting: acid
Ammonia solution is applied: the base neutralizes it
q3.ovoz: When an ant stings, formic acid gets onto the skin and it burns. Sometimes diluted household ammonia, that is, ammonia solution, is applied to the spot: the base neutralizes the acid.

q3.doska:
Indicator: litmus paper
red → acid;  blue → base
q3.ovoz: Use an indicator: litmus paper turns red in an acid and blue in a base. A universal indicator shows the pH value by its color.

q4.doska:
Water → ice: the volume gets bigger
That is why ice floats on water
q4.ovoz: When water turns into ice, its volume gets bigger and it becomes lighter, so ice floats on the surface of water.

q4.doska:
A full glass jar in the freezer cracked
The frozen water had expanded
q4.ovoz: My mother put a full glass jar of water in the freezer and forgot about it. The next day the jar had cracked: the freezing water had expanded and broken the glass.

q4.doska:
In winter a lake freezes from the top
Fish stay alive under the ice
q4.ovoz: Look at nature: in winter a lake freezes from the top, because ice is lighter. Under the layer of ice the water stays liquid, and the fish can survive the winter.

tipik_xatolar: Forgetting that a solubility table is for 100 g of water and using the same number for a different mass
Thinking that all substances, including gases, dissolve better when it is warm
Thinking that in neutralization the pH can go even higher than the pH of the ammonia solution
Believing that water contracts when it freezes: in fact, it expands
Considering melting or dissolving to be a chemical property
strategiyalar: In a table or graph, first read the unit and the conditions
Write a multistep calculation step by step: dissolved, undissolved, settled out
In a pH question, use 7 as the boundary
For a “why” question, write the property and its effect together

maqsad: Distinguish physical and chemical changes, identify the signs of a chemical reaction, apply the law of conservation of mass, and explain exothermic and endothermic processes and the conditions for burning

qadamlar.doska:
Why does vinegar foam when we add baking soda?
TIMSS: on average 43% of grade 8 students answered correctly
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] In the kitchen, if you add baking soda to vinegar, it foams up vigorously. What is this, magic? No, it is a chemical reaction! [2] In the international TIMSS study, on average forty-three percent of students around the world answered questions on this topic correctly. Questions about the signs of a reaction and energy were especially hard, so we will study them thoroughly!

qadamlar.doska:
Physical change: the substance stays the same: melting, freezing, grinding
Chemical change: a NEW substance forms
Examples: burning, rusting, food rotting, bread baking
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] In a physical change, the substance stays itself; only its state or shape changes: ice melting, sugar dissolving in water, tearing paper. [2] In a chemical change, that is, a chemical reaction, a new substance with new properties forms. [3] For example, wood burning, iron rusting, and food spoiling are all chemical changes.

qadamlar.doska:
Gas given off (bubbles) and a color change
A precipitate forms, a smell appears
Heat or light given off or absorbed
Careful: bubbles in boiling water are a physical change!
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Signs of a chemical reaction: a gas is given off, that is, bubbles appear, and the color changes. [2] A precipitate forming in a solution or a new smell appearing are also signs of a reaction. [3] Heat or light being given off, or the opposite, the mixture getting colder, also shows that a reaction is taking place. [4] But be careful: the bubbles in boiling water are water vapor, not a new substance. So do not rely on a single sign; check whether a new substance has appeared.

qadamlar.sarlavha: The law of conservation of mass
qadamlar.doska:
Reactants → products
Atoms are not lost and do not appear from nothing
Mass of reactants = mass of products
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] The substances that react are called reactants, and the substances formed are called products. [2] In a reaction, atoms are not lost and do not appear from nothing; they are only rearranged. [3] That is why the mass of the substances that reacted equals the mass of the substances formed. This is the law of conservation of mass, discovered by Lomonosov and Lavoisier.

qadamlar.doska:
Exothermic: heat is GIVEN OFF: burning, respiration, rusting
Endothermic: energy is ABSORBED: photosynthesis, limestone
Burning needs: fuel + oxygen + high temperature
If one is removed, the fire goes out: a blanket blocks oxygen
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] In exothermic reactions, heat is given off: burning, cellular respiration, iron rusting. [2] In endothermic reactions, energy is absorbed: photosynthesis absorbs light energy, and limestone breaks down only when it is heated. [3] Burning needs three conditions: a fuel, oxygen, and heating to the ignition temperature. [4] If we remove one of them, the fire goes out. For example, if we cover something that is burning with a thick blanket, oxygen cannot get in and the fire goes out.

qadamlar.doska:
In an open glass: vinegar + baking soda = 200 g
After the foaming stops, the scale shows 198 g. Why?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Example one. Vinegar in an open glass and the baking soda to be added to it together weighed two hundred grams on a scale. [2] After the foaming stopped, the scale showed one hundred ninety-eight grams. Where did the mass go?

qadamlar.doska:
The bubbles are $\mathrm{CO_2}$ gas: a product of the reaction
The gas escaped from the open glass into the air: 2 g
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] The bubbles are carbon dioxide gas: it is a new substance formed in the reaction, so this is a chemical reaction. [2] Because the glass was open, this gas escaped into the air. The missing two grams are exactly this gas.

qadamlar.doska:
In a closed container the scale does not change: 200 g
Answer: mass is conserved; the gas escaped
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] If the experiment is done in a closed container, the gas cannot escape, and the scale stays at two hundred grams. [2] Answer: the mass was not lost; it went into the air as a gas. The law of conservation of mass is not broken!

qadamlar.doska:
A) ice melting;  B) a candle burning
C) iron rusting;  D) sugar dissolving in water
Which are chemical? In which is energy given off?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Example two requires reasoning. Four processes are given: ice melting and a candle burning. [2] Also, iron rusting and sugar dissolving in water. [3] Question: which of them are chemical reactions, and in which is energy given off?

qadamlar.doska:
A, D: physical: no new substance
B, C: chemical: $\mathrm{CO_2}$, water, rust form
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] When ice melts, it is still water, and when sugar dissolves, it is still sugar. These are physical changes. [2] When a candle burns, carbon dioxide and water form, and when iron rusts, rust forms. These are chemical reactions.

qadamlar.doska:
Energy is given off: B (heat, light), C (slowly)
A absorbs energy: melting ice needs heat
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] In B, energy is given off quickly as heat and light, while in C, heat is given off very slowly, so slowly that you cannot notice it. [2] Melting ice, on the other hand, absorbs heat, which is why ice cools its surroundings. In an energy question, remember that burning and rusting are exothermic.

qadamlar.doska: We covered a campfire with soil. Which gas stopped getting in?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Now you try: when we covered a campfire with soil, the fire went out. Which gas stopped getting in? Write the name of the gas.
qadamlar.savol: Write the name of the gas

qadamlar.doska: Is burning an exothermic or an endothermic reaction?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] One more question: is burning a reaction that gives off heat, that is, exothermic, or one that absorbs heat, that is, endothermic? Write one word.

qadamlar.sarlavha: How to solve an international question
qadamlar.doska:
1. The key question: did a new substance form?
2. Signs: gas, color, precipitate, smell, heat
3. If the mass decreases, look for gas that escaped
4. Heat given off: exo; absorbed: endo
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] First: for any change, ask yourself: did a new substance form? Then you will know whether it is physical or chemical. [2] Second: in an observation question, recall the list of signs of a reaction and find which one was observed. [3] Third: if the mass decreases in an open container, a gas has escaped; in a closed container the mass does not change. [4] Fourth: if the surroundings get warmer, it is exothermic; if they get colder, it is endothermic. Burning always gives off energy.

qadamlar.doska:
Chemical change = a new substance forms
Signs: gas, color, precipitate, smell, heat, light
Mass is conserved: atoms are only rearranged
Burning is exothermic; remove one condition and the fire goes out
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Remember: in a chemical change a new substance forms, while in a physical change the substance does not change. [2] The signs of a reaction are a gas, a color change, a precipitate, a smell, heat, and light. [3] Mass is conserved in a reaction, because atoms are only rearranged. [4] Burning is an exothermic reaction, and if we remove one of its three conditions, the fire goes out. Wonderful work, now you are a young chemist!

q1.doska:
Physical: the shape changes
Chemical: the substance changes
q1.ovoz: A simple difference: in a physical change only the shape or state changes, but in a chemical change the substance itself turns into a different substance.

q1.doska:
The ice cream melted: it can be frozen again
The egg was cooked: it will not become raw again
q1.ovoz: If ice cream melts, you can freeze it again: it is the same substance. But if you fry an egg, it will never become raw again, because the protein has turned into a new substance.

q1.doska:
Check: did the properties change?
New color, smell, flammability → chemical
q1.ovoz: Check it: if what forms has a completely new color, smell, or flammability, this is a chemical change.

q2.doska:
5 signs: gas, color, precipitate, smell, heat
Sign + new substance = reaction
q2.ovoz: Remember the five signs: gas, color, precipitate, smell, and heat. But the main thing is that a new substance appears.

q2.doska:
A cut apple turns brown
A color change is a sign of a reaction
q2.ovoz: If you cut an apple and leave it, after a while the cut surface turns brown. Substances in the apple have reacted with oxygen in the air, and the color change is the sign of this.

q2.doska:
A pair of experiments: boiling water and baking soda + vinegar
Bubbles in both, but only one is a reaction
q2.ovoz: Compare two experiments: bubbles appear both in boiling water and in baking soda with vinegar. But the bubbles in the water are just water vapor, while those from the baking soda are a new gas, carbon dioxide.

q3.doska:
We took apart a Lego castle and built a car
The number of bricks did not change
q3.ovoz: If you take apart a Lego castle and build a car from the same bricks, the number of bricks does not change. In a reaction, atoms are put back together in just the same way.

q3.doska:
The campfire burned, leaving a little ash
The rest of the mass went into the air as gas and vapor
q3.ovoz: When a big campfire burns out, only a little ash is left. The mass was not lost: most of it rose into the air as carbon dioxide and water vapor.

q3.doska:
Count the atoms: $\mathrm{C + O_2 \rightarrow CO_2}$
Left: 1 C, 2 O;  right: 1 C, 2 O
q3.ovoz: Check by counting the atoms: when carbon burns with oxygen, there is one carbon and two oxygens on the left side, and exactly the same on the right side. The atoms are equal, so the masses are equal too.

q4.doska:
Exo: outward (heat comes out)
Endo: inward (heat is absorbed)
q4.ovoz: The word itself helps: “exo” means outward, that is, heat comes out; “endo” means inward, that is, heat is absorbed.

q4.doska:
Oil caught fire in the kitchen
Mom covered it with a lid and the fire went out
q4.ovoz: One day the oil in a frying pan caught fire. My mother calmly covered the pan with a lid, and the fire went out: oxygen could no longer get in. Never pour water on burning oil!

q4.doska:
Fire triangle: fuel, oxygen, heat
If one side is removed, the triangle breaks
q4.ovoz: Draw a triangle: its three sides are fuel, oxygen, and heat. If you remove one side, the triangle breaks and the fire goes out: water cools it, and a blanket blocks oxygen.

tipik_xatolar: Thinking that any bubbles mean a chemical reaction: the bubbles in boiling are water vapor
Considering sugar dissolving in water to be a chemical reaction
Thinking mass has disappeared if it decreases in an open container: a gas has escaped
Thinking that burning absorbs energy: burning is exothermic
Thinking a blanket puts out a fire by “pressing” on it: it blocks oxygen
strategiyalar: For every change, ask “did a new substance form?”
In an observation question, use the list of signs of a reaction
If the mass changes, check whether the container was open or closed
In an energy question, check whether the surroundings get warmer or colder

maqsad: Explain solids, liquids and gases in terms of particles, recognize changes of state (melting, freezing, evaporation, condensation), and determine what changes and what stays the same during them

qadamlar.doska:
Drops on the outside of a cold glass — where do they come from?
TIMSS: on average 50% of grade 8 students answered correctly
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] In summer, have you ever seen drops appear on the outside of a glass filled with ice-cold lemonade? Where do you think they come from? [2] In the international TIMSS study, on average fifty percent of eighth graders around the world answered questions on this topic correctly. By the end of the lesson, you will be able to solve such questions with confidence!

qadamlar.doska:
Solid: keeps its shape and volume
Liquid: keeps its volume, takes the shape of the container
Gas: keeps neither shape nor volume
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] In a solid, the particles are very close together and vibrate in place, so it keeps both its shape and its volume. [2] In a liquid, the particles are close together but can slide past one another, so it takes the shape of its container. [3] In a gas, the particles are far apart and move quickly, so a gas fills the whole container.

qadamlar.doska:
Melting: solid → liquid;  freezing: liquid → solid
Evaporation: liquid → gas;  condensation: gas → liquid
Temperature does not change during melting and boiling
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Ice melts and turns into water; if water is cooled, it freezes and turns back into ice. [2] A puddle evaporates in the sun, and water vapor in the air condenses on a cold surface and forms drops. [3] While a pure substance is melting or boiling, its temperature stays the same until the change of state is complete, even though it keeps taking in heat.

qadamlar.sarlavha: What changes and what stays the same?
qadamlar.doska:
Stays the same: mass, type of substance, number of particles
Changes: distance between particles, volume, density
This is a physical change
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] When the state changes, the substance does not turn into a different substance: a water molecule is still a water molecule in ice and in vapor, and the mass does not change either. [2] What changes is the distance between the particles and how they move, so the volume and density change. [3] Because no new substance is formed, a change of state is a physical change, not a chemical one.

qadamlar.doska:
Air contains invisible water vapor
It touches a cold surface → water drops
Water does not seep through the wall of the glass!
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] The air we breathe always contains water vapor that we cannot see. [2] When the vapor touches the cold glass, it cools, condenses and collects as drops on the outside of the glass. [3] The glass wall does not let water through, so the drops are not the water from inside but vapor from the air.

qadamlar.doska: 200 g of ice melted. What are the mass and volume of the water?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Let's read the problem: two hundred grams of ice melted completely; we need to find the mass and volume of the water formed.

qadamlar.doska:
Mass is conserved: $m = 200$ g
Ice: $V = \frac{200}{0.9} \approx 222$ cm³
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] When the state changes, mass is conserved, so the water also has a mass of two hundred grams. [2] The density of ice is about zero point nine grams per cubic centimeter, so the volume of the ice was about two hundred twenty-two cubic centimeters.

qadamlar.doska: Water: $V = \frac{200}{1} = 200$ cm³ — the volume decreased
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] The density of water is one gram per cubic centimeter, so the volume of the water is two hundred cubic centimeters: the mass did not change, but the volume became smaller.

qadamlar.doska: Drops on the outside of a glass of iced juice
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Now a TIMSS-style problem: Ali says the iced juice in the glass seeped out through the wall. How can we check this?

qadamlar.doska:
Hypothesis 1: the juice seeped through the wall
Hypothesis 2: vapor in the air condensed
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] If Ali is right, the drops should be colored and sweet like the juice. [2] If the drops come from the air, they will be colorless, ordinary water.

qadamlar.doska:
Experiment: the drops are colorless → from the air
No drops on a glass of warm water
Answer: vapor condenses on a cold surface
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] When we check, the drops turn out to be colorless and tasteless, so the second hypothesis is correct. [2] If we pour warm water into the same glass, no drops appear: so the cause is the coldness of the glass. [3] A complete answer is written like this: water vapor in the air cools on the surface of the cold glass and condenses into drops.

qadamlar.doska: What is it called when water vapor turns into a liquid?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Now answer on your own: what is the process called in which water vapor, a gas, turns into liquid water? Write one word.
qadamlar.savol: Write the name of the process

qadamlar.doska: 50 g of water evaporated completely. What is the mass of the vapor in g?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Fifty grams of water turned completely into vapor in a closed container. What is the mass of the vapor formed, in grams? Write only the number.

qadamlar.sarlavha: How to solve the international question
qadamlar.doska:
1. From which state to which state did it change?
2. Mass and type of substance — stay the same
3. Where do the drops come from? — don't forget the vapor in the air
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] In an international question, first determine which state the substance changed from and to, and name the process. [2] In a question about what does not change, remember: mass and type of substance always stay the same. [3] The question about drops on a cold surface is the hardest part; only seven percent of students worldwide answered it fully: in your answer, mention both the vapor in the air and the cooling.

qadamlar.doska:
Solid — liquid — gas: the distance between particles differs
Melting, freezing, evaporation, condensation
Mass is conserved, volume and density change
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] The difference between the three states lies in the distance between the particles and how they move. [2] Remember the names and directions of the four main processes. [3] When the state changes, mass is conserved, while volume and density change — this is a physical change.

q1.doska:
Solid — standing in tight rows
Liquid — moving in a crowd
Gas — running around a field
q1.ovoz: Imagine the particles are students: in a solid they stand still in rows, in a liquid they move around one another in a crowd, and in a gas they run freely around a big field.

q1.doska: Ice, water, vapor — one substance
q1.ovoz: You put ice into a kettle: first it is a solid lump, then water in the shape of the kettle, and when it boils it spreads through the whole kitchen as vapor. The substance is the same; only the arrangement of the particles has changed.

q1.doska:
Shape? Volume?
Solid: yes, yes
Liquid: no, yes · Gas: no, no
q1.ovoz: Ask two questions: does it keep its shape, and does it keep its volume? Solid — yes to both, liquid — yes only to volume, gas — no to both.

q2.doska:
Add heat: solid → liquid → gas
Cool: gas → liquid → solid
q2.ovoz: When heated, a substance “loosens up” and changes from solid to liquid and from liquid to gas. When cooled, it goes back the opposite way.

q2.doska:
Laundry dried — evaporation
Window fogged up — condensation
q2.ovoz: Wet laundry dries in the sun — the water evaporated. In winter, a cold window in a warm room fogs up — the vapor in the room condensed.

q2.doska: Graph: temperature ↑, flat part during melting, then ↑
q2.ovoz: If we heat ice and plot its temperature on a graph, the line is horizontal during melting: the heat goes into freeing the particles, while the temperature stays the same.

q3.doska: We took apart a Lego house: the number of bricks is the same
q3.ovoz: If we take apart a Lego house and put the bricks in a box, the shape changes, but the number and weight of the bricks stay the same. A change of state works the same way.

q3.doska: The ice melted: the scale reading did not change
q3.ovoz: If we weigh ice in a closed jar on a scale and wait until it melts, the scale reading does not change: the mass was conserved.

q3.doska:
Physical: same substance
Chemical: new substance
q3.ovoz: Ask: was a new substance formed? If not, it is a physical change. Ice melting is a physical change, but paper burning is a chemical change.

q4.doska: Air + cold surface = drops
q4.ovoz: Air contains invisible vapor. When it touches something cold, it turns into water. That is why drops appear only on a cold glass.

q4.doska: A cold bathroom mirror fogs up
q4.ovoz: After a hot shower, the bathroom mirror fogs up: no water came out of the mirror; the vapor in the air turned into drops on the cold mirror.

q4.doska: Even an empty cold glass fogs up
q4.ovoz: Even if you take an empty glass out of the refrigerator, its surface fogs up. There is no water inside, so the drops can only come from the air.

tipik_xatolar: Thinking that the drops on the surface of a cold glass are water that seeped out from inside
Believing that mass decreases or increases during melting or evaporation
Thinking that the molecules themselves get bigger or change when the state changes
Thinking that the temperature keeps rising during boiling
strategiyalar: First identify the starting and final states, then name the process
In a question about what stays the same, choose mass and type of substance
In an open-response question, write both the cause and the result (vapor + cold surface → drops)

maqsad: Follow types of energy and how they change from one to another, relate temperature to particle motion, and learn about thermal expansion, heat transfer and designing a fair test

qadamlar.doska:
Why are there gaps between railroad rails?
TIMSS: on average 37% of grade 8 students answered correctly
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Have you noticed the small gaps left between railroad rails? Today we will find out why, and how energy changes from one form to another. [2] In the international TIMSS study, on average thirty-seven percent of eighth graders around the world answered questions on this topic correctly. By the end of the lesson, you will be able to solve such questions with confidence!

qadamlar.sarlavha: Types of energy and energy transformations
qadamlar.doska:
Kinetic — motion, potential — height
Chemical, electrical, thermal, light
Energy is not lost — it changes from one form to another
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] A moving object has kinetic energy, and an object at a height has potential energy. [2] Batteries and food contain chemical energy, which can change into electrical, thermal or light energy. [3] The law of conservation of energy: energy cannot be created from nothing or destroyed; it only changes from one form to another.

qadamlar.doska:
When heated: particles move faster
The distance between particles increases → the object expands
The particles themselves do not get bigger!
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Temperature is a measure of how fast the particles are moving: when we heat something, they speed up. [2] Faster-moving particles move farther apart, so the object expands; the gaps between rails leave room for expansion in summer. [3] Pay attention: the size of the molecules does not change; only the distance between them increases.

qadamlar.doska:
Heat: from a hot object to a cold object
Conduction: metal is good, wood is poor
Convection — in liquids and gases; radiation — the Sun
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Heat always flows from a hotter object to a colder one until their temperatures are equal. [2] Copper and iron conduct heat well, while wood, plastic and air conduct it poorly — they are thermal insulators. [3] In liquids and gases, heat is carried by currents, that is, by convection, and from the Sun it comes by radiation.

qadamlar.doska:
$Q = c\,m\,\Delta t$
For water $c = 4200$ J/(kg·°C)
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] The amount of heat needed to heat an object equals the product of the specific heat capacity, the mass and the change in temperature. [2] The specific heat capacity of water is four thousand two hundred joules per kilogram per degree, which is a very large value.

qadamlar.doska: 2 kg of water was heated from 20 °C to 70 °C. $Q$ = ?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Problem: we heat two kilograms of water from twenty degrees to seventy degrees. How much heat is needed?

[1] First we find the change in temperature: seventy minus twenty is fifty degrees. [2] We substitute into the formula: four thousand two hundred times two times fifty gives four hundred twenty thousand joules. [3] This equals four hundred twenty kilojoules.

qadamlar.doska: Water from a high tank pours onto a wheel
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Now a TIMSS-style problem: water falling from a high tank turns a wheel. How does the energy change, and how can the wheel be made to turn faster?

qadamlar.doska:
In the tank: potential energy ($E = mgh$)
While falling: potential → kinetic
At the wheel: kinetic → rotational energy
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] The water in the tank has potential energy because it is high up; only seventeen percent of students worldwide answered this question correctly. [2] As the water falls, its potential energy decreases and its energy of motion, that is, kinetic energy, increases. [3] The water hits the paddles of the wheel and gives its kinetic energy to the wheel.

qadamlar.doska:
10 kg, $h = 2$ m: $E = 10 \cdot 10 \cdot 2 = 200$ J
$h = 4$ m: $E = 400$ J — twice as much
Conclusion: place the tank higher or use more water
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Let's calculate: ten kilograms of water at a height of two meters, taking g as ten, has two hundred joules of energy. [2] If we raise the tank to four meters, the energy becomes four hundred joules, that is, it doubles. [3] So, to make the wheel turn faster, we need to place the tank higher or let more water flow.

qadamlar.doska: How many J are needed to heat 1 kg of water by 10 °C?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Use the formula: how many joules of heat are needed to heat one kilogram of water by ten degrees? Write the number.

qadamlar.doska: Pot handle: metal or plastic?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] So that a pot handle does not burn your hand, it should conduct heat poorly. What material should it be made of? Write one word.

qadamlar.sarlavha: How to solve the international question
qadamlar.doska:
1. Write the energy chain: from where → to where
2. In an experiment, only one thing changes
3. In a heated container, the liquid level rises
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] In an energy question, write the start and the end with arrows, for example in a flashlight: chemical, electrical, light and heat. [2] In a question about an experiment, remember the rule of a fair test: one variable changes, and all the others are kept the same. [3] One of the hardest questions: the liquid in a heated container expands and its level rises; only thirteen percent of students answered it correctly.

qadamlar.doska:
Energy changes from one form to another and is conserved
Heating → particles speed up → expansion
Heat flows from hot to cold; $Q = c\,m\,\Delta t$
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Energy is not lost; it only changes its form. [2] When the temperature rises, the particles speed up and move apart, and the object expands. [3] Heat flows from a hot object to a cold one, and we calculate its amount with the formula.

q1.doska: Height → motion → work
q1.ovoz: If you carry a stone up high, potential energy is stored in it. If you let it go, it falls and starts moving — the energy changes into kinetic energy.

q1.doska: Flashlight: battery → current → light + heat
q1.ovoz: You turned on a flashlight: the chemical energy in the battery changes into electrical energy, and in the bulb into light and a little heat. That is why the bulb gets warm.

q1.doska: Energy is like money: it moves from account to account
q1.ovoz: Think of energy as money: it moves from one wallet to another, but the total amount does not decrease.

q2.doska: Hot — the particles “dance”
q2.ovoz: When heated, the particles “dance” faster and take up more space. They themselves do not get bigger.

q2.doska: A glass jar lid opens in hot water
q2.ovoz: If a lid is stuck, you hold it under hot water: the metal lid expands more than the glass and opens easily.

q2.doska: Thermometer: the alcohol expands and rises
q2.ovoz: The liquid in a thermometer expands when heated and rises in the tube — a way to see expansion with your own eyes.

q3.doska: Hot tea → cold spoon
q3.ovoz: If you put a spoon in hot tea, the spoon gets warm: heat moved from the tea to the spoon.

q3.doska: Metal and wooden benches in winter
q3.ovoz: In winter, a metal bench feels colder than a wooden one, even though they are at the same temperature: the metal carries heat away from your hand faster.

q3.doska: Copper rod: the wax pieces fall off one after another
q3.ovoz: If we stick small pins to a copper rod with wax and heat one end, first the nearest one falls, then the farther ones: heat travels along the rod.

q4.doska: More water, more heating → more heat
q4.ovoz: The greater the mass and the more we raise the temperature, the more heat is needed.

q4.doska: A big pot boils more slowly than a small kettle
q4.ovoz: On the same stove, the water in a big pot boils much later than the water in a small kettle, because it needs more heat.

q4.doska: 1 kg of water, 1 °C → 4200 J
q4.ovoz: The key benchmark: heating one kilogram of water by one degree takes four thousand two hundred joules. You find the rest by multiplying from this.

tipik_xatolar: Thinking that the molecules themselves get bigger when heated
Calling the energy of water high up kinetic (it is actually potential)
Thinking that cold also “flows” from one object to another, like heat
Changing two variables at the same time in an experiment
Using the final temperature instead of $\Delta t$ in $Q = c\,m\,\Delta t$
strategiyalar: Write energy transformations as a chain with arrows
In a fair test, separate the variable that changes from the ones that stay the same
When drawing a conclusion from a graph, first read the axis labels and units

maqsad: Understand that light travels in straight lines and is reflected and refracted, that sound is a vibration and needs a medium to travel, and compare the speeds of light and sound

qadamlar.doska:
Lightning is seen first, thunder is heard later
TIMSS: on average 28% of grade 8 students answered correctly
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] During a thunderstorm, you see the lightning first and hear the rumble a few seconds later. Why is that? [2] In the international TIMSS study, on average twenty-eight percent of eighth graders around the world answered questions on this topic correctly. By the end of the lesson, you will be able to solve such questions with confidence!

qadamlar.doska:
In a uniform medium — along a straight line
In a vacuum $\approx 300\,000$ km/s — the fastest
In water $\approx 225\,000$, in glass $\approx 200\,000$ km/s
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] In a uniform medium, light travels in a straight line, which is why shadows form. [2] Light is fastest in a vacuum — about three hundred thousand kilometers per second, and almost the same in air. [3] In water, light is slower, about two hundred twenty-five thousand kilometers per second, and in glass about two hundred thousand kilometers per second.

qadamlar.doska:
Angle of incidence = angle of reflection
Periscope: two mirrors at 45°
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] When a ray is reflected by a mirror, the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection; the angles are measured from the line perpendicular to the surface, called the normal. [2] In a periscope, two mirrors are placed parallel at an angle of forty-five degrees: the ray is turned downward by the first one and toward the eye by the second.

qadamlar.doska:
When the medium changes, speed and direction change
A spoon in water looks “broken”
A lens refracts rays and focuses or spreads them
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] When light passes from air into water or glass, its speed changes, and so its direction bends. [2] A spoon in a glass looking broken at the water surface is the result of refraction. [3] A convex lens focuses rays at one point, while a concave lens spreads them out.

qadamlar.doska:
Sound is the vibration of an object
It needs a medium to travel; none in a vacuum
In air $\approx 340$ m/s, in water $\approx 1500$ m/s
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Every sound comes from a vibrating object: a guitar string, a bell, the vocal cords. [2] Sound is passed on through the particles of air, water or a solid, and it does not travel at all in a vacuum. [3] In air, sound travels about three hundred forty meters per second, in water one thousand five hundred meters per second, and in solids even faster.

qadamlar.doska: Thunder was heard 3 s after the lightning. Distance?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Problem: you saw the lightning and heard the rumble three seconds later. How far away is the lightning?

qadamlar.doska:
The time for light is tiny — we ignore it
$s = v \cdot t = 340 \cdot 3 = 1020$ m
Answer: about 1 km
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Light covers one kilometer in a few millionths of a second, so we can ignore its time. [2] We multiply the speed of sound by the time: three hundred forty times three is one thousand twenty meters. [3] So the lightning struck about one kilometer away.

qadamlar.doska: A bell ringing inside a glass jar
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] A TIMSS-style problem: an electric bell is ringing inside a glass jar, and the air is pumped out of the jar. What do we hear and see?

qadamlar.doska:
As the air decreases, the sound gets fainter
The hammer can still be seen striking
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] As the air is pumped out, there are fewer particles to carry the sound, so the sound gets quieter and quieter until it can hardly be heard. [2] But the bell's hammer can clearly be seen striking, because light travels even through a vacuum.

qadamlar.doska:
Conclusion: sound needs a medium, light does not
If the air is let back in, the sound is heard again
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] A complete answer has two parts: sound needs air to travel, but light does not need a medium. [2] To check, we let the air back in: the sound is heard again, so the cause really was the air.

qadamlar.doska: A ray hits a mirror at 30° to the normal. Angle of reflection?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] A ray strikes a mirror at an angle of thirty degrees to the normal. What is the angle of reflection in degrees? Write the number.

qadamlar.doska: How many meters does sound travel in air in 2 s?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Sound travels in air at three hundred forty meters per second. How many meters does it travel in two seconds? Write the number.

qadamlar.sarlavha: How to solve the international question
qadamlar.doska:
1. Light or sound? Identify the medium
2. Draw the path of the ray straight with a ruler
3. In a vacuum: light yes, sound no
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] In an international question, first identify which phenomenon it is about and which medium the light or sound is passing through. [2] In a periscope or mirror question, draw the path of the ray with straight lines and check that the angles are equal at each mirror. [3] Twenty-two percent of students worldwide answered the question about the bell in the jar correctly: in your answer, write both parts — it can be seen but not heard.

qadamlar.doska:
Light travels in straight lines, is reflected and refracted
Angle of incidence = angle of reflection
Sound is a vibration, needs a medium, slower than light
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Light travels in a straight line, is reflected by a mirror and is refracted at the boundary between media. [2] Always apply the law of reflection relative to the normal. [3] Sound comes from vibration, does not travel without a medium and is much slower than light.

q1.doska:
A flashlight beam is a straight line
Obstacle → shadow
q1.ovoz: In the dark, a flashlight beam goes in a straight line. If you put your hand in its way, a shadow appears behind it — the light does not bend around.

q1.doska: Sunlight reaches Earth in ~8 minutes
q1.ovoz: It is one hundred fifty million kilometers from the Sun to Earth, but light covers that distance in only eight minutes — that is how fast it is.

q1.doska: Speed: vacuum > air > water > glass
q1.ovoz: Remember the order: fastest in a vacuum, almost the same in air, slower in water and even slower in glass.

q2.doska: A ball hitting a wall at an angle bounces back the same way
q2.ovoz: If you throw a ball at a wall at an angle, it bounces off at the same angle. Light reflects from a mirror in the same way.

q2.doska: A submarine periscope
q2.ovoz: A sailor in a submarine sees above the water through a periscope: the upper mirror turns the light downward, and the lower one turns it into his eye.

q2.doska: Mirror at 45° → the ray turns by 90°
q2.ovoz: If a mirror is placed at forty-five degrees to a ray, the ray turns through a right angle. Two such mirrors turn the ray back to its original direction.

q3.doska: A cart going from a fast road onto sand turns
q3.ovoz: When a cart rolls from asphalt onto sand at an angle, one wheel slows down first and the cart turns. Light turns in the same way when it passes into a slower medium.

q3.doska: The bottom of a pool looks shallower
q3.ovoz: The bottom of a pool looks shallower than it really is, because the light coming out of the water is refracted. That is why you should be careful when getting into the water.

q3.doska: A magnifying glass is a convex lens
q3.ovoz: With a magnifying glass, you can focus sunlight onto one point on a piece of paper — a convex lens refracts rays and brings them together.

q4.doska: String vibrates → air vibrates → ear
q4.ovoz: A guitar string vibrates, it makes the air vibrate, and the air makes the eardrum in our ear vibrate — that is how we hear.

q4.doska: In space, astronauts talk by radio
q4.ovoz: There is no air in open space, so astronauts cannot hear each other's voices and talk by radio.

q4.doska: Put your ear to the table
q4.ovoz: If you tap gently on one end of a table and put your ear to the other end, the sound is heard more clearly than through the air: solids carry sound well.

tipik_xatolar: Thinking that sound also travels in a vacuum
Thinking that light travels faster in water and glass than in air
Measuring the angle from the mirror surface (it should be measured from the normal)
In the jar question, writing only “no sound is heard” without giving the reason
strategiyalar: When drawing the path of a ray, check that the angles are equal at each reflection
In a sound question, ask: “Is there a medium?”
When comparing speeds, remember the order: vacuum > air > water > glass (for light)

maqsad: Understand a simple electric circuit, tell series and parallel connections apart, apply Ohm's law, and learn how magnetic poles interact and how to identify a magnet

qadamlar.doska:
Two iron bars: which one is a magnet?
TIMSS: on average 38% of grade 8 students answered correctly
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] You have two identical iron bars in your hands; one is a magnet and the other is not. Using only the bars themselves, how can you tell which one is the magnet? [2] In the international TIMSS study, on average thirty-eight percent of eighth graders around the world answered questions on this topic correctly. By the end of the lesson, you will be able to solve such questions with confidence!

qadamlar.doska:
Source + conductor + device + switch
Current flows only if the circuit is closed
Conductor: metal · insulator: plastic, glass
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] The simplest circuit consists of a power source, wires, a device such as a bulb, and a switch. [2] Current flows only in a closed, unbroken circuit; if the switch is opened, the bulb goes out. [3] Metals conduct current well, while plastic, rubber and glass do not conduct it; they are insulators.

qadamlar.doska:
$I = \frac{U}{R}$
$I$ — ampere (A), $U$ — volt (V), $R$ — ohm (Ω)
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Current is directly proportional to voltage and inversely proportional to resistance: we divide the voltage by the resistance. [2] Current is measured in amperes, voltage in volts, and resistance in ohms.

qadamlar.doska:
Series: one path, $R = R_1 + R_2$
If one bulb breaks, all go out
Parallel: a separate path for each bulb
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] In a series connection, the current flows along one path, the resistances add up, and the current is the same everywhere. [2] That is why, in a series circuit, if one bulb burns out, the circuit is broken and the others go out too. [3] In a parallel connection, each bulb has its own branch; if one burns out, the others stay lit; the outlets in a house are connected this way.

qadamlar.doska:
Two poles: N and S
Like poles repel, unlike poles attract
A coil with current is an electromagnet
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Every magnet has two poles, north and south; they cannot be separated. [2] Two north poles repel each other, while a north and a south pole attract; iron, nickel and cobalt are attracted to a magnet. [3] A magnetic field forms around a wire carrying current; the more turns and the greater the current, the stronger the electromagnet.

qadamlar.doska: 4.5 V battery, bulb $R = 9$ Ω. $I$ = ?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Problem: a bulb with a resistance of nine ohms is connected to a battery with a voltage of four point five volts. Let's find the current.

qadamlar.doska:
$I = \frac{4.5}{9} = 0.5$ A
Two bulbs in series: $R = 9 + 9 = 18$ Ω
$I = \frac{4.5}{18} = 0.25$ A — the current decreased
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] By Ohm's law, we divide four point five by nine and get zero point five amperes. [2] Now we connect two such bulbs in series: the resistances add up to eighteen ohms. [3] The current dropped to zero point two five amperes, so the bulbs glow more dimly.

qadamlar.doska: Bar A and bar B: which one is a magnet?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Now let's return to the opening question: using only the two bars, we need to find the magnet; twenty-eight percent of students worldwide answered this question correctly.

qadamlar.doska:
Attraction is not yet proof!
Repulsion — only if both objects are magnets
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] If the bars attract each other, this proves nothing: a magnet also attracts ordinary iron. [2] Repulsion happens only between two magnets, so it is reliable evidence.

qadamlar.doska:
Touch the end of A to the middle of B
Strong attraction → A is the magnet; no attraction → B is the magnet
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Method: bring the end of bar A close to the middle of bar B; the middle of a magnet hardly attracts at all. [2] If A attracts strongly, A is the magnet; if there is almost no attraction, then the magnet is B, because we brought A close to its middle.

qadamlar.doska: $U = 6$ V, $R = 3$ Ω. What is the current in amperes?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Use Ohm's law: the voltage is six volts and the resistance is three ohms. What is the current in amperes? Write the number.

qadamlar.doska: Three bulbs in series, one burned out. How many stay lit?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Three bulbs are connected in series, and one of them burned out. How many bulbs stay lit? Write the number.

qadamlar.sarlavha: How to solve the international question
qadamlar.doska:
1. Trace the circuit with your finger
2. Series or parallel — count the branches
3. When comparing magnet strength — a fair test
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] In a circuit question, follow the path of the current with your finger, starting from the source: if the path is broken, there is no current. [2] Check whether there are branches: if there is one path, it is series; if there are several, it is parallel. [3] When comparing the strength of magnets, use the same distance and the same pins, and let only the magnet change.

qadamlar.doska:
Current flows only in a closed circuit; $I = \frac{U}{R}$
Series: if one breaks, all go out
Repulsion is the reliable sign of a magnet
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Current flows in a closed circuit and is calculated with Ohm's law. [2] In a series connection there is one path; in parallel, each has its own path. [3] Like poles repel; when identifying a magnet, only repulsion is reliable evidence.

q1.doska: A circuit is a loop: if it breaks, the current stops
q1.ovoz: Imagine a circuit as a closed loop. If the loop is broken in one place, the current cannot flow around it and the bulb goes out.

q1.doska: A light switch opens and closes the circuit
q1.ovoz: When you press the light switch in a room, it closes or opens the circuit. When the switch is off, the circuit is open.

q1.doska: Current is like water flowing in a pipe
q1.ovoz: The battery is a pump, the wires are a pipe, and the bulb is a wheel turned by the water. If the pipe is broken, the water does not flow.

q2.doska: Voltage ↑ → current ↑; resistance ↑ → current ↓
q2.ovoz: If we increase the voltage, the current increases; if we increase the resistance, the current decreases.

q2.doska: Cars move slowly along a narrow street
q2.ovoz: Think of resistance as a narrow street: the narrower the street, the fewer cars get through in a minute.

q2.doska: Triangle: U on top, I and R at the bottom
q2.ovoz: Write U at the top and I and R at the bottom. If you need I, divide U by R; if you need U, multiply I by R.

q3.doska: Series — one path; parallel — many paths
q3.ovoz: Series is a single lane: if one person stops, everyone stops. Parallel is several lanes: if one is closed, the others keep working.

q3.doska: Holiday tree lights and house lights
q3.ovoz: In an old string of holiday tree lights, if one bulb burned out, they all went out — they were connected in series. At home, if the light in one room burns out, the others stay on — they are connected in parallel.

q3.doska: Draw a diagram: are there branches?
q3.ovoz: If there is a place in the diagram where the wire splits in two, it is a parallel connection. If it never splits, it is series.

q4.doska: Like poles repel, unlike poles attract
q4.ovoz: If you bring like poles of two magnets close together, they push away; unlike poles stick together.

q4.doska: A compass needle is a small magnet
q4.ovoz: A compass needle is a small magnet; it points north along Earth's magnetic field. If you bring a magnet near it, the needle turns.

q4.doska: Nail + wire + battery = electromagnet
q4.ovoz: If you wrap insulated wire around an iron nail and connect the ends to a battery, the nail starts to attract pins. If you disconnect the current, they fall off.

tipik_xatolar: Taking attraction as proof that both objects are magnets
Thinking that in a series connection, if one bulb burns out, the others stay lit
In Ohm's law, dividing the resistance by the voltage instead of the voltage by the resistance
Thinking that all metals are attracted to a magnet (aluminum and copper are not)
strategiyalar: Follow the path of the current in a circuit, starting from the source
When identifying a magnet, accept only repulsion as evidence
Before calculating, write down the units: A, V, Ω

maqsad: Understand force, gravity and balanced forces, calculate speed, pressure and density, and apply atmospheric pressure and the conditions for floating to real-life situations

qadamlar.doska:
A bottle closed on a mountain gets crushed in the valley
TIMSS: on average 32% of grade 8 students answered correctly
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] If you screw the cap tightly onto an empty plastic bottle at the top of a mountain and then go down into the valley, the bottle gets crushed. Today we will uncover the secret. [2] In the international TIMSS study, on average thirty-two percent of eighth graders around the world answered questions on this topic correctly. By the end of the lesson, you will be able to solve such questions with confidence!

qadamlar.doska:
A force is a push or a pull, unit N
Gravity always acts downward: $F = mg$
If the forces are equal, the speed does not change
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] A force changes the speed or shape of an object and is measured in newtons. [2] Earth pulls every object toward itself; this force always points downward, and we take g as about ten newtons per kilogram. [3] If opposite forces are equal, the object stays at rest or moves at a constant speed; this is how a parachutist falls steadily.

qadamlar.doska:
$v = \frac{s}{t}$
Units: m/s or km/h
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Speed is the distance traveled per unit of time: we divide the distance by the time. [2] Speed is measured in meters per second or kilometers per hour.

qadamlar.doska:
$p = \frac{F}{S}$, unit Pa
Small area → large pressure
Air pressure decreases as altitude increases
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Pressure is the ratio of the force acting perpendicular to a surface to the area of that surface; it is measured in pascals. [2] That is why a sharp knife cuts well, and why we do not sink into the snow on wide skis. [3] The weight of the layer of air above us creates atmospheric pressure; in the mountains this layer is thinner, so the pressure is lower.

qadamlar.doska:
$\rho = \frac{m}{V}$
$\rho_{object} < \rho_{liquid}$ (object less dense than liquid) → floats
The liquid pushes the object upward — the buoyant force
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Density is the ratio of the mass of a substance to its volume. [2] If the density of an object is less than the density of the liquid, it floats; if it is greater, it sinks. [3] The force with which a liquid pushes a submerged object upward is called the buoyant force, or Archimedes' force.

qadamlar.doska: Object: $m = 60$ g, $V = 50$ cm³. In which liquid does it float?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Problem: there is an object with a mass of sixty grams and a volume of fifty cubic centimeters. In which of these does it float: alcohol, water or glycerin?

qadamlar.doska:
$\rho = \frac{60}{50} = 1.2$ g/cm³
Alcohol 0.8 · water 1.0 · glycerin 1.26
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] First we find the density of the object: sixty divided by fifty is one point two grams per cubic centimeter. [2] Now we write the densities of the liquids: alcohol zero point eight, water one, glycerin one point two six.

qadamlar.doska:
$1.2 > 1.0$ → sinks in water
$1.2 < 1.26$ → floats in glycerin
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] The density of the object is greater than that of water, so it sinks in both water and alcohol. [2] The density of glycerin is greater than that of the object, so the object floats only in glycerin.

qadamlar.doska: A bottle closed on a peak got crushed in the valley. Why?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Now let's solve the opening problem step by step; thirty-three percent of students worldwide answered it correctly.

qadamlar.doska:
On the peak: pressure inside = pressure outside (low)
In the valley: pressure outside is higher
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] When we closed the cap on the peak, the air pressure inside the bottle was equal to the pressure of the thin air outside. [2] As we go down, the outside atmospheric pressure increases, but the air inside does not increase because the bottle is closed.

qadamlar.doska:
Pressure outside > pressure inside → the bottle is crushed
If the cap is opened, air enters and the shape is restored
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] The greater pressure outside pushes the walls of the bottle inward, and it gets crushed. [2] If we open the cap, air comes in, the pressures become equal and the bottle returns to its shape.

qadamlar.doska: A bus traveled 120 km in 2 hours. Speed in km/h?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] A bus traveled one hundred twenty kilometers in two hours. What was its average speed in kilometers per hour? Write the number.

qadamlar.doska: A cube has a density of 0.8 g/cm³. Does it float or sink in water?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] The density of the cube is zero point eight grams per cubic centimeter, and the density of water is one. Does the cube float or sink in water? Write one word.

qadamlar.sarlavha: How to solve the international question
qadamlar.doska:
1. Draw the forces as arrows
2. Floating: compare the two densities
3. Pressure: compare the inside and outside pressure
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] In a question about forces, draw all the forces acting on the object as arrows; gravity always points downward and never disappears. [2] In a floating question, first calculate the density of the object, then compare it with the density of each liquid. [3] In questions about bottles, balloons or ear pain, write the inside and outside pressures separately and compare them.

qadamlar.doska:
Gravity always acts downward; equal forces → speed does not change
$v = \frac{s}{t}$, $p = \frac{F}{S}$, $\rho = \frac{m}{V}$
Pressure is lower at altitude; an object with lower density floats
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Gravity always acts; if the forces are equal, the motion is steady. [2] Remember the three main formulas together with their units. [3] Air pressure decreases as you go higher, and an object with a density lower than the liquid's floats.

q1.doska: Tug-of-war: equal forces → nobody moves
q1.ovoz: In a tug-of-war, if the two teams pull with equal force, the rope does not move. That is balanced forces.

q1.doska: The parachute opened: air resistance = weight
q1.ovoz: When a parachutist jumps, gravity pulls them downward. After the parachute opens, air resistance increases until it equals the weight, and the parachutist falls at a constant speed. But gravity has not disappeared!

q1.doska: Force diagram: ↓ weight, ↑ resistance
q1.ovoz: Draw the object as a dot, with a weight arrow pointing down and a resistance arrow pointing up. If the arrows are equal, the speed does not change.

q2.doska: 60 km every hour → speed 60 km/h
q2.ovoz: If a car travels sixty kilometers every hour, its speed is sixty kilometers per hour. That is what dividing distance by time means.

q2.doska: 600 m to school in 10 minutes
q2.ovoz: If you walk six hundred meters to school in ten minutes, you walk sixty meters every minute.

q2.doska: Triangle: s on top, v and t at the bottom
q2.ovoz: Write distance at the top and speed and time at the bottom. If you need speed, divide distance by time.

q3.doska: The tip of a needle is small → the pressure is large
q3.ovoz: If you press with the same force, a needle makes a hole but a finger does not: the area of the needle's tip is very small, so the pressure is large.

q3.doska: Your ears get blocked on a plane
q3.ovoz: When a plane climbs, the outside pressure decreases and your ears “pop”. This is caused by the difference between the inside and outside pressure.

q3.doska: Air “column”: short on a mountain, tall in a valley
q3.ovoz: Imagine the air above you as a tall column. In a valley, the column is taller and heavier; on a mountain, it is shorter — that is why the pressure is lower.

q4.doska: Wood floats, stone sinks
q4.ovoz: The density of wood is less than that of water, so it floats; the density of stone is greater, so it sinks.

q4.doska: An egg floats in salt water
q4.ovoz: An egg sinks in fresh water. If you add a lot of salt to the water, the density of the water increases and the egg starts to float.

q4.doska: Density column: honey, water, oil
q4.ovoz: If you pour honey, water and vegetable oil into a glass, they form layers by density: the densest, honey, at the bottom and the oil on top.

tipik_xatolar: Thinking that gravity disappears after a parachute opens or when an object moves steadily
Thinking that a heavy object always sinks (in fact, density decides)
Explaining the crushed bottle by the cooling of the air inside, forgetting the pressure difference
Thinking that atmospheric pressure increases with altitude
strategiyalar: Draw the forces acting on each object as arrows
In a floating question, calculate the densities and compare them
In a pressure question, write the inside and outside pressures separately

maqsad: Know Earth's internal structure and its spheres, read contour lines on a topographic map, determine the direction of river flow, and explain how temperature and pressure change as altitude increases

qadamlar.doska:
How do the curved lines on a map show a mountain?
TIMSS: on average 38% of grade 8 students answered correctly
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Have you seen the winding lines on a topographic map? They hold the secret of a mountain's height and steepness. Today we will learn to read that secret. [2] In the international TIMSS study, on average thirty-eight percent of eighth graders around the world answered questions on this topic correctly. By the end of the lesson, you will be able to solve such questions with confidence!

qadamlar.doska:
Crust → mantle → outer and inner core
Lithosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere, biosphere
~71% of Earth's surface is water, fresh water ~3%
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Earth's interior is made of layers: on the outside, the thin crust; beneath it, the thick mantle; and at the center, the liquid outer core and the solid inner core. [2] Earth's outer spheres are the solid lithosphere, the water layer called the hydrosphere, the air layer called the atmosphere, and the layer of life called the biosphere. [3] Water covers about seventy-one percent of Earth's surface, but only about three percent of it is fresh water.

qadamlar.doska:
A contour line joins points at the same height
Lines close together → steep slope; far apart → gentle
The innermost ring is the summit
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] A contour line is a line on a map joining points at the same height above sea level. [2] If contour lines are close together, the slope is steep; if they are far apart, the slope is gentle. [3] The innermost of the closed rings shows a hilltop or mountain summit.

qadamlar.sarlavha: Which way does a river flow on a map?
qadamlar.doska:
A river flows from high to low ground
Valley: contour lines form a “V” pointing uphill
A river crosses the contour lines
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Water always flows from high to low ground, so a river runs from a higher contour line toward a lower one. [2] In a valley, the contour lines bend into the shape of the letter “V”, and its point faces uphill; the river flows through these “V” shapes. [3] A river does not flow along a contour line; it crosses them, in the direction of the steepest drop.

qadamlar.doska:
For every 1 km of height, the temperature drops by ~6 °C
The air gets thinner, the pressure decreases
Altitude zones: forest → meadow → snow
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] As you climb a mountain, the air gets colder: about six degrees for every kilometer. [2] High up, the air is thin, the atmospheric pressure is low and breathing becomes harder. [3] That is why the plants change from the foot of a mountain to its summit, and at the summit there may be snow all year round.

qadamlar.doska: Foot at 600 m: 24 °C. Temperature at the 3600 m summit?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Problem: the foot of a mountain is six hundred meters above sea level, and the air temperature there is twenty-four degrees. What will it be at the summit, at three thousand six hundred meters?

qadamlar.doska:
Height difference: $3600 - 600 = 3000$ m = 3 km
Drop: $3 \cdot 6 = 18$ °C
At the summit: $24 - 18 = 6$ °C
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] First we find the height difference: three thousand meters, that is, three kilometers. [2] If the temperature drops by six degrees for every kilometer, over three kilometers it drops by eighteen degrees. [3] We subtract eighteen from twenty-four: at the summit it will be about six degrees.

qadamlar.doska: Map: lake at 500 m, sea at 0 m. The river's path?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] A TIMSS-style problem: on a map, a mountain lake is on the five-hundred-meter contour line, and the sea is at zero meters. Which way does the river flowing out of the lake go?

qadamlar.doska:
1) Read the contour values: 500, 400, …, 0
2) The river flows downhill, from 500 toward 0
3) Choose the path that goes through the “V” bends
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] First we read the number next to each contour line and find out which side is lower. [2] The river flows from the lake toward the sea, that is, through decreasing heights. [3] The “V” bends pointing uphill show a valley, and the river runs exactly through that valley.

qadamlar.doska: Check: the path never goes uphill
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Let's check the answer: the path we drew must never climb to a higher contour line; nineteen percent of students worldwide answered this question correctly.

qadamlar.doska: 20 °C at the foot. About how many °C 2 km higher?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] The temperature at the foot of a mountain is twenty degrees. About how many degrees will it be two kilometers higher? Write the number.

qadamlar.doska: If the contour lines are close together, is the slope steep or gentle?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Where the contour lines on a map are drawn very close together, what is the slope like: steep or gentle? Write one word.

qadamlar.sarlavha: How to solve the international question
qadamlar.doska:
1. First read the map symbols and numbers
2. Water always flows downhill — check the river's path
3. In an altitude question: temperature ↓, pressure ↓
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] In a map question, first read the map symbols and the contour numbers, and mark which side is higher. [2] After drawing the river's path, check that it never goes uphill. [3] In a question about altitude, write two changes: the temperature drops, and the air gets thinner so the pressure decreases.

qadamlar.doska:
Earth: crust, mantle, core; four spheres
Contour lines close together — steep; the “V” points uphill
Every 1 km: −6 °C; pressure is lower at altitude
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Remember the names of Earth's inner layers and outer spheres. [2] How close the contour lines are shows the slope, and the “V” bends show a valley. [3] For every kilometer of height, the temperature drops by about six degrees, and the pressure decreases.

q1.doska: Earth is like a peach: skin, flesh, pit
q1.ovoz: Compare Earth to a peach: the thin skin is the crust, the thick flesh is the mantle, and the pit is the core.

q1.doska: Even the deepest borehole is only in the crust
q1.ovoz: The deepest hole people have ever drilled is about twelve kilometers deep, and that is only part of the crust. Scientists study the inner layers using earthquake waves.

q1.doska: Litho — stone, hydro — water, atmo — vapor, bio — life
q1.ovoz: Remember the names of the spheres by their word parts: litho means stone, hydro means water, atmo means air or vapor, bio means life.

q2.doska: If we slice a mountain into layers — rings
q2.ovoz: If we make a mountain out of modeling clay, slice it horizontally every centimeter and trace the outlines on paper, we get contour lines.

q2.doska: Hiker: lines close together — a hard climb
q2.ovoz: When a hiker sees a place on the map where the lines are close together, they know the climb there is hard and steep, so they choose a route where the lines are farther apart.

q2.doska: A fist: lines between the knuckles
q2.ovoz: If you put your fist on the table and draw lines at the heights of your knuckles, you get a small ring at the highest point and larger rings lower down.

q3.doska: Water flows down from a hill
q3.ovoz: Take your time: water always flows downhill. Once you find which side is lower on the map, you know the direction of the river.

q3.doska: Rainwater collects in a stream
q3.ovoz: When it rains in the mountains, the water runs down the slopes, collects in the lowest place — a stream — and flows down as a river.

q3.doska: The “V” is an arrow: the river flows against it
q3.ovoz: Imagine the “V” in a valley as an arrow: its point faces uphill, and the river flows the opposite way, downhill.

q4.doska: A mountaintop is cold — there is snow there
q4.ovoz: Even in summer you see snow on high mountain peaks, because the air high up is cold.

q4.doska: You need a jacket when you go up to Chimgan
q4.ovoz: Even on a hot day in Tashkent, if you go up into the Chimgan mountains, the air is cooler and you may need a jacket.

q4.doska: Table: 0 km — 24 °C, 1 km — 18 °C, 2 km — 12 °C
q4.ovoz: Make a table: for each kilometer added, subtract six degrees from the temperature. Then you can find the temperature at any altitude.

tipik_xatolar: Reading contour lines that are close together as a gentle slope
Making a river flow along a contour line or uphill
Thinking that the point of the “V” in a valley faces downhill
Thinking it is warmer at altitude because it is closer to the Sun
strategiyalar: On a map, first read the contour numbers and mark the low and high sides
Check the river's path by making sure the height keeps decreasing
In an altitude question, write the changes in temperature and pressure together

maqsad: Understand the movement of tectonic plates, volcanoes and earthquakes, the evidence for continental drift, the water cycle, and the difference between weather and climate, and draw conclusions based on evidence

qadamlar.doska:
Africa and South America — puzzle pieces?
TIMSS: on average 49% of grade 8 students answered correctly
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Look at a world map: the coasts of Africa and South America fit together like puzzle pieces. Is this a coincidence? [2] In the international TIMSS study, on average forty-nine percent of eighth graders around the world answered questions on this topic correctly. By the end of the lesson, you will be able to solve such questions with confidence!

qadamlar.doska:
Earth's crust is made of large plates
The plates move a few cm per year
Earthquakes and volcanoes — at plate boundaries
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] The lithosphere is not one solid piece; it is made of huge plates floating on the mantle. [2] The plates move very slowly, a few centimeters per year, about as fast as your fingernails grow.
