[3] Conclusion: at the current rate the money is enough, but the margin is very small. It is wise to put a little extra money on the card before buying.

qadamlar.doska: Transfer 150 000 soums, fee 0.5%
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Now it's your turn: you transferred one hundred fifty thousand soums from your card to a friend, and the fee is zero point five percent. How many soums in total were taken from your card?
qadamlar.savol: How many soums were taken in total?

qadamlar.doska: The bank sells 1 USD for 12 900 soums. 50 USD = ?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] The bank sells one dollar for twelve thousand nine hundred soums. How many soums do you need to buy fifty dollars?

qadamlar.doska:
Add up the receipt yourself to check
When comparing, find the unit price
The fee is added to the amount — keep a margin on the card
USD → soums: multiply; the rate may change
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Remember: always add up receipts and bills yourself to check them. [2] When comparing two different packages, find the price of one kilogram or one liter. [3] A card fee is added to the amount, so keep a little extra on the card. [4] When converting dollars to soums, multiply by the rate, and don't forget that the rate can change. You are now a smart shopper!

q1.ovoz: Three loaves of bread at eight thousand each — twenty-four thousand. Two cartons of milk at twelve thousand five hundred each — twenty-five thousand. Tea is fourteen thousand. The total is sixty-three thousand soums. If you pay with one hundred thousand, your change is thirty-seven thousand soums.

q1.doska:
The cashier rang up 2 cartons of milk as 3
The customer who checked the receipt saved 12 500 soums
q1.ovoz: One day a cashier accidentally rang up two cartons of milk as three. The customer checked the quantities on the receipt, found the mistake right away and got twelve thousand five hundred soums back. The receipt is your document.

q2.doska:
Bring them to the same quantity: 1 kg or 1 L
Lower unit price — cheaper
q2.ovoz: To compare two packages, we bring them to the same quantity — one kilogram or one liter. Whichever has the cheaper liter is the better deal.

q2.doska:
3 L: 10/3 bottles of 0.9 L ≈ 33 000;  2 bottles of 1.5 L = 30 000
Comparing by bringing to a common quantity
q2.ovoz: Another method: bring both to the same total quantity, for example three liters. Two one-and-a-half-liter bottles cost thirty thousand, while in small bottles it comes to about thirty-three thousand soums.

q3.doska:
Money sent + fee = money deducted
100 000 + 1 000 = 101 000
q3.ovoz: A fee is a charge for the service. It is added on top of the money being sent: if you send one hundred thousand, at one percent, one hundred one thousand soums is taken.

q3.doska:
My older sister had exactly 500 000 soums on her card
She wants to transfer 500 000 — “insufficient funds”
q3.ovoz: Your older sister tried to transfer exactly the five hundred thousand soums on her card, but the app said “insufficient funds.” The reason is the fee. There must also be money left on the card for the fee.

q4.ovoz: The dollar is a large currency unit, the soum is a small one. When we go from dollars to soums, the number gets bigger — we multiply. When we go from soums to dollars, the number gets smaller — we divide.

q4.doska:
You came back from a trip: 100 USD left over
The bank buys at 12 700 → 1 270 000 soums
q4.ovoz: You came back from a trip with one hundred dollars. The bank buys it from you at its buying rate — for example, twelve thousand seven hundred soums. You receive one million two hundred seventy thousand soums, even though the selling rate is higher.

tipik_xatolar: Thinking a bigger package is always cheaper — not calculating the unit price
Forgetting to add the fee to the amount
Dividing instead of multiplying when converting dollars to soums
Not adding the shipping cost to the total
Confusing the bank's selling and buying rates
strategiyalar: Work out the meaning of every number in the stimulus
When comparing, convert to the unit price
List the extra charges (shipping, fees)
Give the answer in the currency asked for
Evaluate the result by asking, “What if the rate changes?”

maqsad: Make a budget based on income and expenses, calculate the savings share as a percentage, find how long it takes to reach a goal, and evaluate a simple-interest deposit

qadamlar.doska:
Monthly pocket money 300 000 soums: do you need a plan?
PISA financial literacy: baseline — 400 points
Mathematics 2022: Uzbekistan 364, baseline 420
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Hello! Imagine you get three hundred thousand soums of pocket money every month. Will you have money left at the end of the month, or will it run out in two weeks? That depends on your plan. Today we will learn how to plan money. [2] The international PISA study also assesses financial literacy. There, the baseline, Level 2, starts at four hundred points: a student at this level can understand everyday financial documents such as receipts, bills and prices, and make simple decisions. [3] Financial questions rely on mathematics. In 2022, students from Uzbekistan scored an average of three hundred sixty-four points in mathematics, while the baseline is four hundred twenty points. Today let's work together to close this gap!

qadamlar.doska:
Income − expenses = balance
Needs and wants
Balance < 0 → debt;  balance > 0 → savings
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] A budget is a plan of income and expenses. The basic formula: income minus expenses equals the balance. [2] There are two kinds of expenses: needs — food, utility bills, transportation; and wants — cafés, games, new clothes. [3] If the balance is negative, a person falls into debt. If it is positive, it can be put into savings.

qadamlar.doska:
50/30/20: needs / wants / savings
Income 4 000 000 soums:
2 000 000 / 1 200 000 / 800 000 soums
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] One popular rule is fifty, thirty, twenty: fifty percent of income goes to needs, thirty percent to wants, and twenty percent to savings. [2] For example, let the monthly income be four million soums. [3] Two million for needs, one million two hundred thousand for wants, and eight hundred thousand soums for savings. Check: the sum is four million again.

qadamlar.doska:
Number of months = amount still needed ÷ monthly savings
If you get 7.2 months → 8 months (round up)
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] If you are saving for something, first find how much is still missing and divide it by the amount you save each month. [2] If the quotient is a decimal, for example seven point two, the answer is eight months: at the end of the seventh month there is still not enough money.

[1] If you put money in a bank deposit, the bank pays interest. With simple interest: S is the final amount, P is the money deposited, r is the annual interest rate as a decimal, t is the number of years. [2] For example, if we deposit two million soums at twenty percent a year for one year — the interest rate is just an example — at the end of the year there will be two million four hundred thousand soums. [3] Six months is half a year, so t equals zero point five. In half a year it is two million two hundred thousand soums. The time must be written in years — pay attention to the unit!

qadamlar.doska:
Phone 2 600 000 soums. She has 800 000 soums now
If she saves 250 000 soums a month — in how many months?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] The first example. Dilnoza wants to buy a phone that costs two million six hundred thousand soums. Right now she has eight hundred thousand soums. [2] She saves two hundred fifty thousand soums every month. After how many months will she be able to buy the phone?
[1] First we find the missing amount: one million eight hundred thousand soums. [2] We divide it by the monthly savings: seven point two.

qadamlar.doska:
In 7 months: 800 000 + 1 750 000 = 2 550 000 — not enough
In 8 months: 800 000 + 2 000 000 = 2 800 000 ✓
Answer: 8 months
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Let's check: in seven months she will have two million five hundred fifty thousand soums in total — still fifty thousand short of the phone. [2] In eight months, two million eight hundred thousand soums — enough, with some left over. [3] The answer in the language of the situation: Dilnoza will buy the phone after eight months.

qadamlar.sarlavha: How to read a PISA question
qadamlar.doska:
1) Stimulus: table of income and expenses
2) Question: balance, percentage or time?
3) Not needed: last month's data, kWh
4) Unit: monthly or yearly? months or years?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] In planning questions, the stimulus is often a budget table. Mark each row as income or an expense. [2] Break down the question: is it asking for the balance, the savings percentage, or the time needed to reach a goal? [3] The table may also contain numbers unrelated to the amount, such as last month's data or kilowatt-hours — cross them out. [4] And look at the unit: is the income monthly or yearly? Is the interest rate yearly? Is the time in months or years? Bring everything to the same unit.

qadamlar.doska:
Income: father 6 000 000, mother 4 500 000 soums
Utilities 900 000, food 4 200 000 soums
Transportation 1 100 000, loan 2 000 000; electricity 300 kWh
Can the family set aside 20% for savings?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] The second example is in PISA style. The family's monthly income: the father earns six million, and the mother four million five hundred thousand soums. [2] Expenses: utility bills are nine hundred thousand, food is four million two hundred thousand soums. [3] Transportation is one million one hundred thousand, and the loan payment is two million soums. The family used three hundred kilowatt-hours of electricity this month. [4] Question: can the family set aside at least twenty percent of its income for savings?

qadamlar.doska:
Not needed: 300 kWh — the amount is already in utilities
Income: $6\,000\,000 + 4\,500\,000 = 10\,500\,000$
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] First we separate out the unnecessary information: the electricity cost is already included in the utility bills, so the kilowatt-hours are not needed. [2] Total income: ten million five hundred thousand soums.
[1] We add up the expenses, in thousands of soums for convenience: eight million two hundred thousand soums. [2] The balance: two million three hundred thousand soums.

qadamlar.doska:
Share: $2\,300\,000 : 10\,500\,000 \approx 0.219 = 21.9\%$
Check: 20% — 2 100 000;  2 300 000 > 2 100 000 ✓
Interpretation: yes, it can; another 200 000 soums are left
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] We find the share of the balance: two million three hundred thousand divided by ten million five hundred thousand is about zero point two one nine, that is, twenty-one point nine percent. [2] Let's check another way: twenty percent of the income is two million one hundred thousand soums, and the balance is more than that. [3] The answer in the language of the situation: yes, the family can set aside twenty percent for savings, and another two hundred thousand soums will be left as a reserve.

qadamlar.doska: Income 3 000 000 soums, savings — 20%. How many soums?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Now it's your turn: your older brother's salary is three million soums, and he wants to save twenty percent of it. How many soums will he save each month?

qadamlar.doska: Bicycle 1 500 000 soums, saving 200 000 a month
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] A bicycle costs one million five hundred thousand soums. You don't have any money yet, and you save two hundred thousand soums every month. In how many months will you buy the bicycle? Don't forget to round!

qadamlar.doska:
Income − expenses = balance
Savings share = balance ÷ income
If the time is a decimal — round up
Simple interest: $S = P(1 + r t)$, $t$ — in years
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Remember: the basis of a budget is income minus expenses equals the balance. [2] To find the savings share, divide the balance by the income and convert it to a percentage. [3] If the time to reach a goal is a decimal, round up and check the last month. [4] For a simple-interest deposit, the time is always taken in years. You are now the master of your own money!

q1.ovoz: Your pocket money is three hundred thousand soums. One hundred twenty thousand went on transportation and lunch, and ninety thousand soums on games and sweets. The balance is ninety thousand soums — this can be saved.

q1.doska:
Bucket: water flows in (income), leaks out through a hole (expenses)
If more flows out than in — the bucket empties
q1.ovoz: Think of a budget as a bucket: water is poured in from the top — this is income, and it leaks out through holes at the bottom — these are expenses. If there are many holes, the bucket never fills up.

q2.doska:
50% — half;  30% — multiply by 0.3
20% — divide by 5
q2.ovoz: Fifty percent is half of the income, thirty percent is multiplying by zero point three, twenty percent is dividing by five. If you add all three, you should get the income itself.

q2.doska:
A flatbread in 10 pieces: 5 — lunch, 3 — for guests, 2 — for tomorrow
Just like 50/30/20
q2.ovoz: You cut a flatbread into ten pieces: five for lunch, three for guests, and you save two for tomorrow. This is exactly the fifty, thirty, twenty split — some is kept for tomorrow too.

q3.doska:
Every month +250 000: 1 050 000, 1 300 000, ...
Count until you reach it
q3.ovoz: If dividing is hard, keep adding month by month: two hundred fifty thousand is added each month. The month when the total passes the required price is the answer.

q3.doska:
Table: month | total
7 | 2 550 000;  8 | 2 800 000
q3.ovoz: Make a table: months in the first column, total money in the second. The first row that goes over the price is your answer.

q4.doska:
Interest: $2\,000\,000 \cdot 0.2 = 400\,000$ (for 1 year)
For half a year — half: 200 000
q4.ovoz: First find the interest for one year: twenty percent of two million is four hundred thousand. For half a year, the interest is also half — two hundred thousand soums.

q4.doska:
The bank “rents” your money
The rent is the interest
q4.ovoz: Think of a deposit this way: the bank rents your money for a while and pays rent for it — this is interest. The longer you rent it out, the more you are paid.

tipik_xatolar: Rounding down when the time is a decimal: 7.2 → 7 months
Using months instead of years: taking $t = 6$ for 6 months
Calculating the savings percentage relative to expenses
Including unnecessary information (kWh) in the calculation
Dividing the whole price without counting the money already saved
strategiyalar: Mark each row of the table as income or an expense
Bring monthly and yearly values to the same unit
Determine the time by checking the last month
Check the percentage by recalculating it another way
Write the answer in the language of the situation as “yes/no, because ...”

sarlavha: Risk and return: deposits, loans, insurance
maqsad: Compare compound and simple interest, calculate the true cost of a loan and an installment plan, evaluate insurance using expected loss, and recognize the signs of fraud

qadamlar.doska:
A deposit or “30% profit a month” — which one is risky?
PISA financial literacy: baseline — 400 points
Mathematics 2022: Uzbekistan 364, baseline 420
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Hello! On social media you saw an ad saying, “Give us your money, and we guarantee thirty percent profit every month.” A bank, on the other hand, pays much less interest per year. Which one can you trust? Today we will evaluate risk and return with calculations. [2] The international PISA study also assesses financial literacy. There, the baseline, Level 2, starts at four hundred points: a student at this level can understand everyday financial documents such as receipts, bills and prices, and make simple decisions. [3] Financial questions rely on mathematics. In 2022, students from Uzbekistan scored an average of three hundred sixty-four points in mathematics, while the baseline is four hundred twenty points. Today let's work together to close this gap!

qadamlar.doska:
Compound interest: $S = P(1 + r)^n$
1 000 000, 20%, 2 years: $1.2^2 = 1.44$ → 1 440 000
With simple interest: 1 400 000 — a difference of 40 000 soums
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] With compound interest, at the end of each year the interest is added to the principal, and the next year's interest is calculated on this larger amount. The formula: S equals P times one plus r to the power n. [2] If one million soums is deposited at twenty percent a year for two years — the rate is just an example — one point two squared is one point four four, that is, one million four hundred forty thousand soums. [3] With simple interest it would be one million four hundred thousand. The difference is forty thousand: this is interest on interest. The longer the term, the bigger the difference.

qadamlar.sarlavha: The true cost of a loan
qadamlar.doska:
Overpayment = total payments − amount borrowed
12 × 550 000 = 6 600 000;  borrowed 5 000 000
Overpayment: 1 600 000 soums, that is, 32%
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] When you take out a loan, you pay the bank back more than you borrowed. The overpayment is the sum of all payments minus the amount borrowed. [2] For example, you took out a loan of five million soums and pay five hundred fifty thousand soums a month for twelve months. That is six million six hundred thousand soums in total. [3] The overpayment is one million six hundred thousand soums — thirty-two percent of the amount borrowed. Calculate exactly this number before taking out a loan.

qadamlar.doska:
A promise of high returns = high risk
“30% a month”: $1.3^{12} \approx 23$ — 23 times in a year?!
Never tell anyone your SMS code, CVV or password
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] There is a rule in finance: the higher the return, the greater the risk. Nobody can guarantee a high return. [2] Let's calculate the “thirty percent a month” promise: one point three to the twelfth power is about twenty-three. That means the money would supposedly grow twenty-three times in one year! A guarantee like this is a sign of fraud. [3] Another rule: even a bank employee will never ask for your SMS code, the CVV code on the back of your card, or your password. If someone asks, they are a scammer.

qadamlar.doska:
Expected loss = probability × loss
$0.02 \cdot 10\,000\,000 = 200\,000$ soums
Insurance 250 000 soums — protection from a big loss
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Risk can be measured with a number: the expected loss is the probability of the event times the amount of the loss. [2] For example, let the probability that a car has an accident during the year be zero point zero two, and let the repair cost ten million soums. The expected loss is two hundred thousand soums. [3] The insurance premium is two hundred fifty thousand soums — a little more than the expected loss. But it protects you from an unexpected ten-million-soum blow. Insurance is the price of peace of mind.

qadamlar.doska:
10 000 000 soums, 3 years. Bank A: 22%, simple interest
Bank B: 20%, interest added every year (compound)
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] The first example. You want to put ten million soums in a deposit for three years. Bank A pays twenty-two percent a year, but as simple interest. [2] Bank B pays twenty percent a year, but at the end of each year the interest is added to the deposit — compound interest. Which bank is the better choice?

[1] Bank A: one plus zero point two two times three is one point six six. The result is sixteen million six hundred thousand soums. [2] Bank B: one point two cubed is one point seven two eight. Seventeen million two hundred eighty thousand soums.

qadamlar.doska:
Difference: $17\,280\,000 - 16\,600\,000 = 680\,000$ soums
Interpretation: B is better even though its rate is lower
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] The difference is six hundred eighty thousand soums in favor of Bank B. [2] The conclusion in the language of the situation: don't look only at the interest rate — also read how the interest is calculated. Over a long term, compound interest gives more income even at a lower rate.

qadamlar.sarlavha: How to read a PISA question
qadamlar.doska:
1) Stimulus: contract, ad or table
2) Question: total, overpayment or risk?
3) Not needed: product features, color, storage
4) Unit: monthly or yearly interest? months or years?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] In risk and return questions, the stimulus is loan terms, a deposit table or the text of an ad. Read the fine print too. [2] Identify the question: is it asking for the total payment, the overpayment, a percentage, or an evaluation of whether the offer is trustworthy? [3] Ads contain a lot of information unrelated to money, such as the product's color and storage. Cross it out. [4] The most important unit is the interest period: a monthly rate has a much bigger effect than a yearly one. Check whether the term is in months or years.

qadamlar.doska:
Phone (256 GB): cash price 6 000 000 soums
Installment plan: 12 months × 590 000 soums
What percent is the overpayment? Which way is better?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] The second example is in PISA style. In a shop, a phone with two hundred fifty-six gigabytes costs six million soums in cash. [2] With an installment plan, five hundred ninety thousand soums is paid every month for twelve months. [3] Question: what percent is the overpayment on the installment plan, and which way is better?

qadamlar.doska:
Not needed: 256 GB — unrelated to the price
Total: $12 \cdot 590\,000 = 7\,080\,000$ soums
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] First we separate out the unnecessary information: the phone's storage is not needed for the calculation. [2] The total on the installment plan: seven million eighty thousand soums.
[1] The overpayment: one million eighty thousand soums. [2] We divide it by the cash price: zero point one eight, that is, eighteen percent.

qadamlar.doska:
Alternative: saving 590 000 a month — in 11 months
Check: $11 \cdot 590\,000 = 6\,490\,000 \ge 6\,000\,000$ ✓
Interpretation: if you can wait — saving is better
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Let's also look at the alternative: if you save the same five hundred ninety thousand soums every month, in eleven months you can buy the phone with cash. [2] Let's check: in ten months it is five million nine hundred thousand — not enough; in eleven months it is six million four hundred ninety thousand — enough. [3] Conclusion: if you don't need the phone right away, saving up for it saves more than a million. An installment plan is convenient, but it costs eighteen percent more.

qadamlar.doska: 1 000 000 soums, 10% compound interest, 2 years
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Now it's your turn: one million soums was deposited at ten percent a year with compound interest for two years. How many soums will there be after two years?
qadamlar.savol: How many soums will there be?

qadamlar.doska: Probability 0.05, loss 4 000 000 soums. Expected loss?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] The probability that a bicycle is stolen during the year is zero point zero five, and the bicycle costs four million soums. What is the expected loss in soums?
qadamlar.savol: What is the expected loss in soums?

qadamlar.doska:
Compound interest: $S = P(1 + r)^n$
Cost of a loan = total payments − amount borrowed
A guaranteed big profit is a sign of fraud
Expected loss = probability × loss
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Remember: with compound interest, interest is added to interest, so over a long term it gives more than simple interest. [2] To find the true cost of a loan or an installment plan, add up all the payments and subtract the amount borrowed. [3] If a big profit is guaranteed or someone asks for a code — stop, this is a sign of fraud. [4] Measure risk with the expected loss and evaluate insurance based on it. Now you can see financial risk!

q1.ovoz: Calculate year by year: in the first year, the interest is on one million — two hundred thousand. In the second year, the interest is now on one million two hundred thousand — two hundred forty thousand. In total, one million four hundred forty thousand.

q1.doska:
A snowball: it grows as it rolls
Interest also earns new interest
q1.ovoz: Think of a snowball rolling down a mountain: with every turn new snow sticks to it, and the ball grows faster and faster. Compound interest works the same way — the interest itself earns interest.

q1.doska:
Each year × 1.1:  100 000 → 110 000 → 121 000 → 133 100
Seeing it in a table
q1.ovoz: Make a table: each year, multiply the amount by one point one. In three years, one hundred thousand becomes one hundred thirty-three thousand one hundred soums.

q2.doska:
Borrowed: 5 000 000;  paid back: 6 600 000
The difference is the cost of the loan
q2.ovoz: Ask a simple question: how much did I borrow and how much will I pay back? The difference is the true cost of the loan.

q2.doska:
You borrowed 100 thousand from a neighbor and paid back 130 thousand
30 thousand is the “price” of the loan
q2.ovoz: You borrowed one hundred thousand soums from a neighbor and agreed to pay back one hundred thirty thousand later. Thirty thousand is the price of the loan — thirty percent of one hundred thousand.

q3.doska:
Bank: tens of percent a year
“30% a month” — not realistic
q3.ovoz: Reliable bank deposits pay tens of percent a year. Thirty percent a month means thousands of percent a year. If you see a number like that, be suspicious right away.

q3.doska:
A call: “We're from the bank, tell us the SMS code”
The right response: hang up
q3.ovoz: The phone rings: “We're from the bank, your card has been blocked, tell us the SMS code.” This is a classic scam. Hang up and call the bank yourself using its official number.

q4.doska:
2 out of 100 cars have an accident — 0.02
An average loss of 200 000 soums for each
q4.ovoz: Imagine one hundred cars: during the year, two of them have an accident. Two times ten million is twenty million; divided among one hundred cars, that is an average of two hundred thousand each.

q4.doska:
Insurance is like a mahalla hashar
Many people chip in a little to help the one who suffers a loss
q4.ovoz: Insurance can be compared to a hashar, when the community works together: many people put in a little money, and if someone suffers a big loss, they get help from this shared fund.

tipik_xatolar: Calculating compound interest like simple interest: $P(1 + rn)$
Judging the cost of a loan only by the monthly payment
Confusing a monthly interest rate with a yearly one
Believing in a guaranteed high return
Taking the whole loss as the expected loss without multiplying by the probability
strategiyalar: Add up all the payments and compare with the amount borrowed
Identify the interest period (monthly/yearly) and the calculation method (simple/compound)
Calculate the alternative option too
Check an offer that seems too good with a calculation
Measure risk with the expected loss

sarlavha: The financial environment: taxes, contracts, rights
maqsad: Calculate income tax and take-home pay, read and evaluate the payment and late-fee terms of a contract, and know consumer rights and responsibilities

qadamlar.doska:
First job: how much of the salary do you take home?
PISA financial literacy: baseline — 400 points
Mathematics 2022: Uzbekistan 364, baseline 420
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Hello! In a few years you will get your first job. The job ad says “salary five million,” but you take home less. Why? Today we will study taxes, contracts and our rights with calculations. [2] The international PISA study also assesses financial literacy. There, the baseline, Level 2, starts at four hundred points: a student at this level can understand everyday financial documents such as receipts, bills and prices, and make simple decisions. [3] Financial questions rely on mathematics. In 2022, students from Uzbekistan scored an average of three hundred sixty-four points in mathematics, while the baseline is four hundred twenty points. Today let's work together to close this gap!

qadamlar.doska:
Tax = gross salary × rate
12% (example): $5\,000\,000 \cdot 0.12 = 600\,000$
Take-home: 5 000 000 − 600 000 = 4 400 000 soums
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Income tax is paid to the state from the money you earn. It is found by multiplying the gross salary by the tax rate. Taxes are spent on common needs such as schools, hospitals and roads. [2] As an example, let the rate be twelve percent. On a salary of five million soums, the tax is six hundred thousand soums. [3] You take home four million four hundred thousand soums. When reading a job ad, find out whether the salary is before or after tax.

qadamlar.doska:
A contract is a written agreement between the parties
Read: amount, deadline, penalty, cancellation
Signature = consent and obligation
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] A contract is a written agreement between two or more parties about their rights and obligations: a rental, loan, employment or purchase contract. [2] Before signing, be sure to read four things: what the amount is, when the payment is due, what the penalty is if you are late, and how the contract can be canceled. [3] Once you sign, you are considered to have agreed to all the terms — the excuse “I didn't read it” is not accepted.

qadamlar.sarlavha: Late fees — a penalty for being late
qadamlar.doska:
Late fee = debt × daily rate × number of days
$1\,200\,000 \cdot 0.001 \cdot 15 = 18\,000$ soums
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] In many contracts, if a payment is late, a late fee equal to a certain percentage of the debt is charged for each day. The late fee is the debt times the daily rate as a decimal times the number of days late. [2] For example, a payment of one million two hundred thousand soums was fifteen days late, and the late fee is zero point one percent per day — that is, zero point zero zero one. The late fee is eighteen thousand soums.

qadamlar.doska:
A receipt is a document that proves a purchase
Faulty product: exchange or refund
The warranty period is written on the warranty card
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] After every purchase, take the receipt: it proves that you bought the item from this shop at this price. [2] If an item turns out to be faulty, the consumer has the right to demand an exchange or a refund. For this you will need the receipt and the item. [3] The warranty period for appliances is written on the warranty card or in the contract — keep it.

qadamlar.doska:
A: salary 6 000 000 soums (before tax)
B: take-home 5 400 000 soums. Tax 12%. Which is more?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] The first example. Your older brother was offered two jobs. At company A, the salary is six million soums, but this is the amount before tax is withheld. [2] At company B, he would take home five million four hundred thousand soums. The tax rate is twelve percent, as an example. At which company will he take home more money?
[1] We bring both to the same basis — take-home pay. At company A, the tax is seven hundred twenty thousand soums. [2] Take-home: five million two hundred eighty thousand soums.

qadamlar.doska:
5 280 000 < 5 400 000 → more at B
Interpretation: “salary” — before or after tax?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] We compare: at company B he takes home one hundred twenty thousand soums more a month, even though the number in the ad is smaller. [2] Conclusion: compare two offers only on the same basis — before tax or after tax. PISA tests exactly this kind of trap.

qadamlar.sarlavha: How to read a PISA question
qadamlar.doska:
1) Stimulus: contract, bill, job ad
2) Question: tax, take-home pay or penalty?
3) Not needed: address, floor, names of the parties
4) Unit: daily or monthly rate, number of days
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] In questions about the financial environment, the stimulus is an extract from a contract, a utility bill or a job ad. Read each clause separately. [2] Break down the question: is it asking for the tax, the take-home amount, a penalty, or which of the parties is right? [3] A contract contains a lot of information not needed for the calculation, such as the address, the floor and the names of the parties — cross it out. [4] Check the units: is the late fee daily or monthly? How many days late was the payment? Convert the percentage to a decimal correctly.

qadamlar.doska:
Rent: 2 500 000 soums/month, due by the 5th of each month
A late fee of 0.2% for each day late
The apartment is on the 3rd floor. The payment was 12 days late
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] The second example is in PISA style. A university student signed an apartment rental contract: two million five hundred thousand soums a month, paid by the fifth of each month. [2] The contract says: for each day late, a late fee of zero point two percent of the debt. [3] The apartment is on the third floor. This month the student paid twelve days late. What are the late fee and the total payment?

qadamlar.doska:
Not needed: 3rd floor — not needed for the calculation
Per day: $2\,500\,000 \cdot 0.002 = 5\,000$ soums
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] First we separate out the unnecessary information: the floor of the apartment does not affect the late fee. [2] Zero point two percent is zero point zero zero two. The late fee for one day: five thousand soums.
[1] For twelve days: sixty thousand soums. [2] The total payment: two million five hundred sixty thousand soums.

qadamlar.doska:
Check: $2\,500\,000 \cdot 0.002 \cdot 12 = 60\,000$ ✓
Interpretation: being late cost 60 000 soums
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Let's check with a single formula: the debt times the daily rate times the days — sixty thousand again. [2] Back to the situation: being twelve days late cost the student sixty thousand soums. Knowing the deadline in the contract and keeping to it means saving money.

qadamlar.doska: Salary 4 000 000 soums, tax 12%. How much take-home?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Now it's your turn: the gross salary is four million soums, and the income tax is twelve percent. How many soums is the take-home pay?

qadamlar.doska: Debt 800 000 soums, late fee 0.1% per day, 10 days
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] A debt of eight hundred thousand soums for utilities was paid ten days late, and the late fee is zero point one percent per day. How many soums is the late fee?
qadamlar.savol: How many soums is the late fee?

qadamlar.doska:
Take-home = salary − tax = salary × (1 − rate)
Compare offers on the same basis
Late fee = debt × daily rate × days
Read and keep contracts and receipts
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Remember: take-home pay is the gross salary minus the tax. [2] Compare two offers only on the same basis — before tax or after tax. [3] A late fee is the debt times the daily rate times the number of days. [4] Read a contract before signing it, and keep your receipts and warranty cards. You are now a citizen who knows your rights!

q1.ovoz: First find twelve percent of the salary — this is the tax. Then subtract it from the salary — this is the money you take home.

q1.doska:
Everyone adds a little to the common pot
From the pot: schools, roads, hospitals
q1.ovoz: When there is a wedding in the mahalla, everyone chips in a little and a common pot is cooked. Taxes work the same way: every working person contributes a little, and this money is used to build schools, roads and hospitals that everyone uses.
You can also do it with a single multiplication: if the tax is twelve percent, you take home eighty-eight percent. Multiply the salary by zero point eight eight.

q2.doska:
Who? What? How much? By when?
What happens if it is broken?
q2.ovoz: Find the answers to five questions in a contract: with whom, about what, how much money, by when, and what happens if a term is broken.

q2.doska:
A friend rented a phone — a verbal agreement
The phone broke — who pays? Not written down!
q2.ovoz: Two friends made a verbal agreement to rent out a phone for a week. Nothing had been agreed about who would pay if the phone broke — and an argument started. A written contract protects you from exactly this kind of situation.

q3.doska:
0.1% = 0.001
For 1 day: debt × 0.001;  then × days
q3.ovoz: First convert the percentage to a decimal: zero point one percent is zero point zero zero one. Find the late fee for one day and multiply it by the number of days.

q3.doska:
A library book: a fine for every day it is late
The later you are, the bigger the fine
q3.ovoz: If you don't return a library book on time, a fine is charged for every day. A late fee works the same way — the longer the delay, the bigger the penalty.

q4.doska:
Receipt → easy to prove your right
No receipt → hard to prove
q4.ovoz: A receipt is your evidence. If you have it, it is much easier to demand an exchange or a refund for a faulty item.

q4.doska:
New headphones stopped working after a week
To the shop with the receipt and the warranty card
q4.ovoz: Your new headphones stopped working after a week. You took the receipt and the warranty card to the shop and asked them to exchange the headphones. A person who keeps their documents can protect their rights.

tipik_xatolar: Comparing salaries before and after tax directly
Converting a percentage to a decimal incorrectly: taking 0.2% = 0.02
Forgetting to multiply the late fee by the number of days
Including unnecessary information from the contract (floor, address) in the calculation
Not keeping the receipt and the warranty card
strategiyalar: Read each clause of the contract separately
Bring offers to the same basis (take-home pay)
Check when converting a percentage to a decimal: 1% = 0.01
Check the late fee by recalculating it with a single formula
Write the answer in the language of the situation: who, how much, why

sarlavha: Finding the information you need in a text
maqsad: Search by keyword, recognize paraphrases, and find information that meets several conditions in non-continuous texts such as notices and tables

qadamlar.doska:
Bus timetables, notices, instructions — they are all texts
PISA 2022: Uzbekistan in reading — 336 points
OECD average — 476, baseline Level 2 — 407 points
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Every day we look for the information we need in a bus timetable, a school notice, or the instructions for a medicine. Today we will learn to do this quickly and without mistakes. [2] In the international PISA study in 2022, fifteen-year-old students in Uzbekistan scored an average of three hundred thirty-six points in reading literacy. [3] Compare: the OECD average was four hundred seventy-six points, and the baseline level, Level 2, starts at four hundred seven points. So we have a big but achievable goal ahead of us, and today's lesson is one step along that road!

qadamlar.doska:
1. Pick out the keyword in the question
2. Quickly “scan” the text with your eyes
3. Read the sentence you find slowly and in full
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] First read the question carefully and pick out the most important word: who, when, where, how much — what is being asked? [2] Then don't read the text word by word from beginning to end; instead, run your eyes over it quickly, looking for that keyword. [3] Now read the sentence where you found the keyword slowly and in full, because the answer is often in that very sentence or the next one.

qadamlar.doska:
Question: “What time does the museum open?”
In the text: “Visitors are admitted from 9:00”
Look for synonyms of the keyword too!
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] PISA questions often contain a trick. For example, the question asks what time the museum opens. [2] But the word “opens” does not appear in the text at all; instead it says “visitors are admitted from nine o'clock”. [3] So don't look only for the exact same word; also look for its synonyms or an expression with the same meaning.

qadamlar.doska:
Non-continuous texts: tables, graphs, notices, maps
First read the title and the column and row names
The answer is where the right row and column meet
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Not every text is made of paragraphs. Tables, graphs, notices, and maps are called non-continuous texts. [2] In a text like this, first read the title, then the names of the columns and rows; like the key on a map, they show you the way. [3] Then find the row you need and the column you need: the answer is in the cell where they meet.

qadamlar.doska:
“Book Lovers' Contest! For grades 9–11.
Registration: March 1–15, in the library.
Final: March 28, 14:00, in the school hall.”
Question: Where do you register?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Let's read the notice on the school wall: a book lovers' contest for grades nine to eleven. [2] Registration is from March first to March fifteenth, in the library. [3] The final will be on March twenty-eighth at two p.m., in the school hall. [4] The question: where do you register? Let's find it step by step.

qadamlar.doska:
Keyword: “registration”
Found: line 2 → “in the library”
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] The keyword in the question is “registration”. We scan the text with our eyes, looking for this word. [2] We found it in the second line: registration takes place in the library.

qadamlar.doska:
Distractor: “school hall” — this is about the final
Answer: in the library
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Notice that there is another place in the text: the school hall. But it is about the final, not registration; this is a distractor. [2] So the correct answer is in the library. Don't answer as soon as you see a place name; answer only after checking which sentence it belongs to.

qadamlar.doska: According to this notice: on what date is the final?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Now try it yourself. Using this notice, find on what date the final will be held. The keyword is “final”.

qadamlar.sarlavha: Example 2: a table and two conditions
qadamlar.doska:
A: 07:00 → 11:30, 120 000 soum
B: 09:30 → 13:30, 150 000 soum
C: 08:00 → 14:30, 100 000 soum
Question: which is the cheapest way to arrive by 14:00?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] A bus timetable from Tashkent to Samarkand. Bus A leaves at seven and arrives at eleven thirty; the fare is one hundred twenty thousand soum. [2] Bus B leaves at nine thirty and arrives at thirteen thirty; the fare is one hundred fifty thousand soum. [3] Bus C leaves at eight and arrives at fourteen thirty; the fare is one hundred thousand soum. [4] The question: you need to get to Samarkand by fourteen hundred, and you need to choose the cheapest bus. Which one is it?

qadamlar.doska:
Condition 1: arrive by 14:00 → A, B
Condition 2: cheapest → A (120 000 < 150 000)
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] The question has two conditions, and we check them separately. Condition one is to arrive by fourteen hundred: only A and B meet it. [2] Condition two is the cheapest. Of A and B, A is cheaper: one hundred twenty thousand is less than one hundred fifty thousand.

qadamlar.doska:
Trap: C is the cheapest, but it doesn't meet condition 1!
Answer: bus A
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Here is the trap: C is the cheapest in the whole table, and many students choose it. But C arrives at fourteen thirty, so it is late. [2] So the correct answer is bus A. If you check each condition one by one, you won't fall into the trap.

qadamlar.doska: According to this table: how many hours is bus B on the road?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Use the same table again. Bus B leaves at nine thirty and arrives at thirteen thirty. How many hours is it on the road?

qadamlar.sarlavha: How to solve an international question
qadamlar.doska:
1. Read the question twice and count the conditions
2. Look for the keyword and its synonyms
3. Check what you find against every condition
4. Support your answer with an exact place in the text
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] When solving a PISA question, first read the question twice and count how many conditions it has. [2] Then scan the text for the keyword and its synonyms. [3] Compare the information you find with every condition; a distractor often meets only one condition. [4] And finally, ask yourself: on which line of the text is my answer written? If you can point to that place, your answer is correct.

qadamlar.doska:
Keyword → scan → read slowly
Look for paraphrases too
In a table: title → row × column → conditions
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Remember: first the keyword, then scan the text quickly, then read the sentence you found slowly. [2] The exact word from the question may not be in the text, so look for its synonym. [3] In tables and notices, read the title, the rows, and the columns, and check each condition separately. You can do it!

q1.doska:
What is the question asking? → look for that word
Read the sentence you find in full
q1.ovoz: To put it more simply: mark what the question is asking with one word. Find that word in the text and read the whole sentence it is in; the answer is there.

q1.doska:
Looking up a word in a dictionary: we flip quickly by the letters
Once we find the word, we read its definition slowly
q1.ovoz: Remember looking up a word in a dictionary. You don't read every page; you flip quickly, looking at the letters. Once you find the word, you read its definition slowly. It's exactly the same with a text.

q1.doska:
Underline the keyword
Circle it in the text
q1.ovoz: If you are working on paper, underline the keyword in the question, and when you find it in the text, circle it. A mark you can see helps you not to get lost.

q2.doska:
One meaning — different words
opens = admits visitors = starts work
q2.ovoz: The same meaning can be expressed with different words. “Opens”, “admits visitors”, “starts work” all mean the same thing. Any one of them could be in the text.

q2.doska:
Your friend: “Where are you?”
You: “At home”, “In my room” — same meaning
q2.ovoz: If your friend asks “where are you?”, you say “at home” or “in my room”: different words, same meaning. The author of a text may also change the word from the question.

q2.doska:
Write 2–3 synonyms for the word in the question
Look for all of them in the text
q2.ovoz: Another way: before searching, think of two or three synonyms for the keyword in the question and write them in the margin. Then look for all of them in the text.

q3.doska:
Table = rows + columns
Where the right row and column meet — the answer
q3.ovoz: A table is made of rows and columns. Point to the row you need with one finger and the column you need with another; the cell where they meet is the answer.

q3.doska:
Class schedule: “Tuesday” row, “Period 3” column
Where they meet: “Physics”
q3.ovoz: Remember your class schedule at school. To find which lesson is in third period on Tuesday, you look at the cell where the Tuesday row and the third-period column meet.

q3.doska:
In a notice: What? When? Where? For whom?
One line for each question
q3.ovoz: When reading a notice, ask four questions: what, when, where, and for whom. If you mark each answer separately, the notice turns into a small table.

tipik_xatolar: Searching the text only for the exact word from the question and missing a paraphrase
Answering with the first place name or number you come across without thinking (a distractor)
Checking only one of the several conditions in the question
Reading the wrong value from a neighboring row or column in a table
strategiyalar: Count the conditions in the question and check each one separately
Look for the keyword's synonyms as well as the keyword itself
In a non-continuous text, first read the title and the column and row names
Check that you can support your answer with an exact line in the text

sarlavha: Understanding a text: main idea, inferences, connections
maqsad: Identify the topic and main idea of a text, draw inferences not stated in the text based on evidence, and find cause-and-effect relationships

qadamlar.doska:
I read it — but what was it trying to say?
PISA 2022: Uzbekistan in reading — 336 points
OECD average — 476, baseline Level 2 — 407 points
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Sometimes you read a text to the end but can't say what the author was trying to tell you. Today we will learn to understand a text deeply. [2] In the international PISA study in 2022, fifteen-year-old students in Uzbekistan scored an average of three hundred thirty-six points in reading literacy. [3] Compare: the OECD average was four hundred seventy-six points, and the baseline level, Level 2, starts at four hundred seven points. So we have a big but achievable goal ahead of us, and today's lesson is one step along that road!

qadamlar.doska:
Topic — what the text is about (1–2 words)
Main idea — what the author wants to say about the topic
It is often in the first or last sentence
Check: does every sentence support this idea?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] The topic is what the text is about; you can say it in one or two words, for example, “the Aral Sea”. [2] The main idea is exactly what the author wants to say about that topic, and it is expressed as a full sentence. [3] The main idea is often in the first or last sentence of the text, but not always. [4] The way to check is simple: if every sentence in the text explains or proves this idea, you have found it correctly.

qadamlar.doska:
An inference is not written in the text; it follows from evidence
Evidence in the text + your knowledge → inference
An idea with no evidence in the text is a guess, not an inference
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] PISA often asks about something that is not written directly in the text but follows logically from it. This is called drawing an inference. [2] To make an inference, you combine evidence from the text with your own knowledge of the world. [3] But be careful: an idea with no evidence at all in the text is not an inference, just a guess.

qadamlar.doska:
Cause → effect: because, for this reason, as a result
Contrast: but, however, on the contrary
Sequence: first, then, finally
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Connecting words show how sentences are linked. “Because”, “for this reason”, “as a result” link a cause and an effect. [2] The words “but”, “however”, “on the contrary” signal that the idea is turning in the opposite direction. [3] Words such as “first”, “then”, “finally” show the order of events.

qadamlar.doska:
“The Aral Sea was once one of the largest lakes in the world.
Water from the Amu Darya and Syr Darya was taken to irrigate fields.
As a result, little water reached the sea, and it gradually dried up.”
Question: what is the main idea of the text?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Let's read a short text. The Aral Sea was once one of the largest lakes in the world. [2] More and more water from the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers was taken to irrigate fields. [3] As a result, little water reached the sea, and it gradually dried up. [4] The question: what is the main idea of the text? First let's find the connections.

qadamlar.doska:
“As a result” → a cause-and-effect link
Cause: river water was taken for the fields
Effect: the sea gradually dried up
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] The words “as a result” in the third sentence give us a signal: there is a cause and an effect here. [2] The cause is that the rivers' water was taken for the fields. [3] The effect is that the sea gradually dried up.

qadamlar.doska:
A) “The Aral was a large lake” — just one detail
B) “Taking water for the fields dried up the Aral” — everything
Answer: B
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Option A: the Aral was a large lake. This is true, but it is only one detail of the text, and the other sentences do not support it. [2] Option B: taking the rivers' water for the fields dried up the Aral. All three sentences support this idea. [3] So the main idea is B. The main idea covers the whole text, not just one sentence.

qadamlar.doska: In the text about the Aral, which words introduce the effect?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Now find it yourself: in the text about the Aral, which connecting words introduced the effect? Write the phrase.

qadamlar.doska:
“Last year the farmer switched to drip irrigation.
This year the payment for water fell by half,
and the harvest was the same as before.”
Question: what inference can be drawn from the text?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] The second text: last year the farmer switched his field to drip irrigation. [2] This year he paid half as much for water, [3] and the harvest was the same as before. [4] The question: what inference can be drawn from this text? The inference is not stated openly in the text; we draw it ourselves.

qadamlar.doska:
Evidence 1: the payment fell → less water was used
Evidence 2: the harvest did not fall
Inference: this method saves water without reducing the harvest
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Evidence one: the payment for water fell. Our knowledge of the world tells us that less money means less water was used. [2] Evidence two: the harvest was the same as before, that is, it did not fall. [3] We combine the two pieces of evidence: drip irrigation saves water and does not reduce the harvest.

qadamlar.doska:
Wrong: “The harvest grew” — there is no evidence in the text
Check every inference against the words of the text
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Now let's look at a wrong option: “the harvest grew”. There is no evidence for this in the text; on the contrary, it says the harvest was the same as before. [2] That's why for every inference you must be able to point to exact words in the text as evidence.

qadamlar.doska: According to the text, how did the harvest change?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] According to this text, how did the farmer's harvest change: did it increase, decrease, or stay the same? Answer in one or two words.
qadamlar.javob: stayed the same|did not change|unchanged|the same

qadamlar.sarlavha: How to solve an international question
qadamlar.doska:
1. Read the text once in full: what is the topic?
2. Mark the connecting words
3. Check every option against evidence in the text
4. Beware of narrow (single-detail) options
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] In a PISA question, first read the text once in full and identify its topic. [2] Then mark connecting words such as “because”, “as a result”, and “but”; they show the skeleton of the text. [3] Compare the options with the text one by one: an option with evidence stays, and an option without evidence is out. [4] In a question about the main idea, an option that states only one detail is often a trap.

qadamlar.doska:
The main idea covers the whole text
Inference = evidence in the text + knowledge
Connecting words — the road signs of a text
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Remember: the main idea covers the whole text, not just one detail. [2] An inference may not be written in the text, but it always rests on evidence in the text. [3] Connecting words are road signs that show cause, effect, and contrast. Now you will understand texts more deeply!

q1.doska:
Topic: “what is it about?”
Main idea: “what does it say about it?”
q1.ovoz: More simply: the topic answers the question “what is the text about?”. The main idea answers the question “what does it say about that?”.

q1.doska:
Tell a friend about a movie in one sentence
That one sentence is the main idea
q1.ovoz: If you're asked to tell a friend about the movie you saw yesterday in one sentence, you pick out the most important thing. The main idea of a text is exactly that kind of single sentence.

q1.doska:
Give each paragraph a 2–3-word heading
Combine the headings → main idea
q1.ovoz: Another way: write a two- or three-word heading in the margin next to each paragraph. Then, if you combine these headings into one sentence, you get the main idea.

q2.doska:
Text: “Everyone on the street has opened an umbrella”
Inference: it is raining
q2.ovoz: A simpler example: the text says “everyone on the street has opened an umbrella”. The word “rain” isn't there, but we infer that it is raining.

q2.doska:
Detective: footprint + mud → the guest came from the garden
A claim without evidence is a guess
q2.ovoz: Imagine a detective: he sees a muddy footprint on the floor and says the guest came from the garden. There is evidence, so this is an inference. If he said it without evidence, it would just be a guess.

q2.doska:
Table: “What is in the text?” | “What do I know?”
From both → an inference
q2.ovoz: Draw a two-column table: on the left, write what the text says; on the right, write what you yourself know about it. Combine the two to draw an inference.

q3.doska:
After “because” — a cause
After “as a result” — an effect
q3.ovoz: A simple rule: a cause comes after the word “because”, and an effect comes after “as a result” or “for this reason”.

q3.doska:
I didn't sleep → because I watched a movie
As a result, I was late for class
q3.ovoz: From everyday life: I watched a movie at night because it was interesting. As a result, I overslept in the morning and was late for class. That's how a chain of causes and effects is linked.

q3.doska:
Draw a cause ➝ effect arrow
[river water was taken] ➝ [the sea dried up]
q3.ovoz: Write the sentences in little boxes and draw an arrow from the cause to the effect. In a picture, the connection is much easier to see.

tipik_xatolar: Taking a single detail of the text (for example, the first sentence) as the main idea
Confusing the topic and the main idea: “the Aral Sea” is the topic, not the main idea
Choosing an inference that has no evidence in the text and is based only on one's own knowledge
Swapping the cause and the effect
strategiyalar: Give each paragraph a short heading and combine them into one sentence
Mark the connecting words (because, as a result, but)
Look for evidence in the text for every option — rule out options with no evidence
In a main idea question, beware of an option that states only one detail

sarlavha: Evaluating and reflecting: fact and opinion, source reliability
maqsad: Distinguish fact from opinion, evaluate the reliability of a source, identify the author's purpose, and compare two sources on the same topic to draw a well-supported conclusion

qadamlar.doska:
Is everything you read online true?
PISA 2022: Uzbekistan in reading — 336 points
OECD average — 476, baseline Level 2 — 407 points
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Every day we read hundreds of messages on our phones. But are they all true? Today we will learn how to decide whether or not to trust a text. [2] In the international PISA study in 2022, fifteen-year-old students in Uzbekistan scored an average of three hundred thirty-six points in reading literacy. [3] Compare: the OECD average was four hundred seventy-six points, and the baseline level, Level 2, starts at four hundred seven points. So we have a big but achievable goal ahead of us, and today's lesson is one step along that road!

qadamlar.doska:
Fact — information that can be checked
Opinion — someone's judgment or view
Signs of opinion: I think, the best, wonderful, should
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] A fact is information that can be checked, measured, or proved with a document. [2] An opinion is someone's judgment, view, or feeling; another person might judge it differently. [3] An opinion is often revealed by judgment words such as “I think”, “the best”, “wonderful”, “boring”, and “should”.

qadamlar.doska:
Who wrote it? Is the author an expert?
When was it written? Is the information out of date?
Is there evidence? Are sources cited?
Language: “never”, “100%” — signs of exaggeration
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] The first question when evaluating a source is: who wrote it? Is the author known, and an expert in this field? [2] The second question: when was it written? Information about science and technology in particular goes out of date quickly. [3] The third question: is there evidence? A reliable text shows where its numbers and facts come from. [4] Fourth: look at the language. Extreme words like “never” or “one hundred percent guaranteed” are often a sign of exaggeration.

qadamlar.sarlavha: The author's purpose and two sources
qadamlar.doska:
Purpose: to inform, to persuade, to sell, to entertain
Two sources: where do they agree, where do they differ?
If they differ — which is more reliable, and why?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Every author has a purpose: to inform, to persuade, to sell something, or to entertain. [2] If there are two sources on the same topic, first work out where they agree, then where they differ. [3] If they differ, use the reliability questions to explain which source can be trusted more.

qadamlar.doska:
1) “There are three madrasas on Registan Square.
2) They were built in the 15th–17th centuries.
3) It is the most beautiful square in the world.”
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Let's read three sentences. The first: there are three madrasas on Registan Square. [2] The second: they were built in the fifteenth to seventeenth centuries. [3] The third: it is the most beautiful square in the world. Which sentence is an opinion?

qadamlar.doska:
Sentence 1: you can go and count to check → fact
Sentence 2: checked with historical documents → fact
Sentence 3: “the most beautiful” — a judgment → opinion
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] The first sentence is easy to check: you can go and count. So it is a fact. [2] The second sentence is confirmed by historical documents and scholars' research, so it is also a fact. [3] “The most beautiful” in the third sentence is a judgment. Another square might seem more beautiful to someone else. So it is an opinion.

qadamlar.doska: “The book came out in 2020, and it is very boring.”
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Now you try: “This book came out in two thousand twenty, and it is very boring.” Which word in the sentence expresses an opinion?
qadamlar.savol: Write the word that expresses an opinion

qadamlar.doska:
A: a social media post, author unknown
“Drink 5 liters of water a day — you'll never get sick!”
B: an article by a doctor, with sources cited
“How much water you need depends on age, weight, and activity.”
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Two sources on the same topic. Source A is a social media post; its author is unknown. [2] It says: drink five liters of water a day, and you'll never get sick! [3] Source B is an article written by a doctor, with a list of scientific sources at the end. [4] It says that how much water a person needs depends on their age, weight, and activity level.

qadamlar.doska:
A: no author, no evidence, “never” — exaggeration
B: an expert, references given, careful language
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Let's evaluate source A: the author is unknown, there is no evidence, and “you'll never get sick” is an extreme promise, an exaggeration. [2] In source B, the author is an expert, sources are given, and the language is calm and careful.

qadamlar.doska:
Agree: both say drinking water is important
Differ: A — the same for everyone, B — different for each person
Conclusion: B is more reliable — an expert and evidence
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Now let's compare. Where they agree: both sources say that drinking water is important. [2] Where they differ: A prescribes the same amount for everyone, while B says that needs differ from person to person. [3] Conclusion: source B is more reliable, because its author is an expert, it has evidence, and it does not exaggerate.

qadamlar.doska: “Super-vitamin — the very best! Order now!”
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Read this text: “Super-vitamin — the very best! Order now!” What is the author's purpose: to inform, to sell, or to entertain?
qadamlar.savol: to inform / to sell / to entertain

qadamlar.sarlavha: How to solve an international question
qadamlar.doska:
1. Ask about each sentence: can it be checked?
2. Source: who? when? any evidence? purpose?
3. Two sources: agreement → difference → whom we trust
4. Support your answer with “because ...”
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] To tell fact from opinion in a PISA question, ask about each sentence: can this be checked? [2] If you are asked about a source, ask four questions in a row: who wrote it, when, is there evidence, and what is its purpose. [3] If there are two sources, first find where they agree, then where they differ, and decide whom to trust. [4] In an open-response question, just writing “B” is not enough; always say “because” and give a reason from the text.

qadamlar.doska:
Fact — can be checked, opinion — is a judgment
Reliable source: author, date, evidence, calm language
Two sources → agreement, difference, a supported choice
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Remember: a fact can be checked, while an opinion is someone's judgment. [2] The signs of a reliable source: the author is known, there is a date, evidence is given, and the language is calm. [3] Compare two sources and make a well-supported choice. Now you can evaluate what you read critically!

q1.doska:
“It's +30 °C today” — fact (thermometer)
“It's very hot today” — opinion
q1.ovoz: More simply: “it's thirty degrees today” can be checked with a thermometer, so it is a fact. “It's very hot today”: it's hot for some people and not for others, so it is an opinion.

q1.doska:
Two friends saw the same movie: one says “great”, the other “boring”
The movie lasted 2 hours — fact
q1.ovoz: Two friends saw the same movie. One said “great”, the other “boring”. Both expressed opinions. But the fact that the movie lasted two hours is something neither of them can deny.

q1.doska:
Test: “Can you argue against it?”
Yes → opinion; can only be checked → fact
q1.ovoz: Another test: can you argue against the sentence? If people would just argue according to their tastes, it's an opinion. If it can only be settled by measuring or checking, it's a fact.

q2.doska:
Reliable: author + date + evidence
Doubtful: unknown + “100%” + no evidence
q2.ovoz: More simply: a reliable source has an author, a date, and evidence. A doubtful source has an unknown author, promises like “one hundred percent”, and no evidence.

q2.doska:
You have a toothache: whom do you trust?
A dentist or a neighbor you don't know
q2.ovoz: If you had a toothache, whose advice would you trust: a dentist's or a neighbor's you don't know? The expert's, of course. It's the same with texts.

q2.doska:
Points: author +1, date +1, evidence +1, calm language +1
4 points — reliable, 0–1 — doubtful
q2.ovoz: Give each source points: author known, one point; has a date, one point; has evidence, one point; calm language, one point. Four points means reliable; zero or one point means doubtful.

q3.doska:
Ask about the purpose: “What does the author want from me?”
Learn / believe / buy / laugh
q3.ovoz: More simply: ask yourself, what does the author want from me? For me to learn, to believe, to buy, or to laugh?

q3.doska:
Two witnesses: one says “a red car”, the other “a dark red car”
Agreement: the car is red; difference — the shade
q3.ovoz: Two witnesses described an incident: one said “a red car”, the other said “a dark red car”. They agree that the car was red; they differ in a small detail. We compare two sources the same way.

q3.doska:
Venn diagram: A | shared | B
In the middle — what both sources say
q3.ovoz: Draw two overlapping circles. On the left, write what only A says; on the right, what only B says; and in the middle, what both of them say.

tipik_xatolar: Automatically treating a sentence with a number or date as a fact (a number can be part of an opinion too)
Accepting an opinion one agrees with as a fact
Judging a source by its attractive design or many “likes” instead of its content
Looking only at the differences when comparing two sources and ignoring where they agree
Writing a choice without justifying it in an open-response question
strategiyalar: Ask about every sentence: “Can this be checked?”
Evaluate a source with four questions: who, when, evidence, purpose
Mark the judgment words (most, wonderful, boring, should)
Compare two sources in the order: agreement → difference → supported choice

maqsad: Explain and predict everyday phenomena with scientific knowledge and models (the particle model, thermal conductivity, ecological relationships) using a claim–evidence–reasoning structure

qadamlar.doska:
Why? — the most important question in science
PISA 2022: science — 355 points
PISA 2025: 438 points (+83), 48th place out of 91 countries
OECD average — 482 points
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Why does iron feel colder in winter? Why do the fish in a lake suddenly die? Today we will learn to explain phenomena like these scientifically. [2] In the international PISA study in 2022, students in Uzbekistan scored three hundred fifty-five points in scientific literacy. [3] In PISA 2025, the result rose to four hundred thirty-eight points: an increase of eighty-three points, and forty-eighth place out of ninety-one countries! [4] The OECD average is four hundred eighty-two points. As you can see, the gap is closing, and today's lesson will help close it even further.

qadamlar.doska:
Phenomenon → scientific knowledge (law, model) → cause
Claim: what happens
Evidence: what we observed or measured
Reasoning: “because” with which law or model
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] A scientific explanation shows the cause of a phenomenon using scientific knowledge, that is, a law or a model. [2] A good explanation has three parts. The first is the claim: we say what is happening. [3] The second is the evidence: how we know this from observation or measurement. [4] The third is the reasoning: we say “because” and name the law or model that explains it.

qadamlar.doska:
Matter is made of particles that are always moving
When heated: the particles move faster
The distance between particles increases → expansion
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] In science, many phenomena are explained by the particle model: all matter is made of very tiny particles, and they are always moving. [2] If we heat a substance, its particles start to move faster. [3] As a result, the average distance between them increases and the object expands. The particles themselves do not get bigger — this is important!

qadamlar.doska:
“If ..., then ..., because ...”
If we hold a jar's metal lid under hot water,
the lid expands and opens easily
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Scientific knowledge not only explains things but also lets us make predictions. Remember the pattern: if this happens, then that will happen, because... [2] For example, if we hold the metal lid of a tightly closed glass jar under hot water, [3] the metal lid expands more than the glass, and the jar opens easily, because metals expand noticeably when heated.

qadamlar.doska:
In winter, an iron post and a wooden post stand outside
When we touch the iron, it feels colder. Why?
Observation: both are at the same temperature
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] In winter, an iron post and a wooden post stand side by side in a yard. [2] If we touch both, the iron feels much colder. Why is that? [3] First, an important fact: both posts have been standing in the same place for a long time and are at the temperature of the air, so their temperature is the same!

qadamlar.doska:
Iron is a good conductor of heat
Heat flows quickly from the hand into the iron
The skin cools quickly → it feels “colder”
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] The difference is in the materials: iron conducts heat well, while wood conducts it poorly. [2] Heat passes quickly from our warm hand into the iron, and the iron spreads it inward. [3] Our skin cools quickly, and we feel this as “the iron is colder”. In fact, we sense not the temperature but how fast heat leaves our skin.

qadamlar.doska: A metal spoon in hot tea heats up quickly: metal is a good heat
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Now continue yourself: the handle of a metal spoon in hot tea heats up quickly, because metal is a good heat... what? Write one word.

qadamlar.sarlavha: Example 2: the fish in the lake
qadamlar.doska:
Water with fertilizer flowed into a lake from a field
A few weeks later: algae grew enormously
Then the algae died, and after that the fish
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Now a more complex, PISA-style phenomenon. Water containing fertilizer flowed into a lake from a nearby field. [2] Within a few weeks, the algae in the lake grew enormously. [3] Later the algae died, and after them the fish began to die too. Let's explain this chain.

qadamlar.doska:
1) Nitrogen and phosphorus in fertilizer — food for algae
2) Bacteria break down the dead algae
3) The bacteria use up the oxygen in the water
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] The first link: the nitrogen and phosphorus compounds in fertilizer are nutrients for algae, so the algae multiply quickly. [2] The second link: after the algae die, bacteria break down their remains. [3] The third link: while breaking them down, the bacteria respire and use up a lot of the oxygen dissolved in the water.

qadamlar.doska:
4) Oxygen decreases → the fish can't breathe
Wrong: “the fertilizer poisoned the fish” — the chain is incomplete
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] The fourth link: the oxygen in the water decreases, and the fish can't get enough oxygen through their gills, so they die. [2] A common wrong answer: the fertilizer poisoned the fish. The main cause here is different — a lack of oxygen — and it has to be explained with the whole chain.

qadamlar.doska: Which gas in the water do the bacteria use up?
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Which gas in the water do the bacteria breaking down the algae remains use up, causing the fish to die?
qadamlar.savol: Write the name of the gas

qadamlar.sarlavha: How to solve an international question
qadamlar.doska:
1. Retell the phenomenon in your own words
2. Which knowledge is needed: particles, heat, ecology?
3. Write the chain of causes link by link
4. Answer: claim + evidence + “because” reasoning
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] In a PISA question, first briefly retell the phenomenon in your own words: what happened? [2] Then ask yourself: which scientific knowledge explains this — the particle model, heat transfer, or ecological relationships? [3] For a complex phenomenon, write the chain of causes link by link, without skipping any link. [4] Write your answer as a claim, evidence, and reasoning beginning with “because”; an answer like this earns full credit.

qadamlar.doska:
Explanation = claim + evidence + reasoning
Particle model: heated — faster, farther apart
Complex phenomenon — a chain of causes
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] Remember: a scientific explanation consists of a claim, evidence, and reasoning. [2] The particle model: when heated, particles move faster and move farther apart. [3] Explain a complex phenomenon with a chain of causes. Now you can answer the question “why?” like a scientist!

q1.doska:
What happened? → How do we know? → Why?
Claim → evidence → reasoning
q1.ovoz: More simply: answer three questions. What happened? That's the claim. How do we know? That's the evidence. Why? That's the reasoning.

q1.doska:
Doctor: “You have a cold” (claim)
Temperature 38 °C (evidence), a virus (reasoning)
q1.ovoz: Think of a doctor: “you have a cold” is the claim. “Your temperature is thirty-eight degrees” is the evidence. “A virus causes this” is the reasoning.

q1.doska:
A three-story house: evidence at the bottom, reasoning in the middle
On top — the claim
q1.ovoz: Imagine an explanation as a three-story house: the foundation is the evidence, the middle floor is the reasoning, and the roof is the claim. A roof can't stand without a foundation.

q2.doska:
Hot → particles fast → gaps big → expands
Cold → slow → gaps small → contracts
q2.ovoz: More simply: when it's hot, particles move fast and spread apart, and the object expands. When it's cold, they slow down and move closer, and the object contracts.

q2.doska:
A class at recess: if children run — more space is needed
If they sit quietly in class — less space
q2.ovoz: Think of recess: when students run around playing, they need a lot of space. When they sit quietly in class, a little space is enough. Particles “run around” like that when heated.

q2.doska:
Power lines: sag in summer, taut in winter
The cause — thermal expansion
q2.ovoz: Look at the power lines along the street: in summer they sag lower, and in winter they become taut. This is a ready-made demonstration of expansion with heat and contraction with cold.

q3.doska:
Prediction = knowledge + “if ..., then ...”
It must be possible to test it
q3.ovoz: More simply: a prediction uses our knowledge to say what will happen in the future. It takes the form “if..., then...”, and it can be tested.

q3.doska:
You put a full glass bottle of water in the freezer
Prediction: it may crack when it freezes
q3.ovoz: What happens if you put a closed glass bottle full of water in the freezer? We know that water increases in volume when it freezes. So the prediction is: the bottle may crack.

q3.doska:
Knowledge: metal expands when heated
Situation → prediction → testing
q3.ovoz: Draw three steps: first write the knowledge, then the new situation, then the prediction. Finally, think about how the prediction could be tested in an experiment.

tipik_xatolar: Thinking iron is “colder in temperature” than wood — in fact the temperature is the same; the thermal conductivity is different
Thinking the particles themselves get bigger when heated
Skipping the middle links of a chain of causes and writing only the beginning and the end
Replacing a scientific concept with everyday words (“the cold passes into you”)
Stating only a claim in the answer without giving reasoning (“because ...”)
strategiyalar: Briefly retell the phenomenon in your own words
Identify which scientific model or law is needed
Write a complex phenomenon as a chain of causes, link by link
Build your answer as claim + evidence + reasoning

maqsad: Write a scientific question and a hypothesis, identify independent, dependent, and controlled variables, plan a fair test, and spot an unfair test

qadamlar.doska:
Which fertilizer is better? — we find out by experiment
PISA 2022: science — 355 points
PISA 2025: 438 points (+83), 48th place out of 91 countries
OECD average — 482 points
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] A scientist doesn't say “I think”; a scientist does an experiment. Today we will learn how to plan a proper experiment, that is, a fair test. [2] In the international PISA study in 2022, students in Uzbekistan scored three hundred fifty-five points in scientific literacy. [3] In PISA 2025, the result rose to four hundred thirty-eight points: an increase of eighty-three points, and forty-eighth place out of ninety-one countries! [4] The OECD average is four hundred eighty-two points. As you can see, the gap is closing, and today's lesson will help close it even further.

qadamlar.doska:
A scientific question is answered by measurement or experiment
Yes: “Does salt change the boiling point of water?”
No: “Which flower is the most beautiful?”
Hypothesis: “If ..., then ..., because ...”
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] A scientific question is a question that can be answered through measurement, observation, or experiment. [2] For example, “does salt change the boiling point of water?” can be checked with a thermometer, so it is a scientific question. [3] “Which flower is the most beautiful?” is a matter of taste; it can't be measured. [4] A hypothesis is a testable prediction. It is often written in the form “if..., then..., because...”.

qadamlar.doska:
Independent — what we deliberately change (the cause)
Dependent — what we measure (the result)
Controlled — what is kept the same
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] An experiment has three kinds of variables. The independent variable is the quantity we deliberately change, that is, the suspected cause. [2] The dependent variable is the result we measure; it may depend on the independent variable. [3] The controlled variables are quantities kept the same in every trial, because they could affect the result.

qadamlar.doska:
Only ONE variable is deliberately changed
All other conditions stay the same
Control group — for comparison
Repetition and averaging → reliable results
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] The main rule of a fair test: only one variable, the independent variable, is changed. [2] All other conditions are kept the same; otherwise we can't tell what caused the result to change. [3] A control group is a sample that receives no treatment; by comparing with it, we can see the effect. [4] If we repeat the experiment several times and take the average, random errors are reduced and the result is more reliable.

qadamlar.doska:
Question: does the amount of fertilizer affect the growth of beans?
Pots: 0 g, 5 g, 10 g of fertilizer; height after 2 weeks
qadamlar.ovoz: [1] A student wants to carry out an investigation: does the amount of fertilizer affect the growth of beans? [2] She put zero, five, and ten grams of fertilizer into three pots and measured the height of the plants after two weeks. Let's identify the variables.

qadamlar.doska:
Independent: amount of fertilizer (0, 5, 10 g)
Dependent: height after 2 weeks (cm)
Controlled: water, light, soil, temperature, pot
